The Changing Goals of Orthodontic Treatment
I The Development of Orthodontics
The Development of Orthodontics
Fig 1.2
The Development of Orthodontics
Edward H. Angle "father of modern orthodontics" contributed to the development of orthodontics as a specialty
The Development of Orthodontics

Angle's classification of malocclusion in the 1890s was an important step in the development of orthodontics because it not only subdivided major types of malocclusion but also included the first clear and simple definition of normal occlusion in the natural dentition "the mesiobuccal cusp of the upper molar occludes in the buccal groove of the lower molar the teeth are arranged on a smoothly curving line of occlusion".
The Development of Orthodontics

Angle classification has four classes: Normal occlusion and Class I malocclusion share the same molar relationship but differ in the arrangement of the teeth relative to the line of occlusion Fig 1.2 . The line of occlusion may or may not be correct in Class II and Class III malocclusion.
The Development of Orthodontics
Angle and his followers strongly opposed extraction for orthodontic purposes. Less attention came to be paid to facial proportions and esthetics.
The Development of Orthodontics
Charles Tweed and Raymond Begg reintroduced extraction of teeth into orthodontics to enhance facial esthetics and achieve better stability of the occlusal relationships.

New history (7th) The 7th edition expands the early history: Calvin Case advocated carefully considering protrusion and extraction to achieve the best result, and Dr. Paul Simon believed the dentition is invariably related to the skull (his canine-relationship theory was later examined by Broadbent using skulls and a craniostat).
II Modern Treatment Goals: The Soft Tissue Paradigm
Modern Treatment Goals: The Soft Tissue Paradigm
Table 1.1 Angle paradigm vs soft-tissue paradigm — goals, diagnostic emphasis, and stability.
Modern Treatment Goals: The Soft Tissue Paradigm

The soft tissue paradigm states that both the goals and limitations of modern orthodontic and orthognathic treatment are determined by the soft tissues of the face, not by the teeth and bones Table 1.1 .
Modern Treatment Goals: The Soft Tissue Paradigm
The primary goal of treatment becomes soft tissue relationships and adaptations , not Angle's ideal occlusion.
Modern Treatment Goals: The Soft Tissue Paradigm
The secondary goal of treatment becomes functional occlusion .
Modern Treatment Goals: The Soft Tissue Paradigm

The thought process is to establish what these soft tissue relationships should be and then determine how the teeth and jaws would have to be arranged to meet the soft tissue goals. This relates very much to why patients and parents seek orthodontic treatment.

Class I malocclusion (50% to 55%) is by far the largest single group; there are about half as many Class II malocclusions (approximately 15% ) as normal occlusion. Class III (less than 1%) represents a very small proportion of the total.

The Usual Orthodontic Problems: Epidemiology of Malocclusion

The characteristics of malocclusion evaluated in NHANES III (Third National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey) included the irregularity index , which is a measure of incisor alignment Fig 1.4 .

Updated prevalences (7th) The 7th edition revises the NHANES distribution: 30+% at most have normal occlusion, Class II ≈ 15–20+% , and Class III less than ~5% (your summary, from the 6th, gives Class I 50–55%, Class II ~15%, and Class III <1%); the remainder are variations of anteroposterior discrepancies. It also reports open bite >3 mm (was >2 mm) as more prevalent in Blacks, and posterior crossbite at ~7–9% by age group.
Who Needs Treatment?
I Psychological Problems
Psychological Problems
A number of studies in recent years have confirmed that severe malocclusion is likely to be a social handicap .
Psychological Problems

In short, it seems clear that the major reason people seek orthodontic treatment is to minimize psychosocial problems related to their dental and facial appearance. These problems are not "just cosmetic." They can have a major effect on the quality of life.
II Oral Function
Oral Function

Although severe malocclusion surely affects oral function, oral function adapts to form surprisingly well (like mastication, speech and lip-tongue posture). It appears that malocclusion usually affects function not by making it impossible but by making it difficult, so that extra effort is required to compensate for the anatomic deformity.
Oral Function

The great majority of patients, there is no association between malocclusion and TMD . Therefore orthodontics as the primary treatment for TMD almost never is indicated , but in special circumstances (see Chapter 18 ) it can be a useful adjunct to other treatment for the muscle pain.

There is about one chance in three that a child with an untreated Class II malocclusion will experience trauma to the upper incisors

In summary, it appears that both psychosocial and functional handicaps can produce significant need for orthodontic treatment. The evidence is less clear that orthodontic treatment reduces the development of later dental disease.

Type of Treatment: Evidence-Based Selection
Fig 1.19 illustrates, a hierarchy of quality exists in the evidence available to guide clinical decisions.
Type of Treatment: Evidence-Based Selection
The unsupported opinion of an expert is the weakest form of clinical evidence.
Type of Treatment: Evidence-Based Selection
The gold standard for evaluating clinical procedures is the randomized clinical trial , in which patients are randomly assigned in advance to alternative treatment procedures.

Expanded (7th) The 7th elevates the Clinical Practice Guideline (and meta-analyses / systematic reviews) as the highest tier of evidence above the individual RCT, and calls for moving to a core outcomes set that includes patient satisfaction .

There now are two major methods for scoring the severity of malocclusion: the peer assessment rating (PAR) system, developed in the United Kingdom, and the American Board of Orthodontics (ABO) discrepancy index , developed in the United States (Both systems were developed as a way to objectively determine the amount of improvement achieved during treatment but have been shown to correlate reasonably well with expert opinions of orthodontic treatment need)

Growth versus Development
Growth versus Development
Growth and development, although closely related, are not synonymous.
Growth versus Development
Growth usually refers to an increase in size or number. Development is used almost always to refer to an increase in complexity
Growth versus Development
Growth is largely an anatomic phenomenon, whereas development is physiologic and behavioral.
Growth: Pattern, Variability, and Timing
· Pattern
· Pattern
Fig 2.1 Change in body proportions during growth — the cephalocaudal gradient (head 50%→ ~12%).
· Pattern
Fig 2.2 Scammon's curves — neural, general, lymphoid and genital tissue systems grow at different rates.
· Pattern
The concept of pattern reflects proportionality
· Pattern

As Fig 2.1 illustrates, there is more growth of the lower limbs than the upper limbs during postnatal life. All of these changes, which are a part of the normal growth pattern, reflect the "cephalocaudal gradient of growth" is simply means that there is an axis of increased growth extending from the head toward the feet. Even within the head and face, the cephalocaudal growth gradient strongly affects proportions and leads to changes in proportion with growth (mandible tends to grow more and later than the maxilla)
· Pattern

In fetal life, at about the third month of intrauterine development, the head takes up almost 50% of the total body length. By the time of birth, the proportion of the entire body devoted to the head has decreased to 30%
· Pattern
Another aspect of the normal growth pattern is that not all the tissue systems of the body grow at the same rate Fig 2.2
· Pattern
An important aspect of pattern is its predictability .
· Variability
· Variability
Fig 2.4 A child's growth plotted on a standard chart (girl); follow over time vs the population.
· Variability
All people are not alike in the way that they grow.
· Variability

It can be difficult but clinically very important to decide whether an individual is merely at the extreme of the normal variation or falls outside the normal range. One way to do this is to evaluate a given child relative to peers on a standard growth chart Fig 2.4 .
· Variability

These charts can be used in two ways to determine whether growth is normal or abnormal. First, the location of an individual relative to the group can be established. A general guideline is that a child who falls outside the range of 97% of the population should receive special study. Second and perhaps more important, growth charts can be used to follow a child over time to evaluate whether there is an unexpected change in growth pattern.
· Timing
· Timing
Fig 2.7 Velocity curves for girls with different times of menarche — developmental vs chronologic age.
· Timing
From normal variation
· Timing
From influences outside normal experience (e.g., serious illness)
· Timing
From timing effects.
· Timing
Variability in growth arises in several ways:
· Timing
Variation in timing arises because the same event happens for different individuals at different times, the biologic clocks of different individuals are set differently.
· Timing
Some children grow rapidly and mature early, others grow and develop slowly and so appear to be behind, even though, they will catch up.
· Timing
Timing variability can be reduced by using developmental age rather than chronologic age as an expression of growth status. Fig 2.7
Method of Studying Physical Growth
Method of Studying Physical Growth

There are two basic approaches to studying physical growth. The first is based on techniques for measuring living animals (including humans), with the implication that the measurement itself does no harm. The second approach uses experiments in which growth is manipulated in some way.
I Measurement Approaches
Measurement Approaches
Acquiring Measurement Data
Measurement Approaches

Craniometry: based on measurements of skulls found among human skeletal remains. It has the important disadvantage for growth studies that, by necessity, all these growth data must be cross-sectional.
Measurement Approaches
Anthropometry: measure skeletal dimensions on living individuals, using soft tissue points.
Measurement Approaches

Cephalometric Radiology: It has considerable importance not only in the study of growth but also in clinical evaluation of orthodontic patients and combine the advantages of craniometry and anthropometry. Growth studies are done by superimposing a tracing or digital model of a later cephalogram on an earlier one.
Measurement Approaches

Three-Dimensional Imaging: Using (CBCT). But superimposition of 3-D images is much more difficult than the superimpositions used with 2-D cephalometric radiographs. (MRI) also provides 3-D images that can be useful in studies of growth. Three-dimensional photography now makes possible much more accurate measurements of facial soft tissue.
New in 7th The 7th adds that CBCT also reduces flaws within 2D imaging such as head position, superimposition of anatomical structures, and magnification errors.
New in 7th The 7th adds that CBCT also reduces flaws within 2D imaging such as head position, superimposition of anatomical structures, and magnification errors.

It would be much easier and quicker to do a cross-sectional study, gathering data once for any individual and including subjects of different ages, rather than spending many years on a study in which the same individuals are measured repeatedly. however, variability within the sample can conceal details of the growth pattern, particularly when there is no correction for timing variation Fig 2.12 .
II Experimental Approaches
Experimental Approaches
Vital Staining
Experimental Approaches
Fig 2.16 Tetracycline vital staining marks active mineralizing (growth) sites.
Experimental Approaches
Dyes that stain mineralizing tissues are injected into an animal.
Experimental Approaches

Alizarin is a dye, which still is used for vital staining studies, reacts strongly with calcium at sites where bone calcification. Tetracycline is an excellent vital stain that binds to calcium at growth sites in the same way as alizarin. Fig 2.16
Experimental Approaches

The gamma-emitting isotope technetium 99m (99mTc) can be used to detect areas of rapid bone growth in humans, but these images are more useful in diagnosis of localized growth problems such as condylar hyperplasia
Experimental Approaches
Implant Radiology
Experimental Approaches

Inert metal pins are placed in bones anywhere in the skeleton, including the face and jaws and become permanently incorporated into the bone without causing any problems and are easily visualized on a cephalogram. (This method was developed by Professor Arne Björk and coworkers)
III Genetic Influences on Growth
Genetic Influences on Growth

It now has been shown that homeobox Msx and Dix genes , which are known to be critically important in the establishment of body plan, pattern formation, and morphogenesis, are expressed differentially not only in development of the teeth but also in growth of the mandible. Msx-1 predominates in tooth formation and is expressed in basal bone but not in the alveolar process, whereas Msx-2 is strongly expressed there. Dix-1 and Dix-2 are expressed in the dental mesenchyme and in the epithelium of the maxillary and mandibular arch mesenchyme, and other homeobox gene groups have been shown to play a role in dental and facial development.

Updated (7th) The 7th edition restates the Msx expression pattern: Msx-1 is expressed in mesenchyme during tooth development, whereas Msx-2 is expressed in both the epithelial and mesenchymal components of the developing tooth germ (your summary, from the 6th, places Msx-1 in basal bone but not the alveolar process, with Msx-2 strongly expressed there).
The Nature of Skeletal Growth
The Nature of Skeletal Growth
Fig 2.22 Meckel's cartilage and initial mandibular bone formation; the condyle is a secondary cartilage.
The Nature of Skeletal Growth
Hypertrophy , increase in the size of individual cells.
The Nature of Skeletal Growth
Hyperplasia , increase in the number of the cells, a prominent feature of all forms of growth.
The Nature of Skeletal Growth

Secretion of extracellular material , contributing to an increase in size independent of the number or size of the cells themselves. "particularly important in the growth of the skeletal system, where extracellular material later mineralizes"
The Nature of Skeletal Growth
At the cellular level, there are only three possibilities for growth:
The Nature of Skeletal Growth
Growth occurs at all points within the tissue.
The Nature of Skeletal Growth
Hyperplasia primarily and hypertrophy secondarily are its characteristics, secretion of extracellular material can also accompany interstitial growth.
The Nature of Skeletal Growth
Characteristic of all soft tissues and of uncalcified cartilage within the skeletal system.
The Nature of Skeletal Growth

Interstitial growth is a prominent aspect of overall skeletal growth because a major portion of the skeletal system is originally modeled in cartilage. This includes the basal part of the skull, trunk and limbs.
The Nature of Skeletal Growth
Interstitial growth
The Nature of Skeletal Growth
When mineralization takes place so that hard tissue is formed, interstitial growth becomes impossible.
The Nature of Skeletal Growth
Hyperplasia, hypertrophy, and secretion of extracellular material can occur only on the surface, not within the mineralized mass through the activity of cells in the periosteum
The Nature of Skeletal Growth
Direct or Surface Apposition
The Nature of Skeletal Growth
Types of growth:
The Nature of Skeletal Growth
Endochondral ossification , cartilage is transformed into bone. (mandibular condyle)
The Nature of Skeletal Growth
Intramembranous (Mesenchymal) ossification (cranial vault and both jaws.)
The Nature of Skeletal Growth
There are two types of ossification:
The Nature of Skeletal Growth

In the long bones of the extremities, areas of ossification appear in the center of the bones and at the ends, ultimately producing a central shaft called the diaphysis and a bony cap on each end called the epiphysis . Between the epiphysis and diaphysis is a remaining area of uncalcified cartilage called the epiphyseal plate .
The Nature of Skeletal Growth
The mandible of higher animals develops in the same area as the cartilage of the first pharyngeal arch— Meckel's cartilage . Fig 2.22
The Nature of Skeletal Growth

The condylar cartilage develops initially as an independent secondary cartilage, which is separated by a considerable gap from the body of the mandible Fig 2.23 . Early in fetal life, it fuses with the developing mandibular ramus.
The Nature of Skeletal Growth
The maxilla forms initially from a center of mesenchymal condensation in the maxillary process, and endochondral ossification does not contribute directly to formation of the maxillary bone.
The Nature of Skeletal Growth

The balance of apposition and resorption, with new bone being formed in some areas while old bone is removed in others, is an essential component of the growth process. It has two components: modeling and remodeling .
The Nature of Skeletal Growth

Modeling (addition of new bone) adapts structure to function by changing bone size and shape to maintain bone strength as loading of the bone changes. Remodeling occurs via osteocyte apposition and osteoclast resorption in the same area.
Sites and Types of Growth in the Craniofacial Complex
I Cranial Vault
Cranial Vault
Made up of a number of flat bones that are formed directly by intramembranous bone formation
Cranial Vault

The growth process is entirely the result of periosteal activity at the surfaces of the bones. Modeling (addition of new bone) and growth occur primarily at the periosteum-lined contact areas between adjacent skull bones, the cranial sutures .
Cranial Vault
Apposition of new bone at these sutures is the major mechanism for growth of the cranial vault.
Cranial Vault
Periosteal activity also produces both modeling and remodeling changes of the inner and outer surfaces, allows for changes in contour during growth.
II Cranial Base
Cranial Base
Fig 2.25 Synchondroses of the cranial base (basioccipital, sphenoid, ethmoid).
Cranial Base
Fig 2.26 Growth at the spheno-occipital synchondrosis — like a two-sided epiphyseal plate.
Cranial Base
In contrast to the cranial vault, the bones of the cranial base are formed initially in cartilage and these cartilages models are later transformed into bone by endochondral ossification
Cranial Base

As ossification proceeds, bands of cartilage called synchondroses remain between the centers of ossification (basioccipital, sphenoid, and ethmoid bones) Fig 2.25 . Histologically, a synchondrosis looks like a two-sided epiphyseal plate Fig 2.26 .
III Maxilla (Nasomaxillary Complex)
Maxilla (Nasomaxillary Complex)
Fig 2.27 Sutural apposition translates the maxilla downward and forward.
Maxilla (Nasomaxillary Complex)
Fig 2.28 The anterior maxillary surface is resorptive, cancelling some forward growth.
Maxilla (Nasomaxillary Complex)
Fig 2.30 Modeling of the palatal vault (also the nasal floor) — additive downward-forward movement.
Maxilla (Nasomaxillary Complex)
Develops postnatally entirely by intramembranous ossification .
Maxilla (Nasomaxillary Complex)
The growth pattern is "out from under the cranium" which means that as it grows, the maxilla must move a considerable distance downward and forward relative to the cranium and cranial base.
Maxilla (Nasomaxillary Complex)
(1) by apposition of bone at the sutures that connect the maxilla to the cranium and cranial base Fig 2.27
Maxilla (Nasomaxillary Complex)
(2) by surface modeling and remodeling . In contrast to the cranial vault, however, surface changes in the maxilla are quite dramatic and as important as changes at the sutures.
Maxilla (Nasomaxillary Complex)
Because there is no cartilage replacement, growth occurs in two ways:
Maxilla (Nasomaxillary Complex)

Up until about age 6, displacement from cranial base growth is an important part of the maxilla's forward growth. Failure of the cranial base to lengthen normally, as in achondroplasia Fig 5.27 and several congenital syndromes, creates a characteristic midface deficiency .
Maxilla (Nasomaxillary Complex)
At about age 7, cranial base growth stops, and then sutural growth is the only mechanism for bringing the maxilla forward.
Maxilla (Nasomaxillary Complex)

Part of the posterior border of the maxilla is a free surface in the tuberosity region . Bone is added at this surface, creating additional space into which the primary and then the permanent molar teeth successively erupt.
Maxilla (Nasomaxillary Complex)

The effect is additive , on the roof of the mouth. At the same time, bone is removed on the nasal side and added on the oral side, thus creating an additional downward and forward movement of the palate. Fig 2.30
Maxilla (Nasomaxillary Complex)
The anterior part of the alveolar process is a resorptive area , tends to cancel some of the forward growth. Fig 2.28

IV Mandible
Mandible
Fig 2.31 Mandibular growth viewed from a stable structure — chin almost inactive; growth at ramus/condyle.
Mandible
Fig 2.32 As the mandible lengthens, the ramus relocates posteriorly to make room for the molars.
Mandible
Both endochondral and periosteal activity are important.
Mandible
Displacement created by cranial base growth that moves the temporomandibular joint plays a negligible role (with rare exceptions).
Mandible
In contrast to the maxilla:
Mandible

The principal sites of growth of the mandible are the posterior surface of the ramus and the condylar and coronoid processes . There is little change along the anterior part of the mandible (the chin is almost inactive) Fig 2.31
Mandible
Growth is translated downward and forward.
Mandible

The body of the mandible grows longer ↔ by periosteal apposition of bone only on its posterior surface, while the ramus grows higher ↕ by endochondral replacement at the condyle accompanied by surface modeling.
Mandible

In infancy the ramus is located at about the spot where the primary first molar will erupt. Progressive posterior modeling and remodeling create space for the second primary molar and then for the sequential eruption of the permanent molar teeth. Fig 2.32
V Facial Soft Tissue
Facial Soft Tissue
Lip height is relatively short during the mixed dentition years, lip incompetence is maximal during childhood and decreases during adolescence.
Facial Soft Tissue
Lip thickness reaches its maximum during adolescence, then decreases
Facial Soft Tissue
Growth of the Lips
Facial Soft Tissue
Growth of the nasal bone is complete at about age 10 .
Facial Soft Tissue
Growth thereafter is only of the nasal cartilage and soft tissues, both of which undergo a considerable adolescent spurt.
Facial Soft Tissue
Growth of the Nose
Facial Soft Tissue

The nose and chin both become more prominent with adolescent and post-adolescent growth, while the lips do not, so the relative prominence of the lips decreases, this can become an important point in determining how much lip support should be provided by the teeth at the time orthodontic treatment typically ends in late adolescence.
Theories of Growth Control
Theories of Growth Control

Three major theories in recent years have attempted to explain the determinants of craniofacial growth: (1) bone is the primary determinant of its own growth; (2) cartilage is the primary determinant of skeletal growth, while bone responds secondarily and passively; and (3) the soft tissue matrix in which the skeletal elements are embedded is the primary determinant of growth, and both bone and cartilage are secondary followers.
Theories of Growth Control
The major difference in the theories is the location at which genetic control is expressed . (Indirect genetic control is called epigenetic )
Theories of Growth Control
In contemporary thought, the truth is to be found in some synthesis of the second and third theories ; the first, although it was the dominant view until the 1960s, has largely been discarded.
I Level of Growth Control (Sites Vs Centers of Growth)
Level of Growth Control (Sites Vs Centers of Growth)

Distinguishing between a site of growth and a center of growth clarifies the differences between the theories of growth control. A site of growth is merely a location at which growth occurs, whereas a center is a location at which independent (genetically controlled) growth occurs. All centers of growth also are sites, but the reverse is not true.
Level of Growth Control (Sites Vs Centers of Growth)
Sutures, and the periosteal tissues, are not primary determinants of craniofacial growth.
II Cartilage as a Determinant of Craniofacial Growth
Cartilage as a Determinant of Craniofacial Growth
Fig 2.36 The discarded 'cartilage push' view — condyle as an epiphyseal-plate-like growth center.
Cartilage as a Determinant of Craniofacial Growth
Fig 2.37 Cartilage theory of the maxilla — the nasal septum as a possible pacemaker.
Cartilage as a Determinant of Craniofacial Growth
Fig 2.38 Midface deficiency in a man whose nasal septum was removed at age 8.
Cartilage as a Determinant of Craniofacial Growth

If cartilaginous growth was the primary influence, the cartilage at the condyle of the mandible could be considered as a pacemaker for growth of that bone and the modeling of the ramus and other surface changes could be viewed as secondary to the primary cartilaginous growth.
Cartilage as a Determinant of Craniofacial Growth

If this were the true situation, then indeed the cartilage at the mandibular condyle should act as a growth center, behaving basically like an epiphyseal growth cartilage. From this perspective, the mechanism of downward and forward growth of the mandible would be a "cartilage push" from growth at the condyle. Fig 2.36
Cartilage as a Determinant of Craniofacial Growth
BUT, in experimental animals and in children, after a fracture, all of the original bone and cartilage resorb, and a new condyle regenerates directly from periosteum at the fracture site
Cartilage as a Determinant of Craniofacial Growth
Mandible:
Cartilage as a Determinant of Craniofacial Growth

Although there is no cartilage in the maxilla itself, there is cartilage in the nasal septum , and the nasomaxillary complex grows as a unit. Proponents of the cartilage theory hypothesize that the cartilaginous nasal septum serves as a pacemaker for other aspects of maxillary growth. Fig 2.37
Cartilage as a Determinant of Craniofacial Growth

There are few reported cases of early loss of the cartilaginous nasal septum in humans. One individual in whom the entire septum was removed at age 8 after an injury is shown in Fig 2.38 . It is apparent that a midface deficiency developed, but one cannot confidently attribute this to the loss of the cartilage.
Cartilage as a Determinant of Craniofacial Growth

Nevertheless, the loss of growth in experimental animals when this cartilage is removed is great enough to lead most observers to conclude that the septal cartilage does have some innate growth potential

III Functional Matrix Theory of Growth
Functional Matrix Theory of Growth
Table 2.1 Growth of craniofacial units — sites, centers, mode, mechanism, and determinant for each region.
Functional Matrix Theory of Growth

Introduced by Melvin Moss , the theory holds that neither the cartilage of the mandibular condyle nor the cartilaginous nasal septum is a determinant of jaw growth. Instead, growth of the face occurs as a response to functional needs and neurotrophic influences and is mediated by the soft tissue in which the jaws are embedded. In this conceptual view, the soft tissues grow, and both bone and cartilage react to this form of epigenetic control .
Functional Matrix Theory of Growth

The growth of the cranium illustrates this view of skeletal growth very well. Growth of the cranial vault is a direct response to the growth of the brain. Pressure exerted by the growing brain separates the cranial bones at the sutures, and new bone passively fills in at these sites so that the brain case fits the brain.
Functional Matrix Theory of Growth

According to the theory, the major determinant of growth of the maxilla and mandible is the enlargement of the nasal and oral cavities, which grow in response to functional needs, and absence of normal function would have wide-ranging effects.
Functional Matrix Theory of Growth

It has been known for many years that mandibular growth is greatly impaired by ankylosis at the temporomandibular joint, defined as fusion across the joint so that motion is prevented (which totally stops growth) or limited (which impedes growth).
Functional Matrix Theory of Growth
It appears that growth of the cranium occurs almost entirely in response to growth of the brain.
Functional Matrix Theory of Growth
Growth of the cranial base is primarily the result of endochondral growth and bony replacement at the synchondroses, which have independent growth potential.
Functional Matrix Theory of Growth

Growth of the maxilla and its associated structures occurs from a combination of growth at sutures and modeling of the surfaces of the bone. The extent to which growth of cartilage of the nasal septum leads to translation of the maxilla remains unknown.
Functional Matrix Theory of Growth

Growth of the mandible occurs by both endochondral proliferation at the condyle and apposition and resorption of bone at surfaces. It seems clear that the mandible is translated in space by the growth of muscles and other adjacent soft tissues and that addition of new bone at the condyle is in response to the soft tissue changes.
Functional Matrix Theory of Growth

Maturation of Oral Function

Maturation of Oral Function
The principal physiologic functions of the oral cavity are respiration, swallowing, mastication, and speech.
Maturation of Oral Function

Maturation of oral function can be characterized in general as following a gradient from anterior to posterior. At birth, the lips are relatively mature and capable of vigorous suckling activity, whereas more posterior structures are quite immature. As time passes, greater activity by the posterior parts of the tongue and more complex motions of the pharyngeal structures are acquired.
Maturation of Oral Function
Newborn infants are obligatory nasal breathers.
Maturation of Oral Function
Once an airway has been established, the newborn infant's next physiologic priority is to obtain milk. This is accomplished by two maneuvers: suckling (not sucking) and swallowing.
Maturation of Oral Function

"Infantile swallow" is characterized by active contractions of the musculature of the lips, a tongue tip brought forward into contact with the lower lip, and little activity of the posterior tongue or pharyngeal musculature.
Maturation of Oral Function

By the time the primary molars begin to erupt, "juvenile chewing" pattern is well established "moving the mandible laterally as it opens, then bringing it back toward the midline and closing to bring the teeth into contact with the food Fig 3.9 ".
Maturation of Oral Function

Nearly all modern infants engage in some sort of habitual non-nutritive sucking, this is culturally determined to some extent; children in primitive groups who are allowed ready access to the mother's breast indefinitely rarely suck any other object.
Maturation of Oral Function
After the primary molars erupt during the second year of life, drinking from a cup replaces drinking from a bottle and the number of children who engage in non-nutritive sucking diminishes.
Maturation of Oral Function

When sucking activity stops, a continued transition in the pattern of swallow leads to the acquisition of an "adult swallow pattern" (lips relaxed, with the tongue tip placed against the alveolar process behind the upper incisors, and the posterior teeth brought into occlusion during swallowing).
Maturation of Oral Function
As long as sucking habits persist, however, there will not be a total transition to the adult swallow.
Maturation of Oral Function
A complete transition to the adult swallow is complicated by the fact that an anterior open bite can delay the transition even further because of the physiologic need to seal the anterior space.
Maturation of Oral Function

The transition from the juvenile to the "adult chewing pattern" develops in conjunction with eruption of the permanent canines. It is interesting to note that adults who do not achieve normal function of the canine teeth because of a severe anterior open bite retain the juvenile chewing pattern.

Changes in Facial Soft Tissues

The change of greatest significance for orthodontists is that the lips, and the other soft tissues of the face, sag downward with aging . The result is a decrease in exposure of the upper incisors and an increase in exposure of the lower incisors , both at rest and on smile Figs 4.27 . The lips also become progressively thinner, with less vermilion display Fig 4.29 .
Changes in Facial Soft Tissues

It is important to remember in orthodontic treatment that the vertical relationship of the lip to the teeth will change after adolescence. leaving the upper incisors somewhat more exposed than the ideal adult relationship is necessary in treatment of an adolescent , if this relationship is to be ideal later in life Fig 4.30 .

III Changes in Alignment and Occlusion
Changes in Alignment and Occlusion
Fig 4.33 Prolonged Class III / excessive vertical growth — lower incisors tipped lingually (late crowding).
Changes in Alignment and Occlusion

In modern populations, there is a strong tendency for crowding of the mandibular incisors to develop in the late teens and early 20s, no matter how well aligned the teeth were initially. These changes appear as early as age 17 to 18 in some individuals and as late as the mid-20s in others.
Changes in Alignment and Occlusion

Lack of "normal attrition" in the modern diet. With a coarse diet, the width of teeth is reduced as interproximal wear occur. The result in many primitive populations was a reduction in arch circumference of 10 mm or more after completion of the permanent dentition at adolescence. Raymond Begg, concluded that in modern populations the teeth became crowded when attrition did not occur with soft diets, and advocated widespread extraction of premolar teeth to provide the equivalent of the attrition he saw in aborigines. But, it has been observed in other population groups that late crowding may develop even after premolars have been extracted. Thus the Begg theory, although superficially attractive, does not explain late crowding.
Changes in Alignment and Occlusion

Pressure from third molars. In fact, late crowding of lower incisors can and often does develop in individuals whose lower third molars are congenitally missing. There is some evidence that incisor crowding may be lessened by early removal of second molars, which presumably would relieve pressure from third molars, but pressure from third molars clearly is not the total explanation either.

Aging Changes in Teeth and Supporting Structure
Fig 4.35 Increasing crown height in adolescence is 'active eruption', compensating vertical jaw growth.
Aging Changes in Teeth and Supporting Structure

As time passes, additional dentin slowly deposits on the inside of the tooth so that the pulp chamber gradually becomes smaller with increasing age. This process continues relatively rapidly until the late teens, at which time the pulp chamber of a typical permanent tooth is about half the size that it was at the time of initial eruption. Additional dentin continues to be produced at a slower rate throughout life.
Aging Changes in Teeth and Supporting Structure

Apical movement of the gingival attachment (in normal circumstances) results more from vertical growth of the jaws and the accompanying eruption of the teeth than from downward migration of the gingival attachment.
Aging Changes in Teeth and Supporting Structure

In the late teens, the gingival attachment is usually near the cementoenamel junction . In the absence of inflammation, mechanical abrasion or pathologic changes, the gingival attachment should remain at about the same level almost indefinitely.
Aging Changes in Teeth and Supporting Structure

At one time, it was thought that "passive eruption" (defined as an actual gingival migration of the attachment without any eruption of the tooth) occurred. It now appears that as long as the gingival tissues are entirely healthy, this sort of downward migration of the soft tissue attachment does not occur. What was once thought to be apical migration of the gingiva during the teens is really "active eruption" , compensating for the vertical jaw growth still occurring at that time. Fig 4.35

Achondroplasia (an autosomal dominant trait) is rare in humans Fig 5.27 . Harris and Johnson concluded that the heritability of craniofacial (skeletal) characteristics was relatively high but that of dental (occlusal) characteristics was low.

Equilibrium Consideration
A key consideration is that the supporting structures of the dentition (PDL and alveolar bone) are constructed to withstand heavy forces of short duration such as those from mastication.
Equilibrium Consideration
During mastication, the fluid in the PDL space acts as a shock absorber, so that the soft tissues in the PDL are not compressed, although bending of alveolar bone occurs.
Equilibrium Consideration
Only if pressure is maintained long enough to squeeze out the fluid (a few seconds) is there an impact on the soft tissues.
Equilibrium Consideration

Only light force of long duration (6 hours or so per day) is important in determining whether there is enough of an imbalance of forces to lead to tooth movement. Means that if the balance between long-duration pressure from the tongue vs lip or cheek pressure changes, tooth movement would be expected.
Equilibrium Consideration

If an injury to the soft tissue of the lip results in scarring and contracture, the adjacent incisors will be moved lingually as the lip tightens against them Fig 5.28 . On the other hand, if restraining pressure by the lip or cheek is removed, the teeth move outward in response to unopposed pressure from the tongue Fig 5.29A .
Equilibrium Consideration

It seems unlikely, however, that the intermittent short-duration pressures created when the tongue and lips contact the teeth during swallowing or speaking would have any significant impact on tooth position.
Equilibrium Consideration
As with masticatory forces, the pressure magnitudes would be great enough to move a tooth, but the duration is inadequate Table 5.2 .

Tongue Thrusting
"Tongue thrust swallowing" ( Fig 5.37 ) still is often thought to be a cause of malocclusion despite the number of studies that have found no such relationship.
Tongue Thrusting

Laboratory studies have indicated that individuals who place the tongue tip forward when they swallow usually do not have more tongue force against the teeth than those who keep the tongue tip back; in fact, tongue pressure may be lower.
Tongue Thrusting
Swallowing is not a learned behavior but is integrated and controlled physiologically at subconscious levels, so whatever the pattern of swallow, it cannot be considered a habit in the usual sense.
Tongue Thrusting
The mature or adult swallow pattern appears in some normal children as early as age 3 but is not present in the majority until about age 6 and is never achieved in 10% to 15% of a typical population.
Tongue Thrusting
A tongue thrust swallow is a useful physiologic adaptation if you have an open bite, which is why an individual with an open bite usually also has a tongue thrust swallow.
Tongue Thrusting
After a sucking habit stops, the anterior open bite tends to close spontaneously, but the position of the tongue between the anterior teeth persists for a while as the open bite closes.
Tongue Thrusting
"Tongue thrusting" in young children is often a normal transitional stage in swallowing.

Younger children with reasonably normal occlusion, in whom it represents only a transitional stage in normal physiologic maturation

Individuals of any age with displaced incisors (or open bite), in whom it is an adaptation to the space between the teeth.

It is neither necessary nor desirable to try to teach the patient to swallow differently before beginning orthodontic treatment.

Etiology in Contemporary Perspective
Etiology in Contemporary Perspective

Edward Angle and his contemporaries, in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, took for granted that malocclusion was a disease of civilization and blamed it on improper function of the jaws under the "degenerate" modern conditions.
Etiology in Contemporary Perspective

Classic (mendelian) genetics developed rapidly in the first part of the 20th century, its view was that malocclusion is primarily the result of inherited dentofacial proportions, which might be altered somewhat by developmental variations.
Etiology in Contemporary Perspective

As the 21st century moves ahead, a more balanced view seems to be emerging. The research has not yet clarified the precise role of heredity as an etiologic agent for malocclusion. The relatively high heritability of craniofacial dimensions and the relatively low heritability of dental arch variations now have been established, but exactly how this relates to the etiologic process of malocclusions that have both skeletal and dental components remains unknown.
Etiology in Contemporary Perspective
Conclusions about the etiology of most orthodontic problems are difficult because several interacting factors probably played a role.

The first useful orthodontic classification was Angle's classification of malocclusion into Classes I, II, and III.

Periodontal and Bone Response to Normal Function
Tooth movement is primarily a PDL phenomenon .

Forces applied to the teeth can also affect the pattern of bone apposition and resorption at sites distant from the teeth, particularly the sutures of the maxilla and bony surfaces on both sides of the temporomandibular joint. Thus the biologic response to orthodontic therapy includes not only the response of the PDL but also the response of growing areas distant from the dentition.
I Periodontal Ligament Structure and Function
Periodontal Ligament Structure and Function
PDL occupies a space approximately 0.5 mm in width around all parts of the root.
Periodontal Ligament Structure and Function
The major component of the ligament is a network of parallel collagenous fibers .
Periodontal Ligament Structure and Function
The cellular elements , including mesenchymal cells of various types (fibroblasts, osteoblasts, cementoblasts, fibroclasts, osteoclasts, cementoclasts) along with vascular and neural elements
Periodontal Ligament Structure and Function
The tissue fluids .
Periodontal Ligament Structure and Function
Two other major components of the ligament must be considered:
Periodontal Ligament Structure and Function

The principal cellular elements in the PDL are undifferentiated mesenchymal cells and their progeny in the form of fibroblasts and osteoblasts. The same cells can serve both as fibroblasts , producing new collagenous matrix materials, and fibroclasts , destroying previously produced collagen.
Periodontal Ligament Structure and Function
Differentiation of PDL fibroblasts is dependent on the amount of mechanical strain, and that calcitonin induces this differentiation .
Periodontal Ligament Structure and Function
Bone and cementum are removed by specialized osteoclasts and cementoclasts, respectively. These cells are quite different from the osteoblasts and cementoblasts that produce bone and cementum.
Periodontal Ligament Structure and Function
Although the PDL is not highly vascular, it does contain blood vessels and cells from the vascular system.
Periodontal Ligament Structure and Function

Nerve endings are also found within the ligament, both the unmyelinated free endings associated with perception of pain and the more complex receptors associated with pressure and positional information ( proprioception ).
Periodontal Ligament Structure and Function
PDL space is a fluid-filled chamber with retentive but porous walls is a description of a shock absorber .
Updated number (7th) The 7th edition gives the PDL width as approximately 0.2 to 0.4 mm around the root (the line above, from the 6th edition, says approximately 0.5 mm).

Response to Normal Function

Response to Normal Function

Response to Normal Function

During masticatory function, the teeth and periodontal structures are subjected to intermittent heavy forces . Tooth contacts last for 1 second or less ; forces are quite heavy, ranging from 1 or 2 kg while soft substances are being chewed to as much as 50 kg against a more resistant object.
Response to Normal Function

When a tooth is subjected to heavy loads of this type, quick displacement of the tooth within the PDL space is prevented by the incompressible tissue fluid . Instead, the force is transmitted to the alveolar bone, which bends in response.
Response to Normal Function
Bone bending in response to normal function generates piezoelectric currents Fig 8.2 , that appear to be an important stimulus to skeletal regeneration and repair.
Response to Normal Function

If pressure against a tooth is maintained (more than ~1 second), the fluid is rapidly expressed, and the tooth displaces within the PDL space, compressing the ligament itself against adjacent bone. Pain is normally felt after 3 to 5 seconds of heavy force application Table 8.1 .

Prostaglandin and interleukin-1 beta levels increase within the PDL within a short time (minutes) after the application of pressure

Within a few hours at most, the resulting change in the chemical environment produces a different pattern of cellular activity. Cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP) , the "second messenger" for many important cellular functions and cell differentiation, appear after about 4 hours of sustained pressure. ( If a removable appliance is worn less than 4 to 6 hours per day, it will produce no orthodontic effects. )

Prostaglandins stimulate both osteoclastic and osteoblastic activity, and it can be up to 48 hours before the first osteoclasts appear within and adjacent to the compressed PDL.
Effects on the Response to Orthodontic Force

Osteoclasts attack the lamina dura, removing bone in the process of "frontal resorption," and tooth movement begins soon thereafter. At the same time, but lagging somewhat behind so that the PDL space becomes enlarged, osteoblasts (recruited locally from progenitor cells in the PDL) form bone on the tension side and begin remodeling activity on the pressure side.

Heavy Pressure (Undermining Resorption)
Effects on the Response to Orthodontic Force
The course of events is different if the sustained force against the tooth is great enough to totally occlude blood vessels and cut off the blood supply to an area within the PDL.
Effects on the Response to Orthodontic Force
When this happens, rather than cells within the compressed area of the PDL being stimulated, a sterile necrosis (hyalinization) ensues within the compressed area. (within hours)
Effects on the Response to Orthodontic Force

In clinical orthodontics it is difficult to avoid pressure that produces at least some avascular areas in the PDL. (it seems that chewing on a plastic wafer or chewing gum after orthodontic force is applied reduces pain—chewing force briefly displaces the tooth and allows a spurt of blood into compressed areas, thereby reducing the size of necrotic areas in the PDL).

After a delay of several days (3-5 days), cellular elements "within the adjacent bone marrow spaces not from PDL Fig 8.7 " begin to invade the necrotic (hyalinized) area. This process is appropriately described as undermining resorption , because the attack is from the underside of the lamina dura.

First, a delay in stimulating differentiation of cells within the marrow spaces

Second, because a considerable thickness of bone must be removed from the underside before any tooth movement can take place.

The PDL response is determined not by force alone, but by force per unit area, or pressure .
Effects on the Response to Orthodontic Force

In tipping Fig 8.9 the "loading diagram" consists of two triangles, covering half of the total PDL area. On the other hand, pressure in the two areas where it is concentrated is high in relation to the force applied to the crown. For this reason, forces used to tip teeth must be kept quite low (should not exceed ~50 gm) .

In bodily movement (translation) , the total PDL area is loaded uniformly Fig 8.10 . It is apparent that to produce the same pressure in the PDL and therefore the same biologic response, twice as much force would be required for bodily movement as for tipping.

In theory, forces to produce rotation of a tooth around its long axis could be much larger than those to produce other tooth movements, because the force could be distributed over the entire PDL rather than over a narrow vertical strip. In fact, however, it is essentially impossible to apply a rotational force so that the tooth does not also tip in its socket. For this reason, appropriate forces for rotation are similar to those for tipping.
Effects on the Response to Orthodontic Force

Extrusive movements ideally would produce no areas of compression within the PDL, only tension. Like rotation, this is more a theoretical than a practical possibility, because if the tooth tipped at all while being extruded, areas of compression would be created.

Light force is required for intrusion because the force will be concentrated in a small area at the tooth apex Fig 8.11 . As with extrusion, the tooth probably will tip somewhat as it is intruded, but the force still will be concentrated at the apex. Optimum forces in Table 8.3 .

The key to producing orthodontic tooth movement is the application of sustained force , which does not mean that the force must be absolutely continuous. It does mean that the force must be present for a considerable percentage of the time.

Only after force is maintained for approximately 4 hours do cyclic nucleotide levels in the PDL increase, indicating that this duration of pressure is required to produce the "second messengers" needed to stimulate cellular differentiation.

Despite the clinician's best efforts to keep forces light enough to produce only frontal resorption, some areas of undermining resorption are probably produced in every clinical patient.

The heavier forces that produce undermining resorption are physiologically acceptable only if the force level quickly drops to zero so that there is a period of repair and regeneration before the next activation.

The bottom line: heavy continuous forces are to be avoided; heavy intermittent forces, although less efficient, can be clinically acceptable (the more perfect the spring in the sense of its ability to provide continuous force, the more careful the clinician must be that only light force is applied).

Experience has shown that orthodontic appliances should not be reactivated more frequently than at 3-week intervals . A 4- to 6- or 8-week appointment cycle is the usual minimum in clinical practice, and now a 6- or 8-week cycle is more typical.

Undermining resorption requires 7 to 14 days (longer on the initial application of force, shorter thereafter).

If the appliance is springy and light forces produce continuous frontal resorption, there is no need for further activation for 6 to 8 weeks. If the appliance is stiffer and undermining resorption occurs, but then the force drops to zero, the tooth movement occurs in the first 10 days or so, and there is an equal or longer period for PDL regeneration and repair before force is applied again. This repair phase is highly desirable and needed with many appliances.
III Drug Effects on the Response to Orthodontic Force
Drug Effects on the Response to Orthodontic Force
Direct injection of prostaglandin into the PDL has been shown to increase the rate of tooth movement, but this is quite painful and not very practical.
Drug Effects on the Response to Orthodontic Force

Drugs aimed at increasing brain levels of acetylcholine (ACH), the key neurotransmitter in the brain, might accelerate tooth movement by affecting circulating hormone levels. Using them to affect tooth movement would be hard to justify. (The problem is to find something that primarily works locally)
Drug Effects on the Response to Orthodontic Force

Two types of drugs are known to depress the response to orthodontic force and may influence current treatment: prostaglandin inhibitors for pain control (especially the more potent members of this group that are used in treatment of arthritis, such as indomethacin), and the bisphosphonates used in treatment of osteoporosis (e.g., alendronate [Fosamax], ibandronate [Boniva], risedronate [Actonel]).
Drug Effects on the Response to Orthodontic Force
Prostaglandin Inhibitors
Drug Effects on the Response to Orthodontic Force

In the body, prostaglandins are formed from arachidonic acid, which in turn is derived from phospholipids. Corticosteroids reduce prostaglandin synthesis by inhibiting the formation of arachidonic acid; NSAIDs inhibit the conversion of arachidonic acid to prostaglandins.
Drug Effects on the Response to Orthodontic Force
Most over-the-counter analgesics are NSAIDs and therefore are prostaglandin inhibitors (aspirin, ibuprofen, naproxen [Aleve], and many others). (The major exception is acetaminophen )
Drug Effects on the Response to Orthodontic Force

With the low doses and short durations of analgesic therapy, effects on orthodontic movement does not occur, but it can become a problem in adults or children being treated chronically for arthritis pain.
Drug Effects on the Response to Orthodontic Force

Several other classes of drugs can decrease prostaglandin levels and therefore could slow the response to orthodontic force. Tricyclic antidepressants (doxepin, amitriptyline, imipramine), antiarrhythmic agents (procaine), antimalarial drugs (quinine, quinidine, chloroquine). In addition, the anticonvulsant drug phenytoin has been reported to decrease tooth movement in rats, and some tetracyclines (e.g., doxycycline) inhibit osteoclast recruitment, an effect similar to that of bisphosphonates.
Drug Effects on the Response to Orthodontic Force
Bisphosphonates
Drug Effects on the Response to Orthodontic Force

Their use has been associated with an unusual necrosis of mandibular bone . This typically occurs after extraction of a tooth or other injury to the bone ( elective extractions for orthodontic purposes should be avoided for a patient who has been taking any of these drugs .)
Drug Effects on the Response to Orthodontic Force

Stopping the drug does not eliminate all of its effects. It appears that there are two elimination rates: a fast elimination from the surface of the bones within some weeks, and slower elimination from bone structure. Fortunately, most of the drug is only on the surface, which makes orthodontic treatment possible after about 3 months with no further bisphosphonate therapy.
Drug Effects on the Response to Orthodontic Force
Bisphosphonates are the major class of drugs for control of osteoporosis. They are a special concern for two reasons:
Drug Effects on the Response to Orthodontic Force
Bone healing in patients taking bisphosphonates is problematic, and distraction osteogenesis would be a risky procedure.

New in 7th ed — Other Medications Several other patient medications affect tooth movement (mostly animal data): ACE inhibitors (e.g. Losartan) reduce the rate of movement (↓ osteoclastic activity); some antihistamines slow it (↓ osteoclasts); low-dose beta-blockers slow it by interfering with RANKL-mediated osteoclast differentiation . The practical message: know all the medications an orthodontic patient is taking.

Local Injury to Accelerate Tooth Movement
German surgeon Köle revived the idea that cuts between teeth could produce faster tooth movement and introduced the term corticotomy .
Local Injury to Accelerate Tooth Movement

After flap surgery to reflect the gingiva all the way around the arch, vertical cuts were made facially and lingually between the teeth. A banded orthodontic appliance (placed before the surgery) was activated as soon as possible, using relatively stiff archwires and wire ties to generate enough force to create greenstick fractures of the bone around the root apex and bring the teeth into alignment almost instantly.
Local Injury to Accelerate Tooth Movement

More recently, Corticotomy was revived and reconsidered as a stimulus to a regional acceleration of bone remodeling that allows faster tooth movement, rather than movement of blocks of bone that contain a tooth. The surgical technique, with a large flap to fully expose the alveolar bone and cuts between the teeth, still is similar to Köle's, but now lighter force to move teeth more physiologically is recommended, and the surgical approach has been broadened into "accelerated osteogenic orthodontics" (AOO) Fig 8.15 .
Local Injury to Accelerate Tooth Movement

Reduction of treatment time with corticotomy show a reduction in time to alignment. If corticotomy cuts that time in half, the 2- to 3-month reduction in total treatment time would not mean that total treatment time would be twice as fast, because only the initial alignment phase would be faster.
Local Injury to Accelerate Tooth Movement
In short, the benefit of AOO and corticotomy is primarily in reduction of the time to align crowded teeth without extractions .
Local Injury to Accelerate Tooth Movement

Risk includes the possibility of loss of alveolar bone height , which occurs when corticotomy is done without bone grafting, unsightly facial bruising; and the possibility of gingival stripping Fig 8.16 .

New in 7th ed — PAOO & updated evidence
Three other methods intended to accelerate tooth movement have been marketed since the onset of the 21st century:
New in 7th ed — PAOO & updated evidence

Vibration: AcceleDent and Competitors. Based on delivery of high-frequency vibration ( 30 Hz ) to the teeth for approximately 20 minutes per day . The rationale is that this stimulates cell differentiation and maturation so that the bone remodeling necessary for tooth movement occurs more quickly. Studies found no difference in space closure rates or occlusal outcomes . The effectiveness of AcceleDent is highly questionable .
New in 7th ed — PAOO & updated evidence

Tissue-Penetrating Light: Biolux Fig 8.20 . Based on the observation that healing of dental extraction sites seemed to occur more quickly when the sites were exposed to light. Intraoral device (Biolux) is said to excite intracellular enzymes and increase cellular activity in the PDL and bone, increasing the rate of bone remodeling and tooth movement. The conclusion: neither faster tooth movement nor decreased pain has been credibly demonstrated .
New in 7th ed — PAOO & updated evidence

Therapeutic Ultrasound: SmileSonica Aevo Fig 8.21 . It is known that therapeutic ultrasound increases blood flow in treated areas; indeed, it is used routinely in physical therapy to increase blood flow in muscles. The theory is that increased blood flow in the PDL would increase the rate of bone remodeling and tooth movement and also could decrease root resorption; however, there had been no convincing demonstration of effectiveness or efficiency in accelerating tooth movement.

New in 7th ed — Cochrane verdict A Cochrane review of non-invasive acceleration methods reinforces the above: vibration shows no increase in the rate of tooth movement, light (now framed as low-level laser/LED) gives only small, clinically insignificant effects, and ultrasound remains plausible but unproven — none is currently justified as a routine adjunct .

Orthodontic force directly affects the teeth and alveolar bone, but it also can have indirect effects on the jaws more generally.

Sustained light force can inhibit or enhance the maxilla's normal downward and forward growth. Force against mandibular teeth similarly can affect the direction, and perhaps the amount, of growth at the mandibular condyles.

Mobility and Pain Related to Orthodontic Treatment
Mobility
Mobility and Pain Related to Orthodontic Treatment

Orthodontic tooth movement requires remodeling of bone adjacent to the teeth and reorganization of the PDL. Collagen fibers become detached from the bone and cementum, then reattach at a later time. Radiographically, it can be observed that the PDL space widens during orthodontic tooth movement.
Mobility and Pain Related to Orthodontic Treatment

A moderate increase in mobility is an expected response to orthodontic treatment. The heavier the force, however, the greater the amount of undermining resorption expected, and the greater the mobility that will develop. Excessive mobility will usually correct itself without permanent damage.
Mobility and Pain Related to Orthodontic Treatment
Pain
Mobility and Pain Related to Orthodontic Treatment

If appropriate orthodontic force is applied, the patient feels little or nothing immediately. Several hours later, pain usually appears. The pain typically lasts for 2 to 4 days , then disappears until reactivation.
Mobility and Pain Related to Orthodontic Treatment
The pain associated with the initial activation of the appliance is the most severe. It is commonly noted that there is a great deal of individual variation in any pain experience.
Mobility and Pain Related to Orthodontic Treatment
Ischemic areas in the PDL are the major pain source.
Mobility and Pain Related to Orthodontic Treatment

Strategies to temporarily relieve pressure and allow blood flow through compressed areas should help. In fact, if light forces are used, the amount of pain experienced by patients can be decreased by having them engage in repetitive chewing (of sugarless gum, etc.) during the first 8 hours after the orthodontic appliance has been activated.
Mobility and Pain Related to Orthodontic Treatment
Light forces , however, are the key to minimizing pain as a concomitant feature of orthodontic treatment.
Mobility and Pain Related to Orthodontic Treatment

Based on clinical studies, it now is widely accepted that acetaminophen and the over-the-counter NSAIDs are equally acceptable for controlling pain over the 3 to 4 days after an orthodontic activation.
Mobility and Pain Related to Orthodontic Treatment
Allergy
Mobility and Pain Related to Orthodontic Treatment

Nickel is allergenic. Fortunately, most children with a skin allergy to nickel have no mucosal response to stainless steel orthodontic appliances (which are about 8% nickel) and tolerate treatment perfectly well.
Mobility and Pain Related to Orthodontic Treatment

The typical symptoms of nickel allergy in an orthodontic patient are widespread erythema and swelling of oral tissues, developing 1 to 2 days after a stainless steel appliance is placed. For such patients, titanium brackets and tubes can be substituted for stainless steel, and beta-titanium archwires can be used instead of nickel–titanium (NiTi) or steel wires.

Effects on Dental Pulp

Although pulpal reactions to orthodontic treatment are minimal, there is probably a modest and transient inflammatory response within the pulp, at least at the beginning of treatment with no long-term significance.
Effects on Dental Pulp
There is no contraindication to going ahead with orthodontics soon after the pulp therapy, and severe root resorption would not be expected.
Effects on Dental Pulp

One special circumstance is a tooth that experienced severe intrusive trauma and required pulp therapy for that reason. If such a tooth must be repositioned orthodontically, resorption seems less likely if a calcium hydroxide fill is maintained until the tooth movement is completed, then definitive root canal filling is placed.

Cementum adjacent to hyalinized (necrotic) areas of the PDL is "marked" and that clast cells attack this marked cementum. This observation helps explain why heavy continuous orthodontic force can lead to severe root resorption .
Root Resorption

It appears that cementum (and dentin, if resorption penetrates through the cementum) is removed from the root surface, then cementum is restored in the same way that alveolar bone is removed and then replaced.
Root Resorption
Root remodeling, in other words, is a constant feature of orthodontic tooth movement, but permanent loss of root structure would occur only if repair did not replace the initially resorbed cementum.
Root Resorption
Repair of the damaged root restores its original contours, unless the attack on the root surface produces large defects at the apex that eventually become separated from the root surface Fig 8.31 .
Root Resorption

Once an island of cementum or dentin has been cut totally free from the root surface, it will be resorbed and will not be replaced. On the other hand, even deep defects in the form of craters into the root surface will be filled in again with cementum once orthodontic movement stops, so permanent loss of root structure related to orthodontic treatment occurs primarily at the apex .

IV Effects of Treatment on Alveolar Bone Height
Effects of Treatment on Alveolar Bone Height

Pressure in the PDL space is at its peak at the root apex and the alveolar bone crest. In addition, there are two other potential risk factors: the blood supply at the bone crest is diminished relative to the thicker bone beneath it, and the presence of orthodontic appliances increases the amount of gingival inflammation.
Effects of Treatment on Alveolar Bone Height

Fortunately, excessive loss of crestal bone height is almost never seen as a complication of orthodontic treatment. Loss of alveolar crest height averaged less than 0.5 mm and almost never exceeded 1 mm , with the greatest changes occurring at extraction sites. The only exception is the presence of active periodontal disease.

The Basic Properties of Elastic Materials

Beam: in this context, archwires and springs, supported either only on one end (e.g., a spring projecting from a removable appliance) or on both ends (the segment of an archwire spanning between attachments on adjacent teeth) Fig 9.1 .
The Basic Properties of Elastic Materials
If a force is applied to such a beam, its response can be measured as the deflection (bending or twisting) produced by the force Fig 9.2 .
The Basic Properties of Elastic Materials

Force and deflection are external measurements. Stress (force per unit area) and strain (deflection per unit length) are internal measurements and can be calculated from force and deflection by considering the cross-sectional area and length of the beam Fig 9.3 .
The Basic Properties of Elastic Materials
For orthodontic purposes, three major properties of beam materials are critical in defining their clinical usefulness: strength, stiffness, and range .
The Basic Properties of Elastic Materials

The first two points attempt to describe the elastic limit of the material, the point at which any permanent deformation is first observed: (both serve as good clinical estimates of how much force or deflection a wire can withstand before permanent deformation occurs.)
The Basic Properties of Elastic Materials

(1) Proportional limit: the highest point where stress and strain still have a linear relationship (this linear relationship is known as Hooke's law ). Precisely determining this point can be difficult, so a more practical indicator is the yield strength.
The Basic Properties of Elastic Materials
(2) Yield strength: the intersection of the stress–strain curve with a parallel line offset at 0.1% strain .
The Basic Properties of Elastic Materials

(3) The ultimate tensile strength: The maximum load the wire can sustain, it is reached after some permanent deformation and is greater than the yield strength. It determines the maximum force the wire can deliver. It also is important clinically, especially because yield strength and ultimate strength differ much more for the newer titanium alloys than for steel wires.
The Basic Properties of Elastic Materials
Three different points on a stress–strain diagram can be taken as representative of the strength (the maximum load that the material can resist) of a material:
The Basic Properties of Elastic Materials
Strength is measured in units of stress— megapascals (MPa)
The Basic Properties of Elastic Materials
Fig 9.3 Stress–strain curve (material property, geometry-independent).
The Basic Properties of Elastic Materials
Fig 9.4 Resilience (area) & formability (x-axis distance).
The Basic Properties of Elastic Materials

Stiffness (≠ Springiness) is proportional to the slope of the elastic portion of the force–deflection curve Fig 9.2 . The more vertical the slope, the stiffer the wire, the more horizontal the slope, the more flexible the wire.
The Basic Properties of Elastic Materials
Range is defined as the distance that the wire will bend elastically before permanent deformation occurs, measured in millimeters Fig 9.2 .
The Basic Properties of Elastic Materials
If the wire is deflected beyond yield point, it will not return to its original shape, but clinically useful springback will still occur unless the failure point is reached.
The Basic Properties of Elastic Materials
These three major properties have an important relationship: Strength = Stiffness × Range
The Basic Properties of Elastic Materials
Resilience represents the energy storage capacity of the wire, which is a combination of strength and springiness Fig 9.4 .
The Basic Properties of Elastic Materials
Formability is the amount of permanent deformation that a wire can withstand before failing. It represents the amount of permanent bending the wire will tolerate before it breaks.

Definition of Terms
Two Point Contact for Control of Root Position
Force: load applied to an object that will tend to move it to a different position in space, usually measured clinically in weight units of grams or ounces. 1.0 N ≅ 100 gm .
Two Point Contact for Control of Root Position

Center of resistance: For an object in free space, the center of resistance is the same as the center of mass. The center of resistance for a tooth is at the approximate midpoint of the embedded portion of the root (i.e., about halfway between the root apex and the crest of the alveolar bone) Fig 9.18 .
Two Point Contact for Control of Root Position

Moment: a measure of the tendency to rotate an object around some point. Quantitatively, it is the product of the force times the perpendicular distance from the point of force application to the center of resistance and is measured in units of gram-millimeters .
Two Point Contact for Control of Root Position
Couple: two forces equal in magnitude and opposite in direction but not on the same line Fig 9.19 .
Two Point Contact for Control of Root Position

Center of rotation: the point around which rotation actually occurs when an object is being moved. When two forces are applied simultaneously to an object, the center of rotation can be controlled and made to have any desired location.

II Narrow Versus Wide Brackets in Fixed Appliance Systems
Narrow Versus Wide Brackets in Fixed Appliance Systems
Fig 9.24 Wider bracket eases moments / sliding closure.
Narrow Versus Wide Brackets in Fixed Appliance Systems
When the root of a tooth needs to be torqued facially or lingually , the necessary moment is generated within the bracket and the key dimensions are those of the archwire.
Narrow Versus Wide Brackets in Fixed Appliance Systems

When mesiodistal root movement is needed, the moment is generated across the bracket , and bracket width determines the length of the moment arm. The wider the bracket, the easier it will be to generate the moments .
Narrow Versus Wide Brackets in Fixed Appliance Systems

(With a retraction force of 100 gm and a 10-mm distance from the bracket to the center of resistance, a 1000 gm-mm counterbalancing moment will be needed. If the bracket on this tooth is 1 mm wide, 1000 gm of force will be needed at each corner of the bracket, but if the bracket is 4 mm wide, only 250 gm of force at each corner will be necessary).
Narrow Versus Wide Brackets in Fixed Appliance Systems
Binding of the wire against the corners of the bracket is affected by the force with which the bracket contacts the archwire and the contact angle between the wire and the bracket.
Narrow Versus Wide Brackets in Fixed Appliance Systems

The wider bracket reduces both the force needed to generate the moment and the contact angle and is thus advantageous for space closure by sliding Fig 9.24 . But the wider the bracket on a tooth, the smaller the interbracket span (disadvantage).
Narrow Versus Wide Brackets in Fixed Appliance Systems
Reducing interbracket span greatly increases the stiffness of the archwire and decreases its range (exponentially) .
Narrow Versus Wide Brackets in Fixed Appliance Systems

The maximum practical width of a wide bracket is about half the width of a tooth , and narrower brackets have an advantage when teeth are malaligned because the greater interbracket span reduces stiffness.

Effect of Bracket Slot Size in the Edgewise System
When steel archwires replaced gold, a reduction in slot size from 22 to 18 mil was advocated. (Because good torque is possible with steel wires and 18-mil edgewise brackets)
Effect of Bracket Slot Size in the Edgewise System
Sliding teeth along an archwire requires at least 2 mil of clearance to minimize friction. (4 mil is desirable)
Effect of Bracket Slot Size in the Edgewise System
The greater strength of an 18-mil archwire (with 22-slot bracket) compared with a 16-mil wire (with 18-slot bracket) can be an advantage in sliding teeth.
Effect of Bracket Slot Size in the Edgewise System

The 22-slot bracket would have some advantage during space closure but would be a definite disadvantage when torque is needed , 18-slot is the opposite. With steel archwires of 21 mil, springiness and range in torsion are so limited that effective torque with the archwire is essentially impossible. Exaggerated inclinations of smaller rectangular wires (e.g., 19 × 25) are one alternative, but torquing auxiliaries are often necessary with undersized steel wires in 22-slot edgewise brackets.

Friction Versus Binding in Resistance to Sliding

Friction is proportional to the force with which the contacting surfaces are pressed together and is affected by the nature of the surface at the interface (e.g., rough or smooth, chemically reactive or passive, modified by lubricants).

All surfaces, no matter how smooth, have irregularities that are large on a molecular scale, and real contact occurs only at a limited number of small spots at the peaks of the surface irregularities Fig 9.25 . These spots, called asperities , carry all the load between the two surfaces.

At low sliding speeds, a "stick-slip" phenomenon may occur as enough force builds up to shear the junctions and a jump occurs, then the surfaces stick again until enough force again builds to break them.

Resistance to sliding is determined primarily by two things: friction (as the wire contacts the walls or bottom of the bracket) and elastic or inelastic binding (as the wire contacts the corners of the bracket).

Segmented Arch Mechanics
The essence of the segmented arch system is the establishment of units of teeth , so that anchorage and movement segments are clearly defined.
Segmented Arch Mechanics

In segmented arch treatment, lingual arches are used for stabilization in a majority of the patients, and stabilizing wire segments in the brackets of teeth in anchor units also are used routinely. (For this reason, the 22-slot edgewise appliance is favored for segmented arch treatment. The wires used for stabilizing segments usually are 21 × 25 steel )
Segmented Arch Mechanics
Typical segmented arch treatment would call for initial alignment within anterior and posterior segments
Segmented Arch Mechanics
Sliding archwires through brackets almost always is avoided in this technique because resistance to sliding hampers efforts to control anchorage.
Segmented Arch Mechanics

An excellent example of the segmented arch approach is the design of an appliance to simultaneously retract and intrude protruding maxillary central incisors (because lingual tipping of the incisors tends to move the crown downward as the tooth rotates around its center of resistance) Fig 9.48 . This could be done much more easily now by using TADs .
IV Continuous Arch Mechanics
Continuous Arch Mechanics
Extremely complex multi-couple force system is established when the wire is tied into place. (Force analysis is essentially impossible)
Continuous Arch Mechanics

When the wire is tied into place, the initial result is a small movement of one tooth. As soon as that occurs, the force system is changed, and the new system causes a small movement of another tooth. Either way, the result is still another complex force system, which causes another movement, leading to another change in the system, and so on.
Continuous Arch Mechanics
It is a saving grace that a continuous archwire usually does not allow the teeth to move very far from the desired endpoint.
Continuous Arch Mechanics

The advantages and disadvantages of the continuous arch approach are just the reverse of those with the segmented arch approach. Advantages: less chair time and excellent failsafe properties. Disadvantage: Complex force system.
