The key characteristics of any TAD are: its short- and long-term stability (the major indicator of success or failure) and its ease of use (Box 10.2)
Bone Screws
Short-term or primary stability is determined by mechanical retention of the screw in bone, which depends on bone properties, the design of the screw, and placement technique.
Bone Screws
Long-term or secondary stability is defined by the biologic union of the screw to the surrounding bone. It is determined by the implant surface, bone characteristics, and bone turnover.
Bone Screws
Over time, primary stability decreases while secondary stability increases ; clinical stability is the sum of primary and secondary stability and is the major factor in clinical success Fig 10.47 .
Bone Screws
Stability:
Bone Screws

The pitch of the screw threads (how close the threads are to one another). The denser the bone, the closer the threads should be. Because the layer of cortical bone is thin in the dental alveolus, a tighter pitch of the threads near the head of the screw gives greater contact with the cortical bone, higher pull-out strength, and better primary stability.
Bone Screws

The length of the screw. The amount of contact with cortical bone is the major factor in stability, and the amount of soft tissue overlying the bone is an important consideration. (A long screw that passes all the way through the alveolus to reach cortical bone on the other side called a bicortical screw).
Bone Screws
The diameter of the screw. Within the 1.3- to 2.0-mm diameter range, stability and survival are much more strongly related to the amount of cortical bone contact rather than the screw diameter
Bone Screws
A thread-forming screw compresses the bone around the thread as the screw advances, obtains better bone-to-screw contact, and is better adapted for use with alveolar bone.
Bone Screws
A thread-cutting screw improve penetration into denser bone, they perform better in the mandibular ramus, mandibular buccal shelf, zygomatic buttress, and palate.
Bone Screws
The form of the tip . All orthodontic miniscrews are self-tapping (i.e., they create their own thread as they advance). There are two self-tapping designs: thread-forming and thread-cutting.

Introduction to Section IV — Treatment in Preadolescent Children: What Is Different?

Orthodontic treatment rarely is done in the primary dentition, for three reasons: (1) Movement of primary incisors and canines is likely to lead to accelerated root resorption , (2) movement of any of the primary teeth has little effect on where the permanent teeth erupt, (3) growth modification effects in young children are lost to a resumption of growth in the original pattern.
Introduction to Section IV — Treatment in Preadolescent Children: What Is Different?
Primary dentition treatment, usually called very early treatment .
Introduction to Section IV — Treatment in Preadolescent Children: What Is Different?
Preadolescence = mixed dentition / early treatment / preventive and interceptive treatment
Introduction to Section IV — Treatment in Preadolescent Children: What Is Different?

The goals of early treatment must be clearly outlined and understood. If mixed dentition treatment takes too long, there are two problems: (1) Patients can be "burned out" by the time they are ready for comprehensive treatment, (2) the chance of damage to the teeth and supporting structures increases.
Introduction to Section IV — Treatment in Preadolescent Children: What Is Different?
There are important biomechanical differences between complete and partial appliances . The typical fixed appliance for mixed dentition treatment is a " 2 × 4 " or " 2 × 6 " arrangement.
Introduction to Section IV — Treatment in Preadolescent Children: What Is Different?
Anchorage control is both more difficult and more critical in early treatment. Implant-supported anchorage usually is not practical because of the presence of unerupted teeth and immature bone.
Introduction to Section IV — Treatment in Preadolescent Children: What Is Different?

Beware of unerupted teeth. Care must be taken so that the roots of the lateral incisors are not inadvertently tipped into the path of the erupting canines, this can lead to resorption of lateral incisor root .
Introduction to Section IV — Treatment in Preadolescent Children: What Is Different?
Space closure must be managed with particular care. Otherwise, when all teeth are not banded or bonded, the teeth without attachments will tend to be displaced and squeezed out of the arch
Introduction to Section IV — Treatment in Preadolescent Children: What Is Different?

Interarch mechanics must be used sparingly if at all. The side effects of Class II, Class III, or vertical elastics make them risky with partial fixed appliances (with one exception: Cross-elastics can be used in the mixed dentition in the treatment of unilateral crossbite
Introduction to Section IV — Treatment in Preadolescent Children: What Is Different?
If early treatment is carried out in only one arch, the final result is dictated by the untreated arch .
Introduction to Section IV — Treatment in Preadolescent Children: What Is Different?

Retention often is needed between mixed dentition treatment and eruption of the permanent teeth. Overcorrection and careful retention may be even more necessary after early treatment. The final stage of transition from the mixed to the permanent dentition is a particularly unstable time.

I. Posterior Crossbite
I. Posterior Crossbite
Fig 11.13 Lingual-arch maxillary expansion devices (W-arch / quad helix).
I. Posterior Crossbite

If the child shifts on closure or if the constriction is severe enough to significantly reduce the space within the arch, early correction is indicated. If not, treatment can be deferred before midpalatal suture bridging.
I. Posterior Crossbite
Another critical question is whether the posterior crossbite is related to skeletal maxillary retrusion or mandibular protrusion . (means correcting skeletal discrepancy will eliminate crossbite)
I. Posterior Crossbite
On the average, a 1-mm increase in the inter-premolar width increases arch perimeter values by 0.7 mm .
I. Posterior Crossbite

It is important to determine whether the crossbite is skeletal or dental; in the early mixed dentition years the treatment is usually the same because relatively light forces will move teeth and bones.
I. Posterior Crossbite

An expansion lingual arch is the best choice at this age; heavy force from a jackscrew device is needed only when the midpalatal suture has become significantly interdigitated during adolescence. Heavy force and rapid expansion are not indicated in the primary or early mixed dentition. There is a significant risk of distortion of the nose if this is done in younger children.
I. Posterior Crossbite
There are three basic approaches to the treatment of moderate posterior crossbites in children:
I. Posterior Crossbite
Fig 11.14 Minor canine interference → mandibular shift into crossbite.
I. Posterior Crossbite

1. Equilibration to eliminate mandibular shift (apparent crossbite) — A shift into posterior crossbite will be due solely to occlusal interference caused by the primary canines or (less frequently) primary molars. In this case, a child requires only limited equilibration of the primary teeth (often, just reduction of the primary canines) to eliminate the interference and the resulting lateral shift into crossbite Fig 11.12 .
I. Posterior Crossbite
Fig 11.16 Marked bilateral maxillary constriction.
I. Posterior Crossbite

The preferred appliance for a preadolescent child is an adjustable lingual arch that requires little patient cooperation. Both the W-arch Fig 11.15 and the quad helix Fig 11.16 are reliable and easy to use.
I. Posterior Crossbite
W-arch delivers proper force levels when opened 4 to 6 mm wider than the passive width.
I. Posterior Crossbite

Quad helix is a more flexible version of the W-arch, "but the forces are equivalent". The helices in anterior palate are bulky, which can serve as a reminder to aid in stopping a finger habit. The combination of a posterior crossbite and a finger-sucking habit is the best indication for this appliance.
I. Posterior Crossbite
Both the W-arch and the quad helix leave an imprint on the tongue Fig 11.17 . The imprint will disappear when the appliance is removed but can take up to a year to totally do so.
I. Posterior Crossbite
Fig 11.17 W-arch for bilateral maxillary expansion.
I. Posterior Crossbite
With both types of expansion lingual arches, some opening of the midpalatal suture can be expected in a child with primary or mixed dentition.
I. Posterior Crossbite

Expansion should continue at the rate of 2 mm per month until the crossbite is slightly overcorrected "the lingual cusps of the maxillary teeth should occlude on the lingual inclines of the buccal cusps of the mandibular molars at the end of active treatment" Fig 11.18 .
I. Posterior Crossbite
Data show an average palatal expansion of 3.9 mm and an average intermolar expansion of 6.5 mm .
I. Posterior Crossbite
Most posterior crossbites require 2 to 3 months of active treatment and 3 months of retention.
I. Posterior Crossbite

2. Expansion of a constricted maxillary arch — A lateral shift into crossbite is caused by constriction of the maxillary arch, and moderate expansion of the maxillary dental arch is needed for correction Fig 11.13 . "If the permanent first molars are expected to erupt in less than 6 months, it is better to wait for their eruption so that correction can include these teeth." A greater maxillary constriction may allow the maxillary teeth to fit inside the mandibular teeth—if so, there will not be a shift on closure Fig 11.14 , and there is less reason to provide early correction.
I. Posterior Crossbite
Fig 11.18 Quad helix for bilateral constriction.
I. Posterior Crossbite

3. Unilateral repositioning of teeth — Some children do have a true unilateral crossbite because of unilateral maxillary constriction of the upper arch Fig 11.19 . Asymmetric movement can be achieved by using different length arms on a W-arch or quad helix Fig 11.20 . An alternative is to use a mandibular lingual arch to stabilize the lower teeth and attach cross-elastics. If teeth in both arches contribute to the problem, cross-elastics between banded or bonded attachments in both arches Fig 11.21 can reposition both upper and lower teeth. Cross-elastics will extrude the posterior teeth and should be used with caution in children with increased lower face height or limited overbite.

II. Anterior Crossbite
Etiology
II. Anterior Crossbite
It is critically important to differentiate skeletal problems from crossbites due only to displacement of teeth . If the problem is truly skeletal, simply changing the incisor position is inadequate.
II. Anterior Crossbite

Anterior crossbite affecting only one or two teeth almost always is due to lingually displaced maxillary central or lateral incisors . These teeth tend to erupt to the lingual because of the lingual position of the developing tooth buds and may be trapped in that location, especially if there is not enough space Fig 11.23 .
II. Anterior Crossbite
The most common etiologic factor for nonskeletal anterior crossbites is lack of space for the permanent incisors.
II. Anterior Crossbite

If the developing crossbite is discovered before eruption is complete, the adjacent primary teeth can be extracted to provide the necessary space for facial migration of the erupting tooth Fig 11.24 .
II. Anterior Crossbite
Treatment of Nonskeletal Anterior Crossbite
II. Anterior Crossbite
Lingually positioned maxillary incisors limit lateral jaw movements, and these teeth or their mandibular counterparts sometimes sustain significant incisal abrasion.
II. Anterior Crossbite
Gingival recession is a risk for anterior teeth in crossbite, especially for the lower incisors.
II. Anterior Crossbite
In the early mixed dentition, correction of dental anterior crossbites is recommended for two reasons:
II. Anterior Crossbite
Fig 11.27 Anterior crossbite corrected with a removable appliance.
II. Anterior Crossbite
Removable Appliance Therapy
II. Anterior Crossbite

One way to tip the maxillary anterior teeth out of crossbite is with a removable appliance, using fingersprings for facial movement of the maxillary incisors Fig 11.25 or, less frequently, an active labial bow for lingual movement of mandibular incisors.
II. Anterior Crossbite

In the early mixed dentition, the preferred approach is to place the removable appliance without a biteplate and attempt tooth movement, because a biteplate risks the chance that teeth not in contact with the appliance or the opposing arch will erupt excessively. (an exception is very deep bite or child with bruxism habit). If after 2 months the teeth in the opposing arch are moving in the same direction as the teeth to which the force is being applied, the bite can be opened.
II. Anterior Crossbite
If the lingual fingersprings are activated 1.5 to 2 mm , they will produce approximately 1 mm of tooth movement in a month.
II. Anterior Crossbite
The offending teeth should be slightly overcorrected until overbite is adequate to retain the tooth position. One or 2 months of retention with a passive appliance is usually sufficient.
II. Anterior Crossbite
Fig 11.28 Anterior crossbite — 2×4 fixed appliance.

Fixed Appliance Therapy
II. Anterior Crossbite

One of the simplest fixed appliances for correction of maxillary incisors with a moderate anterior crossbite is a maxillary lingual arch with fingersprings (sometimes called whip springs ). They produce tooth movement at the optimum rate of 1 mm per month Fig 11.26 .
II. Anterior Crossbite
2 × 4 fixed appliance is the best choice for a patient with mixed dentition with crowding, rotations, the need for bodily movement, and more permanent teeth in crossbite Fig 11.27 .

Oral Habits and Open Bites
III. Anterior Open Bite
An open bite in a preadolescent child with normal vertical facial proportions is most likely caused by a habit such as thumb sucking.
III. Anterior Open Bite
A disproportionately large lower anterior face height with a severe anterior open bite indicates a skeletal problem (complex open bites).
III. Anterior Open Bite
Effects of Sucking Habits
III. Anterior Open Bite
More prevalent in girls and non-breastfed children.
III. Anterior Open Bite
The extent to which such a habit affects eruption depends on its frequency (hours per day) and duration (months or years).
III. Anterior Open Bite

With frequent and prolonged sucking, maxillary incisors are tipped facially, mandibular incisors are tipped lingually, and eruption of some incisors is impeded. In many children, maxillary intercanine and intermolar width is narrowed, resulting in a posterior crossbite with a V-shaped arch form .
III. Anterior Open Bite
As long as the habit stops before the eruption of the permanent incisors, most of the changes resolve spontaneously with the exception of posterior crossbite .
III. Anterior Open Bite
If a child does not want to quit sucking, habit therapy (especially appliance therapy) is not indicated.
III. Anterior Open Bite
Fig 11.35 Cemented habit crib (38–40 mil).

III. Anterior Open Bite
The simplest approach to habit therapy is a straightforward discussion between the child and the dentist.
III. Anterior Open Bite
Another level of intervention is reminder therapy .
III. Anterior Open Bite
If the reminder approach fails, a reward system can be implemented.
III. Anterior Open Bite

If all these approaches fail and the child really wants to quit, an elastic bandage loosely wrapped around the elbow prevents the arm from flexing and the fingers from being sucked. "only at night and 6 to 8 weeks of intervention"

Appliance Therapy
III. Anterior Open Bite
If the previous methods have not succeeded in eliminating the habit, a removable reminder appliance is contraindicated because lack of compliance is part of the problem.
III. Anterior Open Bite
Fitted with a cemented reminder appliance that impedes sucking can be used.
III. Anterior Open Bite

The preferred method is a maxillary lingual arch with an anterior crib device , making it extremely difficult for the child to place the thumb or other object in the mouth Fig 11.31 . The crib device is effective in extinguishing thumb-sucking in 85% to 90% of patients.
III. Anterior Open Bite
It is a good idea to leave the crib in place for 6 months after the habit has apparently been eliminated.

I. Overretained Primary Teeth

Most overretained primary maxillary molars have either the buccal roots or the large lingual root intact. Most overretained primary mandibular molars have either the mesial or distal root still intact and hindering exfoliation.
I. Overretained Primary Teeth
In general, incisors will erupt lingually and then move facially when overretained primary incisors exfoliate or are removed Fig 11.33 .

Any permanent tooth can erupt ectopically.

Three patterns of deviant eruption are both reasonably frequent and clinically significant, and deserve consideration during the mixed dentition: lateral incisors in both arches, maxillary first molars, and maxillary canines .

Lateral Incisors

II. Ectopic Eruption

Often, loss of one or both primary canines during permanent lateral incisors eruption in both arches indicates a significant lack of enough space for all the permanent teeth, so either major arch expansion or premolar extraction ultimately will be required.
II. Ectopic Eruption
Early loss of one or both maxillary primary canines almost never requires immediate treatment. In contrast, early loss of one or both mandibular primary canines can be a more complex problem.
II. Ectopic Eruption

When both mandibular primary canines are lost as the lateral incisors erupt, either there is a substantial " incisor liability " that can still be accommodated by space management with a lingual arch during the transition and the available leeway space or there is a true arch length shortage Fig 11.34 .

Guidance for treatment decisions comes from doing a space analysis and assessing the incisor position. (discussed in Chapter 12)

The prevalence of a clinically significant midline shift after premature loss of one primary canine was not statistically or clinically greater than what was seen in patients with normal eruption ( 1.3 and 1.0 mm , respectively) and the new data suggest that it is not necessary to hold the midline or extract the contralateral tooth. An early phase of 2 × 4 or 2 × 6 treatment to correct minor midline changes also could be deferred Fig 11.35 .

Maxillary First Molars
II. Ectopic Eruption
Fig 11.40 Ectopic permanent first molar (bitewing).

Usually diagnosed from routine bitewing radiographs.

When only small amounts of resorption ( <1 to 1.5 mm ) are observed Fig 11.36 , a period of watchful waiting is indicated because self-correction is possible. If the blockage of eruption persists for 6 months or if resorption continues to increase, treatment is indicated.
II. Ectopic Eruption

The basic approach is to move the ectopically erupting tooth away from the primary molar it is resorbing. If a limited amount of movement is needed but little or none of the permanent first molar is visible clinically, a 22-mil brass wire looped and tightened around the contact between the primary second molar and the permanent molar is suggested Fig 11.37 .
II. Ectopic Eruption
A steel spring clip separator, available commercially, may work if only a small amount of resorption of the primary molar roots exists Fig 11.38 .
II. Ectopic Eruption

Elastomeric separators wedged mesial to the first molar also can be used to push it distally so it can erupt but are not recommended. " they have the potential to become dislodged in an apical direction and cause periodontal irritation "

If resorption on the distal roots of the primary second molars is severe and if access can be gained to the occlusal surface of the molar, a simple fixed appliance can be fabricated to move the molar distally Fig 11.39 .

If the permanent molar has caused extensive resorption of the primary molar, there may be no choice but to extract the primary tooth. Unless the second premolar is missing and the arch length is purposefully to be reduced and later premolar extraction is planned, a distal shoe that guides the erupting molar should be placed after the extraction.

II. Localized Space Loss (3 mm or Less): Space Regaining
Distal tipping and de-rotation of maxillary molars often are satisfactory to regain 2 to 3 mm .

A removable appliance retained with Adams clasps and incorporating a helical fingerspring adjacent to the tooth to be moved is very effective. This appliance is the ideal design for distally tipping one molar Fig 11.57 . The spring is activated approximately 2 mm to produce 1 mm of movement per month . The molar typically will de-rotate spontaneously as it is tipped distally.

For unilateral mandibular space regaining, the best choice is a fixed appliance . A lingual arch can be used to support the tooth movement and provide anchorage Fig 11.59 .

If space has been lost bilaterally because of lingual incisor tipping "due to early loss of primary canines", there are two choices short of bands and brackets: a lip bumper Fig 11.60 or an adjustable lingual arch Fig 11.61 . III. Mild-to-Moderate Crowding of Incisors With Adequate Space

Irregular Incisors, Minimal Space Discrepancy: "Incisor liability" cause transient crowding of the permanent incisors. Children with normal occlusion indicate that when they go through the transition from the primary to the mixed dentition, up to 2 mm of incisor crowding may resolve spontaneously without treatment.
III. Mild-to-Moderate Crowding of Incisors With Adequate Space

The only reason for treatment may be temporary esthetic improvement; one could consider disking the interproximal enamel surfaces of the remaining primary canines and first primary molars Fig 11.62 (It is possible to gain as much as 3 to 4 mm of anterior space through this procedure, but the teeth may align in a more lingual position and actually make the space problem worse).

IV. Space Deficiency Largely Due to Allowance for Molar Shift: Space Management (Leeway Space)
2.5 mm of leeway space in EACH side of mandible. 1.5 mm of space in EACH side of maxilla.
IV. Space Deficiency Largely Due to Allowance for Molar Shift: Space Management (Leeway Space)

A major component of the projected space deficiency is the allowance for mesial movement of the permanent first molars to a Class I relationship when the second primary molars are lost. For these patients, if the loss of leeway space could be prevented, there would be little or no space deficiency.
IV. Space Deficiency Largely Due to Allowance for Molar Shift: Space Management (Leeway Space)

The current recommendation for children with moderate crowding but little or no space discrepancy is to begin intervention with a lingual arch in the late mixed dentition , just before the second primary molars exfoliate.

Loss of both primary canines or delayed eruption due to crowding is an indication for earlier space management with a lingual arch Fig 11.63 .
IV. Space Deficiency Largely Due to Allowance for Molar Shift: Space Management (Leeway Space)

In the absence of early loss of primary teeth, the major reason for early intervention in a child who has transitional crowding is esthetic concern . If the parents insist on doing something sooner, a combination of early extraction of primary canines and disking to reduce the width of primary molars can provide space to allow the permanent incisors and canines to erupt and align. This can be carried further posteriorly in the arch by disking the second primary molar to allow the first premolars to erupt Fig 11.64 .
IV. Space Deficiency Largely Due to Allowance for Molar Shift: Space Management (Leeway Space)

Because the molars have not been allowed to shift forward into the leeway space when space management is employed, they often are maintained in the end-to-end relationship that is normal before the premolars erupt. For that reason, correction of the molar relationship also must become a goal of treatment.
IV. Space Deficiency Largely Due to Allowance for Molar Shift: Space Management (Leeway Space)

The child whose incisor segment is straight, without anterior arch curvature, extraction of primary canines usually leads to spacing of the incisors or maintenance of essentially the same arch form. Alignment does not improve even when the space is available and a lingual arch is in place to serve as a template for tooth position Fig 11.65 .
IV. Space Deficiency Largely Due to Allowance for Molar Shift: Space Management (Leeway Space)
Correction of incisor rotations or residual irregularity in incisor position requires a fixed appliance.

Unless the incisors are severely protrusive, the long-term plan would be generalized expansion of the arch to align the teeth. The major advantage of doing this in the mixed dentition is improved esthetics.

In the mandibular arch an adjustable lingual arch is the appliance of choice for simple expansion by tipping tooth movement. In the maxilla, either a removable or fixed appliance can be employed.

When an incisor has delayed eruption and there is no impediment such as a supernumerary tooth or other pathology, simple excision of the overlying soft tissue is recommended (see Chapter 11). This usually leads to normal eruption.
Delayed Incisor Eruption

If there is any doubt regarding the potential for eruption or whether there has been adequate exposure of the crown, the tooth should have an attachment bonded to it. Transposition
The teeth most likely to be transposed are mandibular incisors and maxillary premolars , and this usually occurs as a consequence of ectopic eruption.
Transposition
There appears to be a genetic component to this problem.
Transposition

In the early mixed dentition, transposition can develop when distally directed eruption of the permanent mandibular lateral incisor leads to loss of the primary mandibular canine and primary first molar Fig 12.2 . "Either due to substantial 'incisor liability' or true arch length shortage"
Transposition

Interceptive treatment requires repositioning the lateral incisor mesially Fig 12.2C ; this means either bonding the tooth or gaining surgical access to the tooth and applying traction to tip the tooth back to its natural position.
Transposition

One adverse consequence of this early repositioning is potential resorption of the lateral incisor root because it may be brought into contact with the unerupted canine. This is unlikely because of the usual facial position of the unerupted canine but should be considered.
Transposition
Later in the mixed dentition, the more prevalent transposition is of the maxillary canine and first premolar or maxillary canine and lateral incisor Fig 12.3 .
Transposition
Often, the best approach is to move a partially transposed tooth to a total transposed position or to leave fully transposed teeth in that position .

Primary Failure of Eruption

Primary Failure of Eruption
Table 12.1 Distinguishing primary failure of eruption (PFE) from mechanical obstruction / other disorders.
Primary Failure of Eruption
Failure of eruption of permanent posterior teeth when there is no mechanical interference , and now is known to have a genetic etiology Fig 12.4 " PTHR1 mutation ".
Primary Failure of Eruption

The affected teeth are not ankylosed but do not erupt and do not respond normally to orthodontic force, so they cannot be pulled into occlusion. If tooth movement is attempted, usually the affected teeth will ankylose after little or no movement in any direction.
Primary Failure of Eruption
Table 12.1 contrasts the diagnostic characteristics of PFE with the situation of mechanical obstruction.
Primary Failure of Eruption

Acceptance of premolar occlusion in affected quadrants usually is the best long-term option. Prosthetic replacement of the teeth that failed to erupt, or possibly segmental osteotomies or distraction osteogenesis, is almost the only treatment possibility.

Impact of Radiation Therapy and Bisphosphonates

Impact of Radiation Therapy and Bisphosphonates
Shortened roots are the result of high-dose chemotherapy and total body irradiation (TBI) especially when treatment is in the 3- to 5-years age group .
Impact of Radiation Therapy and Bisphosphonates
Some of the irradiated teeth fail to develop, others fail to erupt, and some may erupt even though they have extremely limited root development.

Traumatic Displacement of Teeth
Traumatic Displacement of Teeth
Fig 12.9 Orthodontic management of an intruded permanent tooth (re-eruption window vs surgical repositioning).
Traumatic Displacement of Teeth
Immediately after a traumatic injury:
Traumatic Displacement of Teeth
Teeth that have not been irreparably damaged usually are repositioned with finger pressure to a near normal position and out of occlusal interference
Traumatic Displacement of Teeth

Then stabilized (with a light wire or nylon filament) for approximately 3 to 5 weeks depending on the extent of the injury. If the alveolus has been fractured, then the teeth should be stabilized with a heavy wire for approximately 6 weeks .
Traumatic Displacement of Teeth

Orthodontic treatment to reposition them is indicated. For most patients it is advised to wait 3 to 4 months to begin active treatment, but for more severe periodontal-type injuries (luxation, intrusion, extrusion, or avulsion), some clinicians recommend longer waiting times (of up to 1 year ). On the other hand, if after an injury the teeth have consolidated in a position that causes an occlusal interference, tooth movement should be started earlier to remove the interference.
Traumatic Displacement of Teeth

In either scenario, light force should be used. In orthodontic treatment that begins after significant trauma, even tipping forces can lead to loss of vitality and root resorption for previously traumatized teeth.
Traumatic Displacement of Teeth

Radiographically, periapical radiographs at 2 to 3 weeks, 6 to 8 weeks, and 1 year are indicated to determine periapical pathology. If the apex is complete at the time of the injury, it is more likely that the tooth will become nonvital from luxation injuries.

For teeth with less severe intrusion, orthodontics provides better supporting tissue outcomes than surgical repositioning, and to keep this option open, the intruded teeth should be observed for about 3 weeks before any treatment. Traumatically extruded teeth also are at increased risk for losing pulp vitality. These teeth have reduced bony support and a poor crown–root ratio. Attempts to intrude them result in bony defects between the teeth, and loss of pulp vitality is a major risk (especially for lateral incisors), so orthodontic intrusion is not a good plan . When the discrepancy is minor to moderate, reshaping the elongated tooth by crown reduction may be the best plan Fig 12.8 . On the other hand, avulsed teeth that were not completely seated in the socket during initial injury treatment and are extruded as a result can be successfully orthodontically repositioned if treatment begins immediately.

Another consideration for patients with traumatically injured anterior teeth that cannot be restored is decoronation , until vertical growth is largely completed and an implant can be placed Fig 12.9 . (This adjunctive procedure reduces the chance of ridge resorption and the need for later bone grafting)

An endodontically-treated tooth can be moved without much fear of resorption, and crown-fractured teeth can be orthodontically extruded (to allow crown lengthening/restoration) — more predictable than rapid forced eruption. Decoronation timing: if done before the growth spurt, bone is maintained and even deposited ; even in a non-growing patient bone can be held.
I Ankylosed Primary Molars Without Successors
Ankylosed Primary Molars Without Successors
Fig 12.14 Ankylosed primary second molar without a successor — decoronation preserves bone.
Ankylosed Primary Molars Without Successors
Most have successors and will exfoliate in reasonable time. If the premolar is blocked by the retained crown of an ankylosed primary molar, the remainder of the crown should be extracted.
Ankylosed Primary Molars Without Successors

The teeth that are problematic are ankylosed primary second molars without successors . As other teeth erupt and the ankylosed ones do not, large vertical occlusal discrepancies and vertical periodontal defects on the adjacent permanent teeth can develop. If this occurs and the ankylosed teeth are extracted, a great deal of bone will be lost.
Ankylosed Primary Molars Without Successors

One solution is early extraction of the ankylosed second primary molar before any vertical defect advances too far, and not placing a space maintainer . Letting the first permanent molar drift mesially is desirable for two reasons: It reduces the size of the implant to closer to the size of a second premolar, and the first molar brings bone with it as it moves forward.
Ankylosed Primary Molars Without Successors

The other possibility is decoronation , as described earlier, which is increasingly indicated for patients who still have the growth spurt remaining. For these patients, the vertical defect at the time of implant placement is reduced and bone grafting may not be necessary. It is possible that new bone will form coronal to the buried root structure Fig 12.11 .
Space-Related Problems
I Excess Space
Excess Space
Fig 12.16 Closure of a large diastema with a fixed appliance (segmental archwire, bodily movement).
Excess Space
Fig 12.18 Bonded 17.5-mil multistrand wire to retain diastema closure.
Excess Space
Spacing of Permanent Teeth
Excess Space

In the absence of incisor protrusion, generalized excess space is not a frequent finding in the mixed dentition. It can result from either small teeth in normal-sized arches or normal-sized teeth in large arches. There is little or no advantage to early treatment unless it is for compelling esthetic reasons.
Excess Space
Large Diastema
Excess Space

Closing a large unesthetic diastema ( >2 mm ) that may also be inhibiting eruption of adjacent teeth requires bodily repositioning . Might be result of pathologic conditions, supernumerary teeth, or missing adjacent teeth.
Excess Space

When the situation demands bodily mesiodistal movement and no retraction of the teeth, an anterior segmental archwire from central to central incisor or a segmental archwire including more anterior teeth is needed. Initial alignment of the incisors with a flexible wire is required. Then a stiffer archwire can be employed as the teeth slide together (with 22-slot brackets, 18-mil round or 16 × 22-mil rectangular steel is a good choice) Fig 12.12 .
Excess Space

If the lateral incisors and canines have not erupted when the diastema is closed, a removable retainer will require constant modification. If the overbite is not prohibitively deep, a better alternative approach for retention is to bond a 17.5-mil multistrand archwire to the linguocervical portion of the incisors Fig 12.14 .
Excess Space

If the centrals and laterals have erupted, a removable appliance instead of a lingual bonded retainer is best. The removable appliance will allow the adjustment of the lateral incisal roots when the canines erupt along their distal root surfaces. A bonded retainer will not allow that and may potentially contribute to lateral incisor root resorption.
Excess Space
A frenectomy before treatment is contraindicated, and a posttreatment frenectomy should be done only if unresolved bunching of tissue between the teeth shows that it is necessary.
Excess Space
Fig 12.17 Multiple supernumerary teeth in the anterior maxilla.
Excess Space
Multiple Supernumerary
Excess Space
In a few instances, multiple supernumerary teeth are located superficially, and uncomplicated extractions can be performed without interfering appreciably with the normal teeth.
Excess Space
The guideline is that the more supernumeraries there are, the more abnormal their shape, and the higher their position, the harder it will be to manage the situation Fig 12.13 .
Excess Space

The earlier the supernumeraries can be removed, the more likely that the normal teeth will erupt without further intervention. Conversely, the later the extractions, the more likely it is that the remaining unerupted normal teeth will need surgical exposure, orthodontic traction, or both to bring them into the arch.
II Maxillary Dental Protrusion and Spacing
Maxillary Dental Protrusion and Spacing
Fig 12.19 Closing-loop archwire retracting protrusive maxillary incisors (2×4 appliance).
Maxillary Dental Protrusion and Spacing
Treatment for maxillary dental protrusion during the early mixed dentition is indicated only when teeth are esthetically objectionable or in danger of traumatic dental injury (TDI) .
Maxillary Dental Protrusion and Spacing
The more common cause for maxillary incisor protrusion is a Class II malocclusion that often has a skeletal component, and, in that case, treatment must address the larger problem.
Maxillary Dental Protrusion and Spacing

Early orthodontic treatment for those who have increased overjet, incompetent lips, and a history of permanent dentition TDI before age 9 years makes some sense if the treatment is limited to retraction of the incisors (not early Class II growth modification).
Maxillary Dental Protrusion and Spacing
When the teeth require bodily movement or correction of rotations, a 2 × 4 fixed appliance is required Fig 12.15 .
Maxillary Dental Protrusion and Spacing

Depending on the amount of incisor retraction and space closure, a headgear or Nance appliance , with consideration for vertical facial and dental characteristics, may be necessary for anchorage support.
Maxillary Dental Protrusion and Spacing

If the overbite is deep, it will bring the upper and lower incisors into vertical contact before the upper incisors can be retracted. In some properly selected patients this can be addressed with a biteplate that allows eruption of posterior teeth and reduces the overbite, but it is rare that skeletal Class II malocclusion is not part of the total picture when excessive overjet and overbite both are present . This presents a much more complex treatment problem that requires skeletal change and most likely comprehensive orthodontic treatment.
III Missing Permanent Teeth
Missing Permanent Teeth
The most commonly missing permanent teeth are second premolars (especially mandibular) and maxillary lateral incisors . These two conditions pose different problems:
Missing Permanent Teeth
Fig 12.20 Retaining the primary second molar when the second premolar is congenitally missing.
Missing Permanent Teeth
Fig 12.21 Missing second premolars — extract primary molar early and let the first molar drift mesially.
Missing Permanent Teeth
Missing Second Premolars
Missing Permanent Teeth

A premolar that begins formation very late is likely to be very late in erupting, and may be abnormal in other ways, so careful observation and caution are required. Good premolars seldom form after the child is 8 years of age.
Missing Permanent Teeth

If the patient has an acceptable occlusion, maintaining the primary second molars is a reasonable plan, because many can be retained at least until the patient reaches the early 20s or beyond Fig 12.16 .
Missing Permanent Teeth

Some reduction of their mesiodistal width often is needed to improve the interdigitation of the posterior teeth, but if this is done, there is a risk of resorption of the mesiodistal diverging roots of the primary molar when they contact the adjacent permanent tooth roots.
Missing Permanent Teeth
Even if eventual replacement of the primary molar with an implant or bridge is required, keeping the primary molar as long as possible is an excellent way to maintain alveolar bone in that area.
Missing Permanent Teeth

If the space, profile, and jaw relationships are good or somewhat protrusive, it can be advantageous to extract primary second molars that have no successor at age 7 to 9 and allow the first molars to drift mesially Fig 12.17 . "The pattern of drift is highly variable and unpredictable"
Missing Permanent Teeth

Unless the second premolars are missing in all quadrants, it may be necessary to extract teeth in the opposing arch to reach a near-ideal Class I occlusion. The molar relationship itself is not a problem, but later overeruption of unopposed second molars may become one.
Missing Permanent Teeth

If only one primary molar is missing, unless there has been true unilateral space loss or there is considerable crowding on the contralateral side, restorative rather than conventional orthodontic resolution of the problem is usually indicated.
Missing Permanent Teeth

Another solution to missing second premolars is to combine hemisectioning of the primary tooth and pulp therapy so that the first permanent molar is protracted into the primary molar space without loss of alveolar bone from a more long-standing extraction.
Missing Permanent Teeth
Fig 12.23 Missing maxillary lateral — the erupting canine spontaneously substitutes (generates bone).
Missing Permanent Teeth
Fig 12.24 Closing/retaining a central diastema to maximize mesial drift of the erupting canines.
Missing Permanent Teeth
Missing Maxillary Lateral Incisors
Missing Permanent Teeth
Long-term retention of primary laterals, in contrast to primary molars, is almost never an acceptable plan.
Missing Permanent Teeth

In some patients, the erupting permanent canine resorbs the primary lateral incisor and spontaneously substitutes for the missing lateral incisor, which means that the primary canine has no successor and is "sometimes" retained Fig 12.19 .
Missing Permanent Teeth

Less often, the primary lateral is retained when the permanent canine erupts in its normal position. This usually means that the lateral incisor space is reduced to the size of the primary lateral incisor and the remaining primary incisor is unesthetic.
Missing Permanent Teeth
When the lateral incisors are missing, there are two possible sequelae:
Missing Permanent Teeth

Having the permanent canine erupt in the position of a congenitally missing lateral incisor is advantageous , whether or not the ultimate treatment is substitution of the canine for the lateral or opening space for a prosthetic lateral replacement, because its eruption in that area generates the formation of alveolar bone .
Missing Permanent Teeth

If space closure "canine substitution" is the goal and the primary lateral incisors are replaced by the permanent canines as they erupt, little immediate attention in the mixed dentition is necessary. Sometimes the absence of lateral incisors causes a large diastema to develop between the permanent central incisors. To maximize mesial drift of the erupting permanent canines, this diastema can be closed and retained Fig 12.20 .
Missing Permanent Teeth
Later in the transition to the permanent dentition, the primary canines should be extracted if they are not resorbing, so that some spontaneous closure of the canine space can occur Fig 12.21 .
Missing Permanent Teeth

This space closure option is best when the incisors are slightly protrusive and the molars are tending toward Class II "reciprocal space closure can be employed between the anterior and posterior teeth".
Missing Permanent Teeth
Space closure is usually avoided when the patients have a Class III tendency , because of the possibility of inadvertently creating an anterior crossbite.
Missing Permanent Teeth
Fig 12.25 Selective removal of primary teeth to allow spontaneous canine-space closure.
Missing Permanent Teeth
Autotransplantation
Missing Permanent Teeth

Teeth can be transplanted from one position to another in the same mouth with a good prognosis for long-term success, if this is done when the transplanted tooth has approximately two-thirds to three-fourths (just erupted) of its root formed . This means that the decision for autotransplantation must be made during the mixed dentition.
Missing Permanent Teeth
Transplantation is most commonly used to move premolars into the location of missing maxillary incisors .
Missing Permanent Teeth
For replacement of a maxillary lateral incisor, the mandibular first premolar has the best crown and root form and often is preferred if it is available.
Missing Permanent Teeth
Autotransplantation also can be used to replace missing first molars with third molars.
Missing Permanent Teeth

A combination of careful surgical intervention and positioning of the transplant, 3 months of healing , followed by light orthodontic forces to achieve final tooth position, and restorative treatment to recontour the crown of the transplanted tooth can result in long-term functional and esthetic success. The success rate with this type of treatment is high and predictable.
IV Localized Moderate-to-Severe Crowding (>3 mm)
Localized Moderate-to-Severe Crowding (>3 mm)
Fig 12.28 Midline shift corrected with a supportive lingual arch + coil spring before the canines erupt.
Localized Moderate-to-Severe Crowding (>3 mm)

In a posterior quadrant of the dental arches, this is most likely the result of severe space loss after early loss of a primary molar or ectopic eruption. Typically this prevents eruption of a succedaneous tooth, usually a second premolar.
Localized Moderate-to-Severe Crowding (>3 mm)

If there is enough space in other areas of the dental arches and no indication that comprehensive orthodontics will be needed in the near future, it is often sensible to extract the impacted tooth and close the space . This takes less time than regaining space and encouraging eruption of the impacted tooth.
Localized Moderate-to-Severe Crowding (>3 mm)

If space regaining is the goal after careful weighing of the options, the biomechanical issues are sizable and include unilateral space opening without disruption of the rest of the arch or occlusion.
Localized Moderate-to-Severe Crowding (>3 mm)

In the anterior portion of the arch, the most common localized problem of this type is a shift of the mandibular dental midline . If the midline has moved and no permanent teeth will be extracted, midline correction is needed before the remaining permanent teeth erupt in asymmetric positions and localized crowding becomes worse. "before the canines erupt"
Localized Moderate-to-Severe Crowding (>3 mm)
This is most successfully accomplished by using a supportive lingual arch to maintain molar symmetry and control, bonding of the incisors, and correction of the midline with a coil spring Fig 12.24 .
Localized Moderate-to-Severe Crowding (>3 mm)
In some cases, disking or extraction of a primary canine or molar will be required to provide the necessary room to reestablish the midlines and space.
V Generalized Moderate and Severe Crowding
Generalized Moderate and Severe Crowding
Fig 12.29 Fixed appliance for early correction of irregular / lingually-positioned lower incisors.
Generalized Moderate and Severe Crowding
Fig 12.30 Gaining arch length with a multiple bonded/banded appliance + compressed coil spring.
Generalized Moderate and Severe Crowding
Expansion Versus Extraction in Mixed Dentition Treatment
Generalized Moderate and Severe Crowding
Children with the largest arch length discrepancies often have reasonably well-aligned incisors in the early mixed dentition because both primary canines were lost when the lateral incisors erupted.
Generalized Moderate and Severe Crowding

Potentially severe crowding usually is obvious in the primary dentition, even before a space analysis can be completed. These children have little developmental spacing between primary incisors and occasionally some crowding in the primary dentition.
Generalized Moderate and Severe Crowding

The two major symptoms of severe crowding in the early mixed dentition are severe irregularity of the erupting permanent incisors and early loss of primary canines caused by eruption of the permanent lateral incisors.
Generalized Moderate and Severe Crowding
In the presence of severe crowding, limited mixed dentition treatment will not be sufficient and extraction has to be considered .
Generalized Moderate and Severe Crowding
Expansion for Treatment of Crowding in the Early Mixed Dentition
Generalized Moderate and Severe Crowding
A key question is whether early expansion of the arches gives more stable results than later expansion (in the early permanent dentition); there is lack of data to document its effectiveness .
Generalized Moderate and Severe Crowding
The lower incisor position is normal or somewhat retrusive
Generalized Moderate and Severe Crowding
Lips are normal or retrusive
Generalized Moderate and Severe Crowding
Overjet is adequate
Generalized Moderate and Severe Crowding
Overbite is not excessive
Generalized Moderate and Severe Crowding
There is good keratinized tissue facial to the lower incisors
Generalized Moderate and Severe Crowding
For most children with crowding and inadequate space in the early mixed dentition, some facial movement of the incisors and expansion can be accommodated, especially if:
Generalized Moderate and Severe Crowding
Maxillary dental or skeletal expansion, moving the teeth facially and/or opening the midpalatal suture.
Generalized Moderate and Severe Crowding
Mandibular buccal segment expansion by facial movement of the teeth.
Generalized Moderate and Severe Crowding
Advancement of the incisors and distal movement of the molars in either arch.
Generalized Moderate and Severe Crowding
This early expansion can involve any combination of several possibilities:
Generalized Moderate and Severe Crowding
The ability of expansion in the primary dentition to meet the challenge of anterior crowding is highly questionable and unsubstantiated .
Generalized Moderate and Severe Crowding

A sensible approach to moderate crowding in the early mixed dentition is to perform a space analysis when the incisors erupt and then begin to work toward arch expansion or extraction with the eruption of the remaining permanent teeth. Long-term holding of inadequate space is hard on the teeth and soft tissues and is not merited.
Generalized Moderate and Severe Crowding

To execute the expansion decision, placing a lingual arch after the extraction of the primary canines and ultimately using the lingual arch or another appliance to increase the arch length is a solution.
Generalized Moderate and Severe Crowding

If the incisors are rotated, severely irregular, or spaced, and early correction is felt to be important "esthetically", a fixed appliance will be needed for treatment, either in the mixed or early permanent dentition Fig 12.25 . Lower incisor teeth usually can be tipped 1 to 2 mm facially without much difficulty.
Generalized Moderate and Severe Crowding

To create substantial space and control the tooth movement, it is best to band the permanent molars, bond brackets on the incisors, and use a compressed coil spring on a labial archwire to gain the additional space Fig 12.26 .
Generalized Moderate and Severe Crowding

A somewhat more aggressive approach is to expand the upper arch transversely in the early mixed dentition, not to correct posterior crossbite but specifically to gain more space in the dental arch. (there is no credible long-term postretention evidence that early intervention to expand arches by any other name has any efficacy in providing a less crowded permanent dentition later)
Generalized Moderate and Severe Crowding
It seems unlikely that the soft tissues would react quite differently to transverse expansion at different ages.
Generalized Moderate and Severe Crowding
Fig 12.32 High-pull headgear — the most effective extraoral appliance to move molars distally.
Generalized Moderate and Severe Crowding
Fig 12.33 Intraoral distalizers built around a heavy lingual arch with an anterior acrylic anchorage pad.
Generalized Moderate and Severe Crowding
Expansion in the Late Mixed Dentition: Molar Distalization
Generalized Moderate and Severe Crowding
Transverse expansion to gain additional space can be used in the late as well as the early mixed dentition, and the previous comments also apply to the late mixed dentition.
Generalized Moderate and Severe Crowding
Less than 4-5 mm of "space deficiency" per side, with some tipping of the molars acceptable.
Generalized Moderate and Severe Crowding
Erupted maxillary anterior teeth and ideally, first premolars for anchorage.
Generalized Moderate and Severe Crowding
Normal or retrusive lip and maxillary dental position, because about one-third of the movement will be experienced as facial incisor movement.
Generalized Moderate and Severe Crowding
Likewise, overjet should be limited.
Generalized Moderate and Severe Crowding
The vertical facial dimensions should be normal or with a short-face tendency because the distal movement of the molars can open the bite.
Generalized Moderate and Severe Crowding
The overbite should be somewhat greater than normal owing to the bite opening mechanics.
Generalized Moderate and Severe Crowding

An additional approach in the late mixed dentition is to obtain additional space by repositioning molars distally . Unless TADs are used, which is not recommended before age 12 because of inadequate bone density, intraoral appliances for distal molar movement will be accompanied by facial incisor movement. With this knowledge, there are some indications for this type of treatment:
Generalized Moderate and Severe Crowding

To tip or bodily move molars distally, extraoral force via a facebow to the molars is a straightforward method (either cervical or high-pull headgear can be chosen, but high-pull headgear is an excellent option ) Fig 12.29 .
Generalized Moderate and Severe Crowding

The more the child wears the headgear, the better; 12 to 14 hours per day is minimal . Approximately 400 gm of force per side is appropriate but not particularly friendly to the teeth. The teeth should move at the rate of 1 mm per month (a cooperative child would need to wear the appliance for 3 to 5 months to obtain the 3 mm of correction that would be a typical requirement in this type of treatment).
Generalized Moderate and Severe Crowding

If bodily distal movement of one or both permanent maxillary first molars is needed to adjust molar relationships and gain space, if there are adequate anterior teeth for anchorage, if some anterior incisor movement can be tolerated, and if the overbite is adequate, several other appliances can be considered. All are built around the use of a heavy lingual arch, usually with an acrylic pad against the anterior palate to provide anchorage Fig 12.29 .
Generalized Moderate and Severe Crowding
Fig 12.34 Mandibular fixed appliance bringing the lower incisors forward to relieve crowding.
Generalized Moderate and Severe Crowding
Fig 12.35 TAD-supported molar distalization (late mixed dentition, age 12+) — the primary method now.
Generalized Moderate and Severe Crowding

In the mandibular arch, appliances that change arch dimensions can cause problems with lower second molar eruption, and use of a fixed appliance to bring the lower incisors forward may be more acceptable Fig 12.30 .
Generalized Moderate and Severe Crowding
The primary method now for distalization of molars , which can be used with children 12 years of age and older, is the use of TAD-supported molar-distalizing appliances .
Generalized Moderate and Severe Crowding
No matter how molars were moved distally, if the time before eruption of the premolars will be longer than a few months, it will be necessary to hold them back after they are repositioned.

New in 7th ed The 7th edition adds placement guidance for distalization TADs: screws placed in the palate near the midline (paramedian / the "T-Zone") are more stable, and it names the distal jet (a heavy-lingual-arch distalizer with a Nance acrylic pad) — noting ~one-third of the movement still shows as facial incisor movement even with Nance support .
VI Early (Serial) Extraction
Early (Serial) Extraction
Fig 12.36 Serial extraction for severe arch-length discrepancy (>10 mm/arch) — an adjunct to later treatment.
Early (Serial) Extraction
Simply involves the timed extraction of primary and, ultimately, permanent teeth to relieve severe crowding.
Early (Serial) Extraction
Now viewed as an adjunct to later comprehensive treatment instead of a substitute for it. "it makes later comprehensive treatment easier and often quicker".
Early (Serial) Extraction
It is best used when no skeletal problem exists and the space discrepancy is large, greater than 10 mm per arch .
Early (Serial) Extraction
If the initial space discrepancy is smaller, more residual space must be anticipated.
Early (Serial) Extraction

Although it is possible to use serial extraction to compensate for minor and moderate skeletal Class II and Class III problems (with a usual extraction sequence of only upper teeth in Class II and only lower teeth in Class III problems), this type of treatment is much more complex.
Early (Serial) Extraction

Serial extraction treatment begins in the early mixed dentition period with extraction of primary incisors if necessary, followed by extraction of the primary canines to allow eruption and alignment of the permanent incisors Fig 12.32 .
Early (Serial) Extraction

As the permanent teeth align without any appliances in place, there is usually some lingual tipping of the lower incisors , and overbite often increases during this stage. Labiolingual displacements resolve better than rotational irregularity.
Early (Serial) Extraction
After extraction of the primary canines, crowding problems are usually under control for 1 to 2 years.
Early (Serial) Extraction
The goal is to influence the permanent first premolars to erupt ahead of the canines so that they can be extracted and the canines can move distally into this space.
Early (Serial) Extraction

The maxillary premolars usually erupt before the canines, so the eruption sequence is rarely a problem in the upper arch. In the lower arch, however, the canines often erupt before the first premolars, which causes the canines to be displaced facially. To avoid this result, the lower primary first molar should be extracted when there is one-half to two-thirds root formation of the first premolar. This usually will speed up the premolar eruption.
Early (Serial) Extraction

A complication can occur if the primary first molar is extracted early and the first premolar still does not erupt before the canine. This can lead to impaction of the premolar that requires later surgical removal (If suspected, the underlying premolar can also be extracted at the same time—a procedure termed enucleation . But early enucleation can leave a bone defect that persists).
VII The Borderline Crowding Case: What Do You Do?
The Borderline Crowding Case: What Do You Do?

The wisest course of action, in most cases, is simply to keep the options open for the later comprehensive treatment that these children will need. Unless crowding is severe, maintaining leeway space during the last part of the transition to the permanent dentition increases the chance of successful nonextraction treatment.
The Borderline Crowding Case: What Do You Do?

Early extraction of primary canines often can provide space for some spontaneous alignment of permanent incisors and decrease the chance of canine impaction, but a lower lingual arch to maintain space is needed to keep the nonextraction option open when this is done.
The Borderline Crowding Case: What Do You Do?
Beyond that, the advantages of early appliance therapy are questionable and must be viewed in the context of an increased burden of treatment versus little or no additional benefit.

II Palatal Expansion in Preadolescents (Late Mixed Dentition)
Palatal Expansion in Preadolescents (Late Mixed Dentition)

A fixed jackscrew appliance (either banded or bonded) is necessary Fig 13.4 .

As many teeth as possible should be included in the anchorage unit. In the late mixed dentition, root resorption of primary molars may have reached the point at which these teeth offer little resistance, and it may be wise to wait for eruption of the first premolars before beginning expansion.

Although some studies have reported increases in vertical facial height with maxillary expansion, long-term evidence indicates this change is transitory.

A bonded appliance that covers the occlusal surface of the posterior teeth may be a better choice for a preadolescent child with a long-face tendency because it produces less mandibular rotation than a banded appliance, but in the long term, this is not totally clear. (the older the patient when maxillary expansion is done, the less likely it is that vertical changes will be recovered by subsequent growth).
Palatal Expansion in Preadolescents (Late Mixed Dentition)

In the late mixed dentition, either rapid or slow expansion is clinically acceptable. It now appears that slower activation of the expansion appliance (at the rate of <2 mm per week ) provides approximately the same ultimate result over a 10- to 12-week period as rapid expansion, with less trauma to the teeth and bones. The five-stage midpalatal suture maturation method. This, too, has not been validated.
Palatal Expansion in Adolescents (Early Permanent Dentition)
Recently, Grünheid et al tested several methods including those mentioned earlier and a novel one called the "midpalatal suture density ratio" (MSDR) from cone beam computed tomography (CBCT)
Palatal Expansion in Adolescents (Early Permanent Dentition)
Guidance for decision making regarding the state of the midpalatal suture could be gained from:
Palatal Expansion in Adolescents (Early Permanent Dentition)
Studies showed that only MSDR was significantly correlated and at high enough level to provide clinical value.
Palatal Expansion in Adolescents (Early Permanent Dentition)

Skeletal anchorage for expansion is more likely to be successful in adolescents, because retention of bone screws and plates requires a level of bone maturation that is not reached until mid-adolescence.
Palatal Expansion in Adolescents (Early Permanent Dentition)

By the end of adolescence, for some patients, there is no expansion for 1 or 2 days as each turn of the screw increases the amount of force, until the patient hears and feels suture fracture. For others, increasing pain from the amount of force against the teeth leads to giving up on expansion after that amount of time. Slow expansion would be likely to just move the teeth, not open the suture.
Palatal Expansion in Adolescents (Early Permanent Dentition)

A modern view would be that for these patients, tooth-supported expansion should not be attempted. Instead, micro-implant assisted palatal expansion (MARPE) should be used, with one activation of the screw ( 0.25 mm ) per day, rather than using heavy force against the teeth. Also surgically assisted palatal expansion (SARPE) and segmental osteotomy of the maxilla are the possibilities for the more mature patients.
IV Rapid Palatal Expansion — the Details
Rapid Palatal Expansion — the Details
Fig 13.8 Removable palatal retainer after RPE.
Rapid Palatal Expansion — the Details
With RPE at a rate of 0.5 mm per day (two quarter turns of the screw), a centimeter or more of expansion is obtained in 2 to 3 weeks , with 10 to 20 pounds of pressure across the suture.
Rapid Palatal Expansion — the Details

The space created at the midpalatal suture is filled initially by tissue fluids and hemorrhage, and at this point the expansion is highly unstable. The expansion device must be stabilized so that it cannot screw itself back shut and is left in place for 3 to 4 months . By then, new bone has filled in the space at the suture, and the skeletal expansion is stable. The midline diastema decreases and may disappear during this time. The diastema closes from a combination of skeletal relapse and tooth movement created by stretched gingival fibers, not from tooth movement alone.
Rapid Palatal Expansion — the Details

During retention, the dental expansion is maintained, but the two halves of the maxilla move back toward each other as a result of soft tissue forces, at the same time the teeth move laterally on their supporting bone.
Rapid Palatal Expansion — the Details

After the 3-month retention period, the fixed appliance can be removed, but a removable retainer that covers the palate is often needed as further insurance against early relapse Fig 13.8 . A relatively heavy, expanded maxillary archwire provides retention and support if further treatment is being accomplished immediately.
Rapid Palatal Expansion — the Details
If not, a transpalatal lingual arch or a large expanded auxiliary wire (36 or 40 mil) in the headgear tubes will help maintain expansion while a more flexible wire is used in the brackets.
V Slow Palatal Expansion — the Details
Slow Palatal Expansion — the Details
Fig 13.10 Implant-supported hinged expander — more anterior expansion.
Slow Palatal Expansion — the Details

Slow activation at the rate of less than 2 mm per week , produces about 2 pounds of pressure in a child with mixed dentition, opens the suture at a rate that is close to the maximum speed of bone formation. (The suture can show some opening on radiographs, but no midline diastema appears)
Slow Palatal Expansion — the Details

After 10 to 12 weeks, approximately the same amounts of skeletal and dental expansion are present as were seen at the same time with rapid expansion. The major difference was greater expansion across the canines in the rapid expansion group . This translated to a predicted greater arch perimeter change but similar opening of the suture posteriorly.
Slow Palatal Expansion — the Details

So with use of slow palatal expansion (one turn per day "semi-slow" or every other day) in a typical fixed expansion appliance or with use of a spring, effective expansion with minimal disruption of the suture can be achieved for a child with late mixed dentition.
Slow Palatal Expansion — the Details
Alternative Expansion Approaches (Alt-RAMEC)
Slow Palatal Expansion — the Details

Alternate rapid maxillary expansion and constriction (Alt-RAMEC) was initially devised by Liou for treatment of patients with Class III cleft palate with maxillary transverse and anteroposterior deficiency.
Slow Palatal Expansion — the Details

Alternatively expand and constrict the maxilla on a weekly basis by 1 mm per day (two turns in the morning and two turns in the evening) by using a double-hinged expander. This is done for 7 to 9 weeks, then the patient wears a facemask for maxillary protraction. The goal is to disrupt not only the midpalatal suture but also the lateral and posterior sutures.
Slow Palatal Expansion — the Details
ALT-RAMEC for protraction cannot be recommended now.
Slow Palatal Expansion — the Details

It appears that there was statistically significant transverse change to the maxilla, adjacent sutures, and soft tissues, along with approximately 1 mm of forward and downward movement at A point, but not clinically different transverse changes from what one would see with routine maxillary expansion.
Slow Palatal Expansion — the Details
Implant-Supported Expansion
Slow Palatal Expansion — the Details

Research has shown that bone screws in the palate provide better anchorage and significantly less tooth movement , with a significant difference between the palatally anchored and tooth-borne expanders.
Slow Palatal Expansion — the Details

The goal of treatment with skeletally anchored expanders is not so much to provide heavy force as to apply the force directly against the bone so that there is little or no pressure against the teeth (this provides a way to expand the maxilla in a patient with anodontia or severe hypodontia, and would maximize skeletal change and minimize tooth movement in patients with a normal dentition).
Slow Palatal Expansion — the Details
With a jackscrew attached to skeletal anchors, rapid disruption of the suture would be a disadvantage, so slow rather than rapid expansion is indicated .
Slow Palatal Expansion — the Details
There are a number of designs for expanders, including hinged ones that expand more anteriorly than posteriorly Fig 13.10
Slow Palatal Expansion — the Details
Even with skeletal anchorage, the expansion increases the light but constant pressure against the teeth from the stretched palatal mucosa and soft tissues of the cheeks.
Slow Palatal Expansion — the Details

The general guideline is that after any type of maxillary expansion, the fixed expansion device should remain in place until the new bone formed in the midline suture has had time to calcify and at least partially mature ( 3–4 months ), and that a tooth-supported retainer is needed for another 6 to 12 months after that.
Slow Palatal Expansion — the Details
With RPE, the consensus is that a tooth-supported expansion appliance should remain in place for 3 to 4 months and then can be replaced with a removable retainer or other retention device.
Slow Palatal Expansion — the Details

After slow expansion, the expansion device is not replaced with a tooth-supported retainer for another 12 weeks after expansion is completed. (Note that the time a fixed appliance is kept in place is about the same with RPE and slow expansion)
Slow Palatal Expansion — the Details
With implant-supported expansion, the guideline is about the same as with tooth-supported expansion.
VI Maxillary Expansion and Sleep-Disordered Breathing
Maxillary Expansion and Sleep-Disordered Breathing
Nasal airway and nasopharynx volume are increased by RPE (sometimes by an order of 2 when measured with CBCT in children and adolescents).
Maxillary Expansion and Sleep-Disordered Breathing
There is evidence that nasal resistance usually decreases when minimum cross-sectional area and nasal volume are improved following expansion.
Maxillary Expansion and Sleep-Disordered Breathing

For patients with sleep-disturbed breathing and no adenotonsillar hypertrophy, RPE appears to reduce Apnea–Hypopnea Index (AHI) and arousal index scores. Even in children with mild or severe tonsillar hypertrophy who showed symptoms of sleep-disordered breathing, RPE produced a decreased AHI that was sustained at 36 months .
Maxillary Expansion and Sleep-Disordered Breathing

RPE appears to have a therapeutic effect for children and adolescents with sleep apnea. Does that justify routinely expanding those with normal palatal dimensions into buccal crossbite? For those with demonstrated resistance to nasal air flow, the answer is yes. Without that, exactly how RPE would accomplish improved breathing is not clear, and routine expansion is questionable.
VII Clinical Management of Palatal Expansion Devices
Clinical Management of Palatal Expansion Devices

During the late mixed dentition years, if the primary second molars are firm, they can be banded along with the permanent first molars. Alternatively, only the permanent first molars can be banded and the supporting framework extended anteriorly, contacting the other posterior primary and erupting permanent teeth near their gingival margins.
Clinical Management of Palatal Expansion Devices
A comparison of four-band versus two-band devices showed that the four-band devices provided more transverse expansion and arch perimeter . If first premolars are available, they should be banded.
Clinical Management of Palatal Expansion Devices

A factor in the decision between a bonded and banded expander is the vertical effect of maxillary expansion. Regardless of the skeletal effect, expansion creates dental interferences as soon as the posterior teeth begin to move laterally, and the effect is to rotate the mandible downward and backward.
Clinical Management of Palatal Expansion Devices

Almost always there is a permanent increase in face height after expansion because of eruption of both maxillary and mandibular posterior teeth before a solid cusp–fossa relationship of the teeth is established.
Clinical Management of Palatal Expansion Devices

For one who had an open bite, this makes the open bite worse. In theory, the splint on top of the teeth with a bonded expander would interfere with eruption of the posterior teeth in both arches, and there is some (weak) evidence that this is the case in the short term.
Clinical Management of Palatal Expansion Devices
It may be reasonable to use a bonded expander in long-face or open bite patients who need expansion rather than a banded one.
Clinical Management of Palatal Expansion Devices
For patients with a deep bite, it seems to make no difference in the vertical effects of expansion which type of expander is used.
VIII Treatment of Transverse Mandibular Constriction
Treatment of Transverse Mandibular Constriction
Unlike the maxilla, the mandible has no midline suture . It started as two halves, but they fused early in fetal life, and the midline is solid bone.
Treatment of Transverse Mandibular Constriction
Although removable appliances that look like midpalatal expanders can be used, they can only move the teeth (and do not do that very well).
Treatment of Transverse Mandibular Constriction
Mandibular transverse expansion was impossible until distraction osteogenesis became available.
Treatment of Transverse Mandibular Constriction

There still is a limitation: The expansion is much greater anteriorly than in the molar region, and the condyles rotate slightly but do not move laterally. Fortunately, this amount of condylar rotation is tolerated without creating any problems.
IX Restriction of Excessive Transverse Growth
Restriction of Excessive Transverse Growth
Restriction of transverse growth in both jaws is exceptionally difficult, almost impossible .
Restriction of Excessive Transverse Growth
Lingual arch during the preadolescent period would maintain molar width but does not affect skeletal growth or arch width across the premolars and canines.
Restriction of Excessive Transverse Growth
The major problem this creates is posterior crossbite in a patient with normal maxillary arch width and very large mandibular arch width (Patients of that type usually have a wide tongue)
Restriction of Excessive Transverse Growth

Expand the maxillary arch to match the wide lower arch (that increases maxillary width more anteriorly than posteriorly, just the reverse of what is needed to match a mandibular arch that widens posteriorly)
Restriction of Excessive Transverse Growth

Tolerate the crossbite (Patients with posterior crossbite have a problem only when it forces a mandibular shift on closure, and without that, there are neither functional nor esthetic reasons for correcting it).
Restriction of Excessive Transverse Growth
That leaves the orthodontist with two options:
Restriction of Excessive Transverse Growth
A segmental maxillary osteotomy can provide more expansion posteriorly than anteriorly. That simply is not indicated for a condition that really is not a problem for the patient.
Restriction of Excessive Transverse Growth
The best option: Take that type of posterior crossbite of the problem list and tolerate it.
Class III Growth Modification
I Concepts of Class III Treatment
Concepts of Class III Treatment
Almost any combination of deficient maxillary growth and excessive mandibular growth can be found in patients with Class III malocclusion (about equally likely).
Concepts of Class III Treatment

Extraoral force could pull the growing maxilla forward if done in the early mixed dentition period, led to a great increase in treatment aimed at promoting maxillary growth. In contrast, extraoral force via a chin cup anchored against the cranium has been shown to produce more downward and backward rotation of the mandible than true growth restraint.
Concepts of Class III Treatment
Class III elastics between bone anchors above the posterior maxilla and in the anterior mandible is now the most effective and invasive growth-modifying method orthodontists have ever had .

It is known now that skeletal growth has a circadian rhythm . Most growth occurs during the evening hours when growth hormone is being secreted; active eruption of teeth occurs during the same time period, typically between 8 pm and midnight or 1 am. (To take practical advantage of this time period, it is suggested that children wear functional appliances from after the evening meal until they awaken in the morning, which should be approximately 12 hours per day ).

A good appointment schedule is to recall the child at 1 and 2 weeks after insertion for inspection of the tissues and the appliance. The treatment of these short-face Class II patients is a balance between the anteroposterior and the vertical reactions to treatment. For this to be accomplished, all vertical eruption is blocked while an appliance with the mandible advanced is used, which will create a posterior open bite when the appliance is not in place. When the Class II jaw relationship is corrected, the posterior bite block gradually is cut away from the lower molars and premolars while correct overbite is maintained anteriorly, so that slow eruption of lower posterior teeth back into occlusion can occur.

Midline Discrepancies
