Midline Discrepancies

If a dental midline discrepancy results from a skeletal asymmetry , it may be impossible to correct it orthodontically, and treatment decisions will have to be made in the light of camouflage versus surgical correction.
Midline Discrepancies

The midline often can be corrected by using asymmetric Class II (or Class III) elastic force . As a general rule, it is more effective to use Class II or Class III elastics bilaterally with heavier force on one side than to place a unilateral elastic.
Midline Discrepancies

It is also possible to combine a Class II or Class III elastic on one side with a diagonal elastic anteriorly to bring the midlines together Fig 17.2 . (only for small discrepancies because asymmetric elastic use has asymmetric vertical side effects capable of producing an unesthetic anterior occlusal plane cant)
Midline Discrepancies

Fortunately, midline discrepancies in the finishing stage usually are not this severe and are caused only by lateral displacements of maxillary or mandibular teeth that are likely to be accompanied by a mild Class II or Class III relationship on one side. In this circumstance:
Midline Discrepancies

If "functional shift" contributing to the discrepancy. The correction in this instance is to alter the transverse arch relationships (usually careful coordination of the maxillary and mandibular archwires, perhaps reinforced by a posterior cross-elastic). Occasionally, the entire maxillary arch is slightly displaced transversely relative to the mandibular arch so that with the teeth in occlusion, relationships are excellent, but there is a lateral shift to reach that position. Correction again would involve posterior cross-elastics but in a parallel pattern (i.e., from maxillary lingual to mandibular buccal on one side and the reverse on the other side).
II Tooth Size Discrepancies
Tooth Size Discrepancies

IPR is the usual strategy to compensate for discrepancies caused by excess tooth size. With tooth size deficiency, leave space between some teeth, which may or may not ultimately be closed by restorations.
Tooth Size Discrepancies
As a general guideline, a 2-mm tooth size discrepancy noted from Bolton analysis is the threshold for clinical significance.
Tooth Size Discrepancies
When IPR is part of the original treatment plan, most of the enamel reduction should be done initially, but final reduction can be deferred until the finishing stage.
Tooth Size Discrepancies
Precise finishing is easier if the buildup is done during the finishing stage of the orthodontic treatment. (It is important to verify that the root position is close to ideal before restoration)
Tooth Size Discrepancies

If the restoration is delayed until the orthodontic treatment is completed, it should be done as soon as possible after the patient is in retention. This requires an initial retainer to hold the space, and a new retainer immediately after the restoration is completed. (The main reason for waiting until after the orthodontic appliance has been removed would be to allow any gingival inflammation to resolve itself).
Tooth Size Discrepancies

Tooth size problems often are caused by small maxillary lateral incisors. Leaving a small space distal to the lateral incisor can be esthetically and functionally acceptable, but a composite resin buildup usually is the best plan for small incisors. (Two methods):
Tooth Size Discrepancies

More generalized small deficiencies can be masked by altering incisor position in any of several ways. To a limited extent, torque of the upper incisors can be used to compensate: leaving the incisors slightly more upright makes them take up less room relative to the lower arch and can be used to mask large upper incisors, whereas slightly excessive torque can partially compensate for small upper incisors.
III Root Paralleling
Root Paralleling

During space closure with the edgewise appliance, if proper moment-to-force ratios have been used, little if any root paralleling will be necessary as a finishing procedure (it is likely that some degree of root paralleling at extraction sites often will be necessary)
Root Paralleling

It is wise to obtain a panoramic radiograph when major tooth movement has been completed, to check for both root positioning errors and root resorption that might dictate ending treatment early or taking a break from the final active treatment for 3 to 4 months to allow cementum to heal.
Root Paralleling

With the 18-slot appliance, the typical finishing archwire is either 17 × 22 or 17 × 25 steel. These wires are flexible enough to engage narrow brackets even if mild tipping has occurred, and the archwire will generate the necessary root paralleling moments. To correct more severe tipping, a 17 × 25 beta-Ti (TMA) or even a 17 × 25 nickel‒titanium (M-NiTi, not superelastic A-NiTi) wire might be needed initially, with a steel archwire used for final expression of torque.
Root Paralleling

With wider 22-slot brackets with the use of sliding rather than loop mechanics to close extraction sites, there is usually even less need for root paralleling as a finishing procedure. If root-positioning is needed, steel archwires (19 × 25 steel, for instance) are much too stiff. A 21 × 25 beta-Ti wire is the best choice for a finishing archwire under most circumstances, and if significant root positioning is needed, 21 × 25 M-NiTi should be used first.
Root Paralleling

If rectangular NiTi wires are used in the finishing stage, M-NiTi (compared to A-NiTi) almost always is the better choice. Why? Because in finishing stage, appropriate stiffness at relatively small deflections , rather than range, is the primary consideration.
Root Paralleling

A root-paralleling moment is a crown-separating moment . When a full-dimension rectangular wire is placed in the maxillary arch, spaces are likely to open between the incisors in nonextraction as well as extraction cases. Tying the maxillary incisors together (with a segment of elastomeric chain from the mesial bracket of one upper lateral incisor across to the mesial bracket of the other) is necessary during finishing.

This wire's torsional stiffness is less than that of 17 × 25 steel, but the shorter interbracket distances with 22-slot twin brackets bring its performance in torsion close to that of the smaller steel wire. Braided rectangular steel wires are available in a variety of stiffnesses and can be useful in 22-slot finishing.

A solid 21 × 25 steel wire cannot be recommended because of its stiffness and the resulting extremely high forces and short range of action. If a solid steel wire of this size is used (the major reason would be surgical stabilization), it should be preceded by 21 × 25 beta-Ti.

Using light final arches must include any first- or second-order bends used in the rectangular finishing arches. It is usually unnecessary for the patient to wear light posterior vertical elastics during this settling, but they can be used if needed. These light arches will quickly settle the teeth into final occlusion and should remain in place for only a few weeks at most.

Replacing the rectangular archwires at the very end of treatment with light round arches that provide some freedom for movement of the teeth and using light vertical elastics to bring the teeth together.

The difficulty with undersized round wires at the end of treatment is that precise control of anterior teeth is lost. It was not until the 1980s that orthodontists realized the advantage of removing only the posterior part of the rectangular finishing wire, leaving the anterior segment (typically canine-to-canine) in place, and using laced elastics to bring the posterior teeth into tight occlusion Fig 17.12 . Control of Rebound and Posturing
After Class II or Class III correction, the teeth tend to rebound back toward their initial position
Control of Rebound and Posturing
In a typical patient with Class II anterior deep bite, the teeth should be taken to an end-to-end incisor relationship , with both overjet and overbite totally eliminated.
Control of Rebound and Posturing

Posturing vs Rebound: Sometimes when Class II elastic force or its equivalent is used, patients begin to posture the mandible forward so that the occlusion looks more corrected than it really is; if the appliances are removed at that point, the patient is likely to slip back toward a Class II molar relationship and increased overjet. This should not be confused with rebound, which is due only to tooth movement. Rebound is a 1- to 2-mm phenomenon; posturing can lead to 4 to 5 mm of relapse.
Control of Rebound and Posturing

When an appropriate degree of overcorrection has been achieved, the force used with the elastics should be decreased or the wear interval reduced (8 to 12 hours per day) while the elastics are continued for another appointment interval.

At that point, interarch elastics should be discontinued, 4 to 8 weeks before the orthodontic appliances are to be removed, so that changes due to rebound or posturing can be observed. If changes do occur, another period of elastics is needed.

Special Finishing Procedures to Avoid Relapse
Two major causes:
I Control of Unfavorable Growth
Control of Unfavorable Growth

Changes resulting from continued growth in a Class II, Class III, deep bite, or open bite pattern contribute to a return of the original malocclusion and in that sense constitute relapse. Controlling this type of relapse requires a continuation of active treatment after the fixed appliances have been removed.
Control of Unfavorable Growth

This "active retention" takes one of two forms. One possibility is to continue extraoral force in conjunction with orthodontic retainer. The other, which is much more acceptable to the patient, is use of a modified functional appliance rather than a conventional retainer after the completion of fixed appliance therapy. (discussed in more detail in Chapter 18 )

Control of Rebound After Tooth Movement
There are two ways to deal with this phenomenon: overtreatment and adjunctive periodontal surgery
Control of Rebound After Tooth Movement
Correction of Class II or Class III malocclusion: Overtreatment of 1 to 2 mm, elastic wear can be reinstituted if there is excessive rebound.
Control of Rebound After Tooth Movement

Crossbite correction: It should be overcorrected by at least 1 to 2 mm, doing this early in treatment should improve stability when transverse relationships are established precisely during the finishing phase.
Control of Rebound After Tooth Movement

Crowded and irregular teeth: It is wise to hold the teeth in a slightly overcorrected position for at least a few months (during the first phase of treatment). As a general rule, however, it is not wise to build this overcorrection into rectangular finishing archwires .
Control of Rebound After Tooth Movement

Rotation correction: Rotated teeth should be maintained in an overcorrected position as long as possible, but even then, these teeth are often candidates for the periodontal procedures described later.

Circumferential supracrestal fibrotomy (CSF): Developed by Edwards, cuts are made interproximally on each side of a rotated tooth and along the labial and lingual gingival margins unless, as is often the case, the labial or lingual gingiva is quite thin.

The "Papilla Split": Make an incision in the center of each gingival papilla, sparing the margin but separating the papilla from just below the margin to 1 to 2 mm below the height of the bone buccally and lingually Fig 17.18 . It is particularly indicated for esthetically sensitive areas.

Foundations
I Development of Aligner Treatment
Development of Aligner Treatment
Aligners are digitally designed custom plastic trays that move teeth in small increments from the present malocclusion toward the planned setup.
Development of Aligner Treatment

Mass production only became feasible once digital software and 3D printing were affordable. Almost no one was treated with aligners until Align Technology gained FDA clearance for Invisalign in 1998 .
Development of Aligner Treatment
Today more than 30% of orthodontic cases in the United States are treated with aligners.
Development of Aligner Treatment
Most common wear schedule: one new aligner every 7 days (10- and 14-day schedules are also used, especially when large posterior movements are planned).
Development of Aligner Treatment

In complex cases, the modern strategy is to prioritize the hardest goals first in the initial attachment design and staging (extraction-space closure, open-bite correction, the worst rotations), then address easier movements in later/refinement aligners.
II Aligners vs Fixed Appliances
Aligners vs Fixed Appliances
The diagnosis and treatment goals do not change with aligners — the same biology of tooth movement, the same use and limits of growth, and the same alveolar boundary conditions apply.
Aligners vs Fixed Appliances

What changes is the biomechanics of force delivery : force comes from a plastic with a much smaller elastic range than a metal archwire, and that plastic suffers time-dependent decay of force (stress relaxation) .
Aligners vs Fixed Appliances
The biological (PDL) response is identical ; only the mechanical delivery differs.
III Benefits & Limitations
Benefits & Limitations
The three benefits that drove aligner innovation: esthetics, easier oral hygiene, and no food restrictions .
Benefits & Limitations
Esthetics: can be near-invisible, but a large print layer size leaves a "stair-step" effect , and anterior attachments are visible — warn the patient up front.
Benefits & Limitations

Oral hygiene: removable for brushing/flossing; a systematic review showed lower plaque index and probing depths. Decalcification risk is NOT eliminated — drinking acidic/sugary liquids with aligners in, or reseating dirty aligners, causes a decay pattern different from braces: widespread, including cusp tips and incisal edges .
Benefits & Limitations
No food restrictions: removed for eating, avoiding the breakage/setbacks of fixed appliances.
Benefits & Limitations

Bite propulsion: two layers of posterior plastic prop the bite open and tend to intrude posterior teeth — helpful for open-bite control and for avoiding the inadvertent extrusion that fixed appliances cause in high-angle cases.
Benefits & Limitations
Unusual tooth anatomy is handled more consistently than with conventional bracket placement.

Treatment Goals & the Virtual Setup
Cases sort into efficiently treated , less predictable , and poor candidates without a hybrid technique (summarised in Table 18.2).
Treatment Goals & the Virtual Setup
A digital setup lets you simulate the final occlusion before starting — valuable for Bolton/tooth-size discrepancies and unusual anatomy.

Erupting Teeth in Adolescents
Aligners freeze tooth anatomy at the moment of the scan. Eruption "wells" (voids) can be built in to allow passive eruption.
Erupting Teeth in Adolescents
If teeth erupt further, a new scan is needed for adaptation; fully engaging an erupting tooth is slow.
Erupting Teeth in Adolescents
When goals allow, delaying until full eruption is the most efficient approach.
VI Management Differences, Cost & Compliance
Management Differences, Cost & Compliance
A complete digital setup to the ideal finish is made at the start .
Management Differences, Cost & Compliance
Minor tracking errors are fixed by better wear, more time in the current tray, or relieving binding contacts .
Management Differences, Cost & Compliance
Removable design → fewer emergencies (no broken wires/loose brackets; occasional attachment re-bond).
Management Differences, Cost & Compliance
Significant root movement is hard — which is also a management benefit (less unwanted root movement).
Management Differences, Cost & Compliance
Because the plan is fixed at the start, longer visit intervals are possible — most practices see aligner patients every 8–16 weeks .
Management Differences, Cost & Compliance
AI remote-monitoring can catch tracking issues early but is still new and inconsistent in studies.
Management Differences, Cost & Compliance
Cost: outsourced fabrication is expensive, partly offset by fewer visits / less chair time.

Exam pearl — compliance Compliance is the dominant challenge in adolescent aligner therapy. Interrupted wear causes fit problems and delay; poor compliance forces a switch to braces in roughly 1 of 6 patients (across two studied offices).
Intra-Arch Tooth Movements
VII Spacing
Spacing

Aligners are good for simple spacing . Many spacing cases also have proclination, so the ideal movement is tipping teeth upright — which suits aligners (tipping is easy, root movement/couples are hard ).
Spacing
Maximize surface contact with the tooth; in spacing, this means engaging the interproximal area until the space closes.
Spacing
If the resulting bite-deepening is undesirable → posterior attachments to seat the aligner and intrude the anterior teeth.
Spacing
If extrusion is wanted (mild anterior open bite) → anterior attachments to keep front teeth seated.
Spacing
Attachments are added when vertical control or root tip is needed. Tipping incisors lingually produces relative (geometric) extrusion :
Spacing
For larger spaces needing bodily movement , use a broad or split (two-part) attachment to create an effective couple.
Spacing
Staging: close spaces evenly and finish them near the end ; if one contact closes early next to a large space, it can help to keep it open until the big space closes.
Spacing

Complete space closure is harder than with braces (scan inaccuracy interproximally, production error, low-stiffness plastic). Aids: over-correction aligners (a "virtual elastic chain" — but they can unseat or over-intrude if worn on already-closed contacts) and measuring residual space with a leaf gauge , then planning fully closed contacts in refinement.
VIII Mild Crowding & Rotations
Mild Crowding & Rotations

With braces, the archwire naturally creates space and guides arch dimension. With aligners, each tray dictates incisor position and arch width — space must be deliberately created and verified above the system's known error.
Mild Crowding & Rotations

Teeth that "barely pass" on screen will bind in the mouth . Prevent it with programmed spaces during derotation / "zero collision tolerance," floss-check contacts at every visit, and IPR/restage as needed.
Mild Crowding & Rotations

Rotations: aligners apply force perpendicular to the tooth surface , so they rotate incisors well but round teeth (canines, premolars) poorly — the moment arm to the center of resistance is tiny. Over-correction of rotations is often required.
Mild Crowding & Rotations
Maxillary lateral incisors tend to intrude during derotation → place seating attachments on them.
IX Complex Crowding
Complex Crowding

As rotation/crowding worsen, follow the basics — good attachment design + deliberate space creation . Severe rotations may need an adjunct: bonded buttons with elastics or power chain for a direct rotational moment while the aligner controls the other planes.

Exam pearl — the 50% rule For all intra-arch movements, the clinical result differs from the plan — from stress relaxation, compliance, or an imperfect force system. Research estimates only ~ 50% of planned movement is realized , so refinements are the norm (the aligner equivalent of repositioning a bracket).
Arch-Level Correction · A-P · Vertical · Transverse
X Class II Correction
Class II Correction
Strategic options match fixed appliances (dento-alveolar movement, differential growth, camouflage — see Ch 16); only force application differs.
Class II Correction
Elastics are the usual tool — attached directly to the aligner or to buttons . Outcome mirrors braces-and-elastics; only the tool differs.
Class II Correction

Functional appliances can precede or be built into aligners (Herbst/MARA before aligners, Twin Block then aligners, or the Invisalign MA system). Research shows the change is mostly dento-alveolar, not skeletal .
Class II Correction
Extractions: upper-premolar camouflage is possible but space closure is hard with aligners — many extraction cases are better in fixed appliances.

Critical — incisor torque Class II mechanics tip maxillary incisors lingually . Far less root movement occurs than planned, so torque must be over-corrected in the virtual setup to hold the final incisor inclination.
XI Class III Correction
Class III Correction
Mechanics mirror Class II with reversed force vectors (aligner cuts or buttons for elastics).
Class III Correction

Best scenario: late Class III growth that drives a developing negative overjet after comprehensive treatment — aligners with minimal movement + Class III elastics predictably regain positive overjet when only limited movement is needed.
Class III Correction
IPR to camouflage: best for mandibular tooth-size excess with molars near Class I.

Exam pearl — IPR math Each 1 mm of retraction needs ~ 2 mm of IPR (1 mm per side). A ¼-cusp (≈2 mm) Class III therefore needs ~ 4 mm of total IPR — which quickly exceeds what is reasonable in more severe cases (then consider lower-incisor extraction or surgery — see Ch 21/22).
XII Open-Bite Correction
Open-Bite Correction

Aligners are useful in mild–moderate open bite : posterior plastic supports posterior intrusion and allows anterior extrusion , with fewer of the inadvertent posterior-extrusion side effects that re-open the bite.
Open-Bite Correction
Direct extrusion along the long axis leaves little surface to grip — so move teeth labially first to create surface, then retract + extrude together .
Caveat — express ~⅔ Posterior intrusion / anterior extrusion only partly express — roughly two-thirds ( ~67% ) of the programmed bite closure . Build over-correction into the plan.
XIII Deep-Bite Correction
Deep-Bite Correction

Deep bite is harder than open bite with aligners — it is difficult to intrude anteriors or extrude posteriors while occluding on two layers of plastic — yet it is a very common required movement (post-treatment relapse of lower crowding / upper spacing).
Deep-Bite Correction
Design for strong posterior aligner retention ; even then, leveling forces are weaker than fixed appliances generate.
Deep-Bite Correction
Bite ramps on the lingual of the maxillary anterior teeth remove posterior occlusal contacts and allow lower-premolar extrusion; place on selected teeth as needed.

Exam pearl — the 33% rule Multiple studies found only ~ 33% of predicted deep-bite correction expresses clinically — the least predictable vertical movement . Over-correct substantially, and remember deep-bite leveling depends on force over the whole arch (why fixed appliances add 2nd molars and stiff wires).
XIV Transverse Correction
Transverse Correction
Options: fixed expander, aligner-alone with careful attachments, or inter-arch (cross) elastics.
Transverse Correction
Skeletal width in an adolescent → fixed RPE gives the most consistent correction (see Ch 13). After expansion, stabilize with a bonded TPA or simply avoid the supporting teeth in early aligners.
Transverse Correction
Bone-borne MARPE can be used in older adolescents and left in place during aligner wear .
Transverse Correction

Dental (or mild-skeletal compensation) → aligners alone ; easier when un-crossed teeth flank the crossbite tooth. Cross elastics help but watch extrusive side effects (better controlled with aligners due to the temporary posterior intrusion).

Exam pearl A University of Minnesota study comparing digital setups to real outcomes found maxillary transverse change is often not fully achieved with aligners — over-correction is required for every transverse plan .
Hybrid & Special Situations
XV Hybrid Treatment & Impacted/Ectopic Teeth
Hybrid Treatment & Impacted/Ectopic Teeth
Hybrid = inter-arch elastics for the bite, intra-arch elastics for displaced teeth, buttons + chains for severe rotations, partial fixed appliances, or short-duration full braces.
Hybrid Treatment & Impacted/Ectopic Teeth
Method 1 — patient-worn elastics from a hook on the impacted tooth to the aligner (needs compliance and adequate span).
Hybrid Treatment & Impacted/Ectopic Teeth
Method 2 — limited fixed attachments (transpalatal arch, TAD, or limited brackets) for a more consistent force system.
Hybrid Treatment & Impacted/Ectopic Teeth
Impacted/ectopic teeth: an aligner cannot apply force beneath the gingiva. Two hybrid methods:
Treatment of choice These methods are reserved for when fixed appliances are refused or impossible . For impacted teeth, fixed appliances remain the treatment of choice .
XVI Complex Space Closure / Root Uprighting
Complex Space Closure / Root Uprighting
Severely tipped lower second molar: uprighting needs force on the mesial surface (inaccessible to an aligner) — limited fixed appliances are usually more efficient.
Complex Space Closure / Root Uprighting
Large space closure needing TAD anchorage: limited fixed appliances are often more efficient.
Complex Space Closure / Root Uprighting
Protraction of 2nd/3rd molars to compensate for a missing first molar.
Complex Space Closure / Root Uprighting
When most of a case suits aligners but a few movements don't, hybrid treatment is reasonable:
XVII Finishing Cases Started in Fixed Appliances
Finishing Cases Started in Fixed Appliances
Braces are sometimes removed before goals are met — white-spot lesions , a request before a special event (prom, photos), or burnout . Aligner finishing can complete the remaining goals.
Caveat Aligner finishing relies on good compliance — which may be exactly what was lacking in the scenarios that led to early brace removal.
Strategies for Success
XVIII Digital Setup & Staging
Digital Setup & Staging

Simulations have no biological limits — any crowding can "correct" without extraction, any open bite "close" non-surgically. The clinician supplies the realistic goals; because movements under-express, over-correction is built into the setup (typical amounts in Table 18.3).
Digital Setup & Staging
Teeth need space to move — keep contacts open for rotation/extrusion; binding stops movement (check contacts each visit).
Digital Setup & Staging
Surface area & retention are king — large attachments where needed; slightly open contacts; rescan if tissue levels change.
Digital Setup & Staging
Move smoothly using all aligners — don't delay the most-displaced tooth to mid-treatment, and don't run every movement at max speed; both hurt tracking.
Digital Setup & Staging
In complex cases, prioritize select movements early , then refine the smaller ones with purpose-designed attachments.
Digital Setup & Staging
Key staging principles:
XIX Attachment Design
Attachment Design

"Optimized" attachments (mainly Invisalign) combine a bonded attachment with aligner-fabrication modifications (e.g., extra activation for a rotation plus clearance on the far side). They must be removed and re-added at refinement to keep that activation; any attachment left on is simply read as the new tooth geometry.
Attachment Design
Value each attachment — many movements work without one; avoid putting an attachment on nearly every tooth.
Attachment Design
Aligners do not load only the attachment — they apply force across multiple tooth surfaces; sometimes an attachment's only job is to improve seating.
XX Case Monitoring & Compliance
Case Monitoring & Compliance
Patients usually receive 6–12 aligners , each worn ~1 week. Educate them on what to watch for, or use virtual photo monitoring.
Case Monitoring & Compliance
Minor tracking issues: check contacts, do light IPR, add time in the stage; specially designed pliers can dimple the plastic to add pressure or improve retention and recapture a non-tracking tooth.
Case Monitoring & Compliance
Significant tracking issues → new scan to reset the staging and refine the plan.

Why Is Retention Necessary?
Why Is Retention Necessary?
Fig 19.1 The major causes of relapse: elastic recoil of gingiva, cheek/lip/tongue pressure, and differential jaw growth.
Why Is Retention Necessary?
Most orthodontic treatment results are potentially unstable, and therefore retention is necessary for three major reasons that are summarized in Fig 18.1
I Reorganization of the Periodontal and Gingival Tissues
Reorganization of the Periodontal and Gingival Tissues

Even if tooth movement stops before the orthodontic appliance is removed, restoration of the normal periodontal architecture will not occur as long as a tooth is strongly splinted to its neighbors, as when it is attached to a rigid orthodontic archwire. For that reason, holding the teeth with passive archwires cannot be considered the beginning of retention.
Reorganization of the Periodontal and Gingival Tissues

Bone bending as each tooth is displaced slightly relative to its neighbor as the patient chews is necessary for recovery from the splinting effect of a fixed orthodontic appliance. Once the teeth can respond individually to the forces of mastication, reorganization of the PDL occurs over a 3- to 4-month period , and the slight mobility present at appliance removal disappears.
Reorganization of the Periodontal and Gingival Tissues
Shock-absorbing properties of the periodontal system
Reorganization of the Periodontal and Gingival Tissues
Prolonged imbalances in tongue‒lip‒cheek pressures or pressures from gingival fibers that are resisted by "active stabilization" due to PDL metabolism
Reorganization of the Periodontal and Gingival Tissues
This PDL reorganization is important for stability because of the periodontal contribution to the equilibrium:
Reorganization of the Periodontal and Gingival Tissues

The disruption of the PDL produced by orthodontic tooth movement probably has little effect on stabilization against occlusal forces (short intermittent?), but it reduces or eliminates the active stabilization.
Reorganization of the Periodontal and Gingival Tissues

The gingival fiber networks are also disturbed by orthodontic tooth movement and must remodel to accommodate the new tooth positions. Both collagenous and elastic fibers are present in the gingiva, and Reitan showed many years ago that the reorganization of both occurs more slowly than in the PDL.
Reorganization of the Periodontal and Gingival Tissues

Within 4 to 6 months , the collagenous fiber networks within the gingiva have normally completed their reorganization, but the elastic supracrestal fibers remodel extremely slowly and can still displace a tooth more than a year after removal of an orthodontic appliance (fiberotomy is useful)
Reorganization of the Periodontal and Gingival Tissues

Teeth require daily (essentially full-time) retention after comprehensive orthodontic treatment for the first 3 to 4 months after a fixed orthodontic appliance is removed. But that retainers are reasonably effective if worn at level of 8-12 hours per day .
Reorganization of the Periodontal and Gingival Tissues

To promote reorganization of the PDL, the teeth should be free to flex individually during mastication, as the alveolar bone bends in response to heavy occlusal loads during mastication. This requirement can be met by removable appliance worn regularly except during meals or by a fixed retainer that is not too rigid.
Reorganization of the Periodontal and Gingival Tissues

Because of slow response of the gingival fibers, retention should be continued for at least 12 months if the teeth were quite irregular initially but can be reduced to part-time after 3 to 4 months. After approximately 12 months, it may be possible to discontinue retention in nongrowing patients, but gradual discontinuation of the appliances can test this process and the stability.
Reorganization of the Periodontal and Gingival Tissues

More precisely, in the absence of growth, the teeth should be stable by 1 to 2 years after treatment if they ever will be. Some patients who are not growing will require permanent retention because of lip, cheek, and tongue pressures that are too great for active stabilization to balance.
Reorganization of the Periodontal and Gingival Tissues
Patient will continue to grow usually need retention until growth has slowed to the low levels that characterize adult life.
Reorganization of the Periodontal and Gingival Tissues
This timetable for soft tissue recovery from orthodontic treatment outlines the principles of retention against intra-arch instability. These are:
II Occlusal Changes Related to Growth
Occlusal Changes Related to Growth
Fig 19.5 Deep-bite retention — upper retainer with a bite plane; lower incisors meet the baseplate, posteriors not separated.
Occlusal Changes Related to Growth
Fig 19.7 Open-bite retention — palate-covering retainer with posterior bite blocks controls eruption.
Occlusal Changes Related to Growth

Skeletal problems in all three planes of space tend to recur if growth continues. Transverse growth is completed first , which means that long-term transverse changes are less of a problem clinically than changes from late anteroposterior and vertical growth.
Occlusal Changes Related to Growth
In late adolescence, continued growth bite problem in the first place is a major cause of recurrence after orthodontic treatment and requires careful management during retention.
Occlusal Changes Related to Growth
Retention When a Class II Growth Pattern Exists
Occlusal Changes Related to Growth
Recurrence of a Class II relationship must result from some combination of tooth movement (short-term) and differential growth of the maxilla relative to the mandible (long-term).
Occlusal Changes Related to Growth

Even with good retention, 1 to 2 mm of anteroposterior change caused by adjustments in tooth position is likely to occur after treatment, particularly if Class II elastics were employed (lower incisor far forward in unstable position "lip pressure"). This change occurs relatively quickly after active treatment stops.
Occlusal Changes Related to Growth
As a general guideline, if more than 2 mm of forward repositioning of the lower incisors occurred during treatment, permanent retention is very likely to be required. (remember Fig 7.5 )
Occlusal Changes Related to Growth
First, if headgear was used in treatment, is to continue its use on a reduced basis (at night, for instance) in conjunction with a retainer to hold the teeth in alignment.
Occlusal Changes Related to Growth

The other method is to use a functional appliance of the activator or Bionator type to hold both tooth position and the occlusal relationship. (the construction bite for the functional appliance is taken without any mandibular advancement "Passive")
Occlusal Changes Related to Growth
The slower long-term recurrence that occurs in some patients results primarily from differential jaw growth. This can be controlled in either of two ways:
Occlusal Changes Related to Growth
Use of a functional appliance as an extra retainer from the beginning makes sense for a patient with a severe growth problem.
Occlusal Changes Related to Growth

For patients with less severe problems, it may be more rational to use only conventional maxillary and mandibular retainers initially and replace them with a functional appliance to be worn at night if relapse is beginning to occur after a few months.
Occlusal Changes Related to Growth

A potential difficulty is that the functional appliance will be worn only part-time (at night), and daytime retainers of conventional design also will be needed to control tooth position during the first few months.
Occlusal Changes Related to Growth

This type of retention is often needed for 24 months or more after the daytime retainer has been discontinued in patients who had a skeletal problem initially. The guideline is this: the more severe the initial Class II problem and the younger the patient at the end of active treatment, the more likely that either headgear or a functional appliance will be needed during retention.
Occlusal Changes Related to Growth
Retention When a Class III Growth Pattern Exists
Occlusal Changes Related to Growth
Recurrence from continuing mandibular growth is very likely and extremely difficult to control .
Occlusal Changes Related to Growth

Applying a restraining force to the mandible, as from a chin cup, is not nearly as effective in a patient with Class III malocclusion as a modified functional appliance in a patient with Class II issues.
Occlusal Changes Related to Growth
If face height is normal or excessive after orthodontic treatment and recurrence occurs from mandibular growth, surgical correction after the growth has expressed itself may be the only answer.
Occlusal Changes Related to Growth
In mild Class III problems, a positioner may be enough to maintain the occlusal relationships during posttreatment growth.
Occlusal Changes Related to Growth
Retention After Deep Bite Correction
Occlusal Changes Related to Growth

Accomplished most readily by using a removable upper retainer made so that the lower incisors will encounter the baseplate of the retainer if they begin to slip vertically downward. The retainer does not separate the posterior teeth. Fig 18.5
Occlusal Changes Related to Growth

A maxillary removable retainer with a bite plane often is needed for several years after fixed appliance orthodontics is completed. Bite depth can be maintained by wearing the retainer only at night, after stability in other regards has been achieved.
Occlusal Changes Related to Growth
Retention After Anterior Open Bite Correction
Occlusal Changes Related to Growth
Relapse into anterior open bite can occur by any combination of depression of the incisors and elongation of the molars .
Occlusal Changes Related to Growth

If thumb-sucking continues after orthodontic treatment, relapse is all but guaranteed. Tongue habits, particularly tongue-thrust swallowing, are often blamed for relapse into open bite, but the evidence to support this contention is not convincing.
Occlusal Changes Related to Growth
In patients who do not place some object between the front teeth, return of open bite is almost always the result of elongation of the posterior teeth, particularly the upper molars .
Occlusal Changes Related to Growth
Controlling eruption of the upper molars therefore is the key to retention in patients with an open bite.
Occlusal Changes Related to Growth

The preferred method to do that is a palate-covering removable appliance (modified Hawley retainer) with bite blocks between the posterior teeth Fig 18.7 . "soft tissue stretch" "advantage: control lower teeth as well"
Occlusal Changes Related to Growth
High-pull headgear to the upper molars, in conjunction with a standard removable retainer to maintain tooth position, also can be effective. "control only upper teeth"
Occlusal Changes Related to Growth

Vacuum-formed retainers with thickened plastic over the posterior occlusal surfaces may be useful for retention of these patients. (More trials are needed to clarify their usefulness in retaining open bite cases)
Occlusal Changes Related to Growth
Retention of Lower Incisor Alignment
Occlusal Changes Related to Growth

Continued mandibular growth (late mandibular growth) in normal or Class III patients is strongly associated with crowding of the lower incisors (lip pressure). Also accompanies the downward and backward rotation of the mandible seen in skeletal open bite problems.
Occlusal Changes Related to Growth
It makes sense therefore to routinely retain lower incisor alignment until mandibular growth has declined to adult levels (i.e., until the late teens in girls and into the early 20s in boys ).
III Timing of Retention: Summary
Timing of Retention: Summary
Essentially full-time for the first 3 to 4 months (removable retainers should be removed while eating).
Timing of Retention: Summary
Continued on a part-time basis for at least 12 months for remodeling of gingival tissues.
Timing of Retention: Summary
If significant growth remains, continued part-time until completion of growth.
Timing of Retention: Summary
Lower incisors will require retention at least until late teens.
Removable Retainers
I Hawley Retainer (preferred upper)
Hawley Retainer (preferred upper)
Fig 19.8 Hawley retainer — canine-to-canine labial bow + molar clasps; palate gives a bite plane.
Hawley Retainer (preferred upper)
Because it covers the palate, it automatically provides a potential bite plane to control overbite.
Hawley Retainer (preferred upper)
The ability of this retainer to provide some tooth movement "active" was an important asset when bands are removed "to close spaces caused by bands".
Hawley Retainer (preferred upper)

It is important that the retainer allow the posterior teeth to settle into occlusion after appliance removal, and slightly trimming the acrylic lingual to the posterior teeth so that an eruption path exists is an important clinical adjustment of the Hawley retainer.
Hawley Retainer (preferred upper)
The standard Hawley labial bow extends across a first premolar extraction space, tending to wedge it open.
Hawley Retainer (preferred upper)
A common modification of the Hawley retainer is a bow soldered to the buccal section of Adams clasps on the first molars so that the action of the bow helps hold the extraction site closed.
Hawley Retainer (preferred upper)

Alternative designs for extraction cases are to wrap the labial bow around the entire arch, using circumferential clasps on second molars for retention, or to bring the labial wire from the baseplate between the lateral incisor and canine and bend or solder a wire extension distally to control the canines. (does not provide an active force to keep an extraction space closed but avoids having the wire cross through the extraction site and gives positive control of canines that were labially positioned initially)
Hawley Retainer (preferred upper)
In extraction cases: Fig 18.8
Hawley Retainer (preferred upper)
A circumferential clasps on the terminal molar may be preferred over the more effective Adams clasp if the occlusion is tight
Hawley Retainer (preferred upper)
For any patient who once had an excessive overbite, light contact of the lower incisors against the baseplate of the retainer is desired.
II Wraparound (Clip) Retainers (preferred lower)
Wraparound (Clip) Retainers (preferred lower)
Fig 19.10 Mandibular wraparound / 'spring (clip)' retainer — wire-reinforced; prevents spaces reopening.
Wraparound (Clip) Retainers (preferred lower)
Consists of a plastic bar (usually wire-reinforced) along the labial and lingual surfaces of the teeth.
Wraparound (Clip) Retainers (preferred lower)
Retainers of this type are particularly indicated when the goal is to prevent spaces from reopening . (Primary indication)
Wraparound (Clip) Retainers (preferred lower)
Maxillary anterior clip-on retainers can be useful in adults with long clinical crowns, but usually would not be tolerated in younger patients because of occlusal interferences.
Wraparound (Clip) Retainers (preferred lower)

In a mandibular extraction case, usually it is a good idea to extend a canine-to-canine wraparound distally on the lingual aspect only to the central groove of the first molar Fig 18.10 . This is called a Moore retainer .
III Clear (Vacuum-Formed) Retainers
Clear (Vacuum-Formed) Retainers
The most widely used retainer for the maxillary arch.
Clear (Vacuum-Formed) Retainers
In terms of effectiveness of maintaining incisor alignment, there is no difference between these retainers and a bonded wire retainer.
Clear (Vacuum-Formed) Retainers

The thickness of the material over the occlusal surface of the teeth can become a problem, because separation of the posterior teeth in occlusion may develop. The combination of a vacuum-formed upper and a fixed lower retainer is better than maxillary and mandibular vacuum-formed retainers.
Clear (Vacuum-Formed) Retainers
The retainer maintains alignment but does not control deepening of the bite as well as a palate-covering Hawley retainer.
Clear (Vacuum-Formed) Retainers
After 6 to 9 months , a vacuum-formed retainer tends to crack and discolor to the point that it has to be replaced.
Clear (Vacuum-Formed) Retainers
There are limitations to vacuum-formed retainers:

New evidence (7th) The 7th adds that patients using a clear retainer report greater satisfaction with their treatment than those with other retainer types and are more likely to wear it regularly (better compliance); newer materials also have better long-term survival .

New caution (7th) Using the final active aligner as a retainer is not as effective as other retainers — the active-aligner material is more flexible and less durable; a more rigid material designed specifically as a retainer is preferred .
IV Positioners as Retainers
Positioners as Retainers
Positioners now are used primarily as finishing devices for patients with an open bite.
Positioners as Retainers
For patient with a tendency towards Class III relapse, a positioner made with the jaws rotated somewhat downward and backward may be useful.
Positioners as Retainers
A positioner with the teeth set in a slightly exaggerated "supernormal" from the original malocclusion can be used for patient with a skeletal Class II or open bite growth pattern.
Positioners as Retainers
It is less effective in controlling growth than a functional appliance or nighttime headgear.
Positioners as Retainers

Positioner does have one major advantage over a standard removable or wraparound retainer, though; it maintains the occlusal relationships as well as intra-arch tooth positions . (can be a consideration for patients with an unfavorable growth pattern)
Fixed Retainers (Three major indications)
I Maintenance of Lower Incisor Position During Late Growth
Maintenance of Lower Incisor Position During Late Growth
Fig 19.12 Bonded canine-to-canine lower retainer (28–30-mil), fabricated on a cast with a carrier.
Maintenance of Lower Incisor Position During Late Growth
Fig 19.13 Place a bonded lingual retainer immediately after appliance removal.
Maintenance of Lower Incisor Position During Late Growth

An excellent retainer to hold these teeth in alignment is a fixed lingual bar , attached only to the canines and resting against the flat lingual surface of the lower incisors above the cingulum Fig 18.11 . (28–30-mil steel)
Maintenance of Lower Incisor Position During Late Growth
Long-term recall of patients who had worn a bonded lower retainer for more than 20 years showed no negative effect on periodontal health.
Maintenance of Lower Incisor Position During Late Growth
It is also possible to bond a fixed lingual retainer to all or some of the incisor teeth. The major indication for this variation is a tooth or teeth that have been severely rotated .
Maintenance of Lower Incisor Position During Late Growth

If the span of the retainer wire is reduced by bonding an intermediate tooth or teeth, a more flexible wire should be used. (not to hold the teeth rigidly during retention to allow reorganization of PDL) Fig 18.12
Maintenance of Lower Incisor Position During Late Growth
A good choice for a fixed retainer with adjacent teeth bonded is 17.5-mil braided steel archwire.
II Maintenance of Diastema Closure
Maintenance of Diastema Closure
Fig 19.14 Bonded flexible wire to maintain a maxillary central diastema.
Maintenance of Diastema Closure
Fig 19.15 A wire bonded to the four maxillary incisors as a fixed retainer.
Maintenance of Diastema Closure
Fig 19.16 Inadvertent tooth movement from fixed lingual retainers — an active wire torques the roots.
Maintenance of Diastema Closure

A removable retainer is not a good choice for prolonged retention of a central diastema. ("jiggling" tooth movement that accompanies back-and-forth closure is potentially damaging to the periodontium)
Maintenance of Diastema Closure
The best retainer for this purpose is a bonded section of flexible wire . Fig 18.13 Fig 18.14
Maintenance of Diastema Closure
Extending the bonded wire to the premolars increases the chance of bonding failure and is indicated only rarely.
Maintenance of Diastema Closure
Loss of lower incisor alignment from inadvertent tooth movement is more likely when wires break
Maintenance of Diastema Closure

When a wire breaks, it is likely to become distorted at the same time, and that can lead to activation of the wire even if it was passive previously. Canine-to-canine wires must be larger and are unlikely to break.
Maintenance of Diastema Closure

It is possible for problems to arise when the retainer remains bonded. With spiral wires, tooth movement due to a wire that was slightly distorted as it was being bonded could be the problem, and downward deflection of the wire could occur if the bonds to the incisors failed but the canines remained bonded. Fig 18.16
Maintenance of Diastema Closure

Although it has been suggested that a dead soft wire is a safer choice in this situation, there is no evidence that this is correct; long-term problems can occur with dead soft wire as with flexible twist wire.
Maintenance of Diastema Closure
Patients with fixed retainers should be seen in the initial retention period by the orthodontist, perhaps for the first 2 years when bond failure rates are greatest.
Maintenance of Diastema Closure
Inadvertent Tooth Movement With Fixed Lingual Retainers
III Maintenance of Spaces in the Dental Arch
Maintenance of Spaces in the Dental Arch
Fig 19.17 Fixed retainer maintaining space for an eventual posterior restoration / missing premolar.
Maintenance of Spaces in the Dental Arch
A fixed retainer is also the best choice to maintain a space where an implant eventually will be placed.
Maintenance of Spaces in the Dental Arch
The preferred retainer for maintaining space for posterior restorations is a heavy intracoronal wire bonded to the adjacent teeth Fig 18.20 .
Maintenance of Spaces in the Dental Arch

Anterior spaces need a replacement tooth, which can be attached to a removable retainer (needs full-time wear and is satisfactory for short periods). If an implant or permanent bridge will be delayed for a long time while adolescent vertical growth is completed, it is better to place a fixed retainer in the form of a temporary bonded bridge .
Active Retainers
I Realignment of Irregular Incisors
Realignment of Irregular Incisors
Fig 19.20 Steps in a canine-to-canine clip-on spring appliance to realign re-crowded lower incisors.
Realignment of Irregular Incisors
Re-crowding of lower incisors is the major indication for an active retainer to correct incisor position.
Realignment of Irregular Incisors

If late crowding has developed (due to late mandibular growth), it often is necessary to reduce the interproximal width of lower incisors before realigning them, so that the crowns are not forced labially into an obviously unstable position. (flattening the contact areas increases the inherent stability of the arch)
Realignment of Irregular Incisors

Enamel reduction should not be overdone, but if necessary, the width of each lower incisor can be reduced up to 0.5 mm on each side without going through the interproximal enamel. If an additional 2 mm of space can be gained, reducing each incisor 0.25 mm per side , it is usually possible to realign these teeth after moderate relapse.
Realignment of Irregular Incisors
After interproximal reduction to achieve appropriate space, there now are two ways to complete the realignment: an active canine-to-canine clip-on device Fig 18.21 , or a short series of aligners .
Realignment of Irregular Incisors

If there is more than a modest degree of relapse, however, a fixed appliance for retreatment must be considered. With bonded brackets on the lower arch from premolar to premolar, space can be opened and superelastic nickel‒titanium (NiTi) wires can be used to bring the incisors back into alignment quite efficiently.
II Correction of Occlusal Discrepancies: Modified Functional Appliances as Active Retainers
Correction of Occlusal Discrepancies: Modified Functional Appliances as Active Retainers
A typical use for an activator or Bionator as an active retainer would be in a male adolescent who had slipped back 2 to 3 mm toward a Class II relationship after early correction.
Correction of Occlusal Discrepancies: Modified Functional Appliances as Active Retainers
It would look exactly like the functional appliance retainer, except that the bite was taken to advance the mandible the 2 to 3 mm needed to correct the occlusion.
Correction of Occlusal Discrepancies: Modified Functional Appliances as Active Retainers
An active retainer is expected primarily to move teeth—no significant skeletal change is anticipated.
Correction of Occlusal Discrepancies: Modified Functional Appliances as Active Retainers

An activator or Bionator as an active retainer is indicated only if not more than 3 mm of occlusal correction is sought. Over this distance, correction can be achieved by restraining the eruption of maxillary teeth posteriorly and directing the erupting mandibular teeth anteriorly.

Adjunctive Versus Comprehensive Treatment
Adjunctive Versus Comprehensive Treatment
In general, orthodontists consider adults as those whose growth is essentially completed. The mean cutoff age for females is 18, but for males it is 20 or 21.
Adjunctive Versus Comprehensive Treatment

Adjunctive orthodontic treatment for adults is, by definition, tooth movement carried out to facilitate other dental procedures necessary to control disease, restore function, and/or enhance appearance.
Adjunctive Versus Comprehensive Treatment
Comprehensive orthodontics for adults tends to be difficult and technically demanding.

Treatment Planning Considerations
Uprighting Posterior Teeth

Should both the second and third molars be uprighted? If the third molar would move it into a position in which good hygiene could not be maintained or it would not be in functional occlusion. Comprehensive Treatment in Adults
I Psychologic Considerations
Psychologic Considerations
A patient with internal motivation is more likely to respond well psychologically than externally motivated.
Psychologic Considerations
Patients with an inadequate or pathologic personality Fig 19.23 are more likely to have a complex set of unrecognized expectations for treatment.
Psychologic Considerations
If patient thinks that appearance or function of the teeth is creating a severe problem but an assessment simply does not corroborate that, orthodontic treatment should be approached with caution.
Psychologic Considerations
Adults, as a rule, are less tolerant of discomfort and more likely to complain about pain after adjustments and about difficulties in speech, eating, and tissue adaptation.
II Temporomandibular Dysfunction as a Reason for Orthodontic Treatment
Temporomandibular Dysfunction as a Reason for Orthodontic Treatment
Types of Problems
Temporomandibular Dysfunction as a Reason for Orthodontic Treatment
TMD patients are classified in four large groups: masticatory muscle disorders, TM joint disorders, chronic mandibular hypomobility, or growth disorders. Fig 19.24
Temporomandibular Dysfunction as a Reason for Orthodontic Treatment
Because muscle spasm and joint pathology can coexist, the distinction in many patients is difficult.
Temporomandibular Dysfunction as a Reason for Orthodontic Treatment
Men with severe malocclusion, occlusal characteristics are directly associated with health-related quality.
Temporomandibular Dysfunction as a Reason for Orthodontic Treatment

Displacement of the disc is increasingly frequent as age increases and can arise from a number of causes. One possibility is trauma to the joint such that the ligaments that oppose the action of the lateral pterygoid muscle are stretched or torn. (the ligaments do not restore the disk to its proper position when the jaw is closed). The result is a click on opening and closing.
Temporomandibular Dysfunction as a Reason for Orthodontic Treatment

The click and symptoms associated with it can be corrected if an occlusal splint is used to prevent the patient from closing the jaw beyond the point at which displacement occurs. The resulting relief of pain influences patients and dentists to seek either restorative or orthodontic treatment to increase facial vertical dimension. (not a treatment procedure that should be undertaken lightly) (Usually there are better ways of handling disc displacement than orthodontic treatment)
Temporomandibular Dysfunction as a Reason for Orthodontic Treatment

To produce myofascial pain, the patient must be clenching or grinding the teeth for many hours per day, presumably as a response to stress. It is impossible to say that occlusal discrepancies of any given degree will lead to TMD symptoms, although recent multicenter research has at least clarified the possibilities.
Temporomandibular Dysfunction as a Reason for Orthodontic Treatment

It is possible to demonstrate that some types of occlusal discrepancies predispose patients who clench or grind their teeth to the development of TMD symptoms. It must be kept in mind, however, that it takes two factors to produce myofascial pain: an occlusal discrepancy and a patient who clenches or grinds the teeth.
Temporomandibular Dysfunction as a Reason for Orthodontic Treatment
Treatment Indications
Temporomandibular Dysfunction as a Reason for Orthodontic Treatment
Three broad approaches to myofascial pain symptoms can be considered: reducing the amount of stress; reducing the patients' reactions to stress; or improving the occlusion.
Temporomandibular Dysfunction as a Reason for Orthodontic Treatment

Drastic alteration of the occlusion, by either restorative dental procedures or orthodontics, is logical only if the less invasive stress-control and stress-adaptation approaches have failed. (this may involve orthognathic surgery to reposition the jaws)
Temporomandibular Dysfunction as a Reason for Orthodontic Treatment

Orthodontic intervention can appear almost magical in the way that TMD symptoms disappear long before the occlusal relationships have been corrected. (grinding or clenching sensitive teeth might break the habit)
Temporomandibular Dysfunction as a Reason for Orthodontic Treatment
The changing occlusal relationships also contribute to breaking up the habit patterns that contributed to the muscle fatigue and pain.
Temporomandibular Dysfunction as a Reason for Orthodontic Treatment

Prolonged use of Class II or Class III elastics may not be well tolerated in adults who have had TMD problems and should be avoided (prolonged use of elastics should be avoided in most other adult patients as well).
Temporomandibular Dysfunction as a Reason for Orthodontic Treatment

Sometimes, the clenching and grinding that originally caused the problem tend to recur after the orthodontic treatment is completed, the use of interocclusal splints in this situation may be the only way to keep symptoms from recurring.
Temporomandibular Dysfunction as a Reason for Orthodontic Treatment

Occasionally, orthodontic treatment is made more complicated by previous splint therapy. "open the bite posteriorly" Fig 19.27 (Placing orthodontic attachments on the posterior teeth and using light vertical elastics can be used to bring the posterior teeth back into occlusion)
III Periodontal Considerations
Periodontal Considerations
The prevalence of periodontal disease as a function of age in a large group of potential orthodontic patients with severe malocclusion is shown in Fig 19.29 .
Periodontal Considerations

The odds are that any patient over the age of 35 has some periodontal problems that could affect orthodontic treatment, and mucogingival considerations are important in treatment of the younger adult group.
Periodontal Considerations
The best indicator that disease may be present is a history of disease. At present, persistent bleeding on gentle probing is the best indicator of active and presumably progressive disease.
Periodontal Considerations
Treatment of Patients With Minimal Periodontal Involvement (10% of the periodontal patients)
Periodontal Considerations
In children and adolescents, even if gingivitis develops in response to the presence of orthodontic appliances, it almost never extends into periodontitis. This cannot be taken for granted in adults.
Periodontal Considerations
Two characteristics are important regarding recession: the width of the attached gingiva (not all keratinized gingiva is attached) and the thickness of the gingival tissue.
Periodontal Considerations
Lingually tipped lower incisors in patients with a prominent chin have a high risk of recession, and thin gingival tissue probably is the reason
Periodontal Considerations

Gingival graft (before orthodontic treatment) must be considered in adults with minimal attached gingiva or thin tissue, particularly those for whom arch expansion will be used to align incisors and those who will have surgical mandibular advancement or genioplasty (because surgical incisions stretch the gingiva as they heal)
Periodontal Considerations
Moderate Periodontal Involvement (80% of the periodontal patients)
Periodontal Considerations

Treatment procedures to facilitate the patient's long-term maintenance, such as osseous recontouring or repositioned flaps to compensate for areas of gingival recession, are best deferred until the final occlusal relationships have been established.
Periodontal Considerations

The general guideline for preliminary restorative treatment is that temporary restorations should be placed to control caries, with the definitive restorative dentistry delayed until after the orthodontic phase. (Composite resin is now the preferred temporary restorative material while orthodontics is being carried out. Cast restorations should be delayed until after the final occlusal relationships have been established)
Periodontal Considerations
Use a fully bonded orthodontic appliance (rather than of bands)
Periodontal Considerations
Use self-ligating brackets or steel ligatures (rather than elastomeric rings)
Periodontal Considerations
For more plaque control in periodontally involved adults:
Periodontal Considerations
During comprehensive orthodontics, a patient with moderate periodontal problems must be on a maintenance schedule (2 to 4 month intervals is the usual plan).
Periodontal Considerations
Severe Periodontal Involvement (10% of the periodontal patients)
Periodontal Considerations
Orthodontic treatment can be carried out without further loss of alveolar bone if good control of the periodontal condition is maintained.
Periodontal Considerations
Periodontal maintenance should be scheduled at more frequent intervals (every 4 to 6 weeks)
Periodontal Considerations
Orthodontic treatment goals and mechanics must be modified to keep orthodontic forces to an absolute minimum Fig 19.32
Periodontal Considerations
The treatment itself must be modified in two ways:
Periodontal Considerations
The crown‒root ratio is a significant factor in the long-term prognosis for a tooth that has sustained periodontal bone loss.
Periodontal Considerations

In adults with bone loss and an anterior deep bite, the orthodontist should not hesitate to remove part of the crown of elongated lower incisors as an alternative to intrusion (simplify orthodontic leveling of the arch and improve the periodontal prognosis).
Periodontal Considerations
Space closure in areas of major bone loss sometimes leads to an improvement in bone height if at least one wall of the periodontal pocket remains.
IV Prosthodontic-Implant Interactions
Prosthodontic-Implant Interactions
Problems Related to Loss of Tooth Structure
Prosthodontic-Implant Interactions

The ideal buccolingual position of a worn or damaged maxillary tooth would be influenced by how the restoration was planned. If crowns are planned, the tooth should be in the center of the dental arch without tight contact with the opposing arch. But if a facial veneer is to be used for an incisor or canine the orthodontist should place the tooth more lingually, in contact with its antagonist in the lower arch.
Prosthodontic-Implant Interactions

Better restorations can be done if the orthodontist provides slightly more space than is required, so there is room for the restorative dentist to finish and polish proximal surfaces. The slight excess space can then be closed with a retainer.
Prosthodontic-Implant Interactions

If only a small amount of tooth structure has been lost (fractured incisal edge)‒it may be possible to elongate the damaged tooth so that the incisal edges line up. The result, however, will be uneven gingival margins. More than 1 to 2 mm of elongation rarely is a good plan unless patient never exposes the gingiva.
Prosthodontic-Implant Interactions
Gingival Esthetic Problems
Prosthodontic-Implant Interactions
Two categories: excessive/uneven display of gingiva, and gingival recession after periodontal bone loss.
Prosthodontic-Implant Interactions
Substituting a canine on one side will result in uneven gingival margins unless great care is taken to extrude the canine and reduce its crown height.
Prosthodontic-Implant Interactions
The best approach to "black triangles" problem is to remove some interproximal enamel so that the incisors can be brought closer together.
Prosthodontic-Implant Interactions
Missing Teeth: Space Closure Versus Prosthetic Replacement
Prosthodontic-Implant Interactions

If there is buccolingual narrowing of the alveolar process in the extraction site, closing the extraction space requires a reshaping of the cortical bone that comprises the buccal and lingual plates of the alveolar process. Cortical bone will respond to orthodontic force in most instances, but the response is significantly slower. Uprighting (~6 months) Vs Space closure (~3 years)
Prosthodontic-Implant Interactions
Often, it is better judgment to open a partially closed old extraction site and replace the missing tooth.
Prosthodontic-Implant Interactions

Sometimes, closure of the space where a hopelessly involved tooth was extracted results in an improvement of the periodontal situation. Unless at least one bony wall remains, however, it is better to move teeth away from such an area in preparation for a prosthetic replacement, because normal bone formation cannot be expected as the tooth moves into the defect.
Prosthodontic-Implant Interactions

However, there is an exception. First molars and incisors are lost in some adolescents and young adults to aggressive juvenile periodontitis (due to Aggregatibacter actinomycetemcomitans). It often is possible to orthodontically close the extraction sites, bringing the second permanent molar forward. The second molar brings its own investing bone with it, and the large bony defect disappears. This favorable response is attributed to some combination of three factors: the relatively young patients, the fact that the original attack was almost entirely on the first molars, and the change in the bacterial flora.
Prosthodontic-Implant Interactions

In an older patient who lost a first molar to periodontal disease, it is unlikely that the other teeth have been totally spared or that the bacterial flora have changed, and it would not be good judgment to attempt to close the space.
Prosthodontic-Implant Interactions

The patient should be ready for definitive prosthodontic treatment as soon as possible after the orthodontic appliances are removed (place bone grafts in areas that will receive implants while orthodontic treatment is being carried out) (osseointegration during the orthodontic treatment is advantageous)
Prosthodontic-Implant Interactions
Almost always, a fixed orthodontic retainer is the best choice to maintain a space for an implant.
Prosthodontic-Implant Interactions
In the anterior area, patients often prefer a temporary resin-bonded bridge.
Prosthodontic-Implant Interactions

A damaged and ankylosed maxillary incisor or canine in a teenager poses a special problem, alveolar atrophy will occur if the tooth is extracted before vertical growth is completed and the implant can be placed. In this situation, the alveolar bone can be "banked" by removing the crown of the offending tooth but retaining the endodontically treated root, or simply decoronating the tooth without endodontic treatment.
Prosthodontic-Implant Interactions

An implant too soon creates a major problem. The implant becomes the equivalent of an ankylosed tooth and will appear to intrude as vertical development continues and the other teeth erupt Fig 19.39 .

In summary:

A new 7th-edition chapter (Larson, Larson & Blevins), summarised in our own words from the textbook. The benefits/limitations mirror the adolescent chapter (Ch 18, Table 18.1) — but because adults are non-growing, often restored, and frequently periodontally compromised , those same issues bite harder.
Figures are taken from the chapter; click any figure to zoom. The compliance numbers and the "what limits adults" list are the most testable points.
Foundations
I Aligners vs Fixed Treatment in Adults
Aligners vs Fixed Treatment in Adults

Adults are esthetics-conscious and want minimal lifestyle disruption — a large driver of aligner demand. Treatment is esthetic, though attachments and aligners are slightly visible (not truly "invisible" — warn the patient).
Aligners vs Fixed Treatment in Adults
Aligners offer flexible appointment timing and even virtual visits, but diagnosis, attachment placement, IPR, and attachment removal all require in-person visits .
Cross-ref Overall benefits/limitations are the same as the adolescent chapter — see Ch 18, Table 18.1 . Methods of attaching Class II/III elastics are also shown in Ch 18 .
II Benefits & Limitations in Adults
Benefits & Limitations in Adults
Esthetic preference usually favors aligners — but daily habits matter : frequent coffee-sipping or all-day snacking (which lower wear time) can make braces the better choice .
Benefits & Limitations in Adults
More exposed tooth structure from continued passive eruption → more surface area for better aligner engagement/retention .
Benefits & Limitations in Adults
Heavily restored dentitions are common; porcelain and metal are hard to bond brackets to, so aligners are often preferable .

Exam pearl — speed of movement Iwasaki et al.: tooth translation is ~ 1.5× faster in growing than non-growing individuals . So velocity is hard to predict in adults — you may have to lengthen wear (e.g. 7 → 10 days) or re-stage at a slower velocity (new trays). It is also hard to tell whether poor tracking is from compliance, mechanics, or slow biology .
Exam pearl — RCT For mild malocclusion, a randomized trial found aligners and braces gave similar quality, but aligners took several months longer .
III Challenges in Adult Patients
Challenges in Adult Patients
Key adult issues: lack of growth, restorations, worn/missing teeth, more multidisciplinary care, and compliance .
Challenges in Adult Patients
No skeletal change → A-P and vertical correction are difficult or impossible without surgery ; corrections must come from tooth movement alone.
Challenges in Adult Patients
Aging dentition: localized wear/parafunction, restorations that improved crown shape while leaving roots poorly positioned.
Challenges in Adult Patients
Missing teeth are common — idealizing space for implants is a frequent reason adults seek treatment.

Critical — control perio first & mind the vertical Vertical control is critical in adults — there is no continued ramus growth to compensate for careless posterior extrusion . And active periodontal disease must be controlled with the dentist/periodontist BEFORE treatment , or it worsens during care. Coordinate final implant/build-up spacing with the whole dental team early.
Cross-ref General adult-treatment challenges are detailed in Ch 20 ; the biologic basis of force/time is in Ch 8 .

Exam pearl — wear time & compliance Recommended wear is 20–22 hr/day . Tooth movement does not begin until ≥ 4 hours of force , so 20 h delivers far more daily movement than 12 h — "reduced-wear" marketing claims fight basic biology. A study of >2500 adults found 36% full, 38% fair, ~ 25% poor compliance. Comprehensive cases run 12–36 months , but tolerance tends to wane after ~12 months — for cases expected to exceed ~12–15 months, stress the long-term commitment up front.
Comprehensive Treatment
IV Mild Difficulty
Mild Difficulty
The most predictable adult cases are intra-arch — crowding or spacing within an arch with minimal root movement.
Mild Difficulty

IPR is commonly used to create space: easy to diagnose Bolton discrepancies on a digital setup; useful when a mild A-P deviation exists but the posterior occlusion is stable and worth keeping (adjust overjet with IPR instead).
Mild Difficulty

Black triangles (open gingival embrasures) from gingival recession and anterior overlap are an adult esthetic problem — IPR + aligners reshape the contact, build a longer connector, and eliminate them.
V Moderate Challenges
Moderate Challenges

With experience, bigger rotations, crossbites, A-P moves, and overbite change become feasible — but a systematic review warns predictability of many movements is still low and refinement is needed in nearly every case .
Moderate Challenges
For larger crowding/spacing, it is even more critical to create adequate space and verify tracking throughout.
Moderate Challenges
A-P change in adults is purely dental — keep teeth healthy within the alveolar bone.

Exam pearl — molar derotation for Class II Maxillary first molars typically rotate forward around the lingual root . Derotating around that lingual root distalizes the buccal cusps and gains 1–2 mm of A-P correction — often critical for Class II molar correction. Note that restorations built to the old malocclusion won't interdigitate well in the new Class I, and a worn incisor becomes more obvious after overbite correction (discuss restorative work).
VI Complex Cases
Complex Cases
(1) the computer/technician staging usually needs significant modification ;
Complex Cases
(2) the amount of planned movement is reduced from what algorithms predict;
Complex Cases
(3) adjunctive appliances (limited braces, TADs) are more often added;
Complex Cases
(4) progress records and revision/refinement aligners are needed — often more than once.
Complex Cases
Complex cases look deceptively like simple ones but differ in four ways :
Complex Cases
This means much greater doctor involvement . In anterior open-bite closure, large posterior open bites are deliberately programmed to reach the finish.
Complex Cases

With extractions + aligners , secure anchorage (attachments or space around anchor teeth during retraction — see Ch 18), and design staging to keep root control . Well-selected extraction cases do well with good compliance.

Exam pearl — the golf analogy In big cases, set an intermediate goal , then re-stage from that midpoint to the finish — "a chip and a short putt beats one long putt." It is the aligner equivalent of taking progress records and repositioning brackets.
Hybrid & Vertical Problems
VII Hybrid Treatment
Hybrid Treatment
Adults need hybrids more often (more tipped/missing teeth, occlusal change, no growth).
Hybrid Treatment
Significant open bite: active splints on miniscrews (see Ch 20) can pre-treat — converting a major open bite into a mild one needing only posterior settling.
Hybrid Treatment
A single complex arch may need fixed appliances + miniscrews ; the other arch is treated with aligners (e.g., a unilateral open bite closed with a hybrid technique).
VIII Root Uprighting
Root Uprighting
Teeth tip into edentulous spaces over time. Uprighting with aligners alone is possible when there is good exposed surface area + a large attachment (or two) to build an uprighting couple.
Root Uprighting
If exposed surface is inadequate, limited braces create a more efficient force system — before or alongside aligners.
IX Deep-Bite Correction
Deep-Bite Correction

Deep-bite correction is achievable but even harder in adults than adolescents because of the lack of vertical growth . Use anterior bite ramps/turbos + retentive posterior attachments , and procline incisors where appropriate.

Exam pearl — proclination, not true intrusion On superimposition, some true incisor intrusion occurs, but much of adult deep-bite correction actually comes from incisor PROCLINATION . Deep-bite cases with generalized spacing are even harder — closing the space uprights the incisors and deepens the bite again.

When to choose braces — or aligners For severe overbite , consider lower braces (or committing to braces from the start) — these are often the cases most important to fully correct for restorative space. But if there is already severe lower-incisor wear with exposed dentin , there may be no room or clearance to place lower braces — then aligners may be the best available option even if inefficient.
Limited Treatment
X Crowding (Relapse Touch-ups)
Crowding (Relapse Touch-ups)
A big aligner advantage: individual teeth move with fewer side effects (root movement is hard, so unwanted movement is too), using the full dentition as anchorage .
Crowding (Relapse Touch-ups)

Minor post-retention relapse is corrected very efficiently — you predictably keep the posterior occlusion while fixing the few teeth that moved, often with few or no attachments (e.g., 10 aligners over ~6 months).
XI Spacing (Diastema)
Spacing (Diastema)
Mild spacing — especially midline diastema — is treated with limited aligners and minimal attachments.
Spacing (Diastema)
Always check Bolton tooth-size discrepancy and overbite — both will cause maxillary spacing to reopen if not addressed. Mild maxillary IPR also reduces the chance of a black triangle after closure.
XII Minor Occlusal Changes
Minor Occlusal Changes

Late mandibular growth or a mandibular-advancement (sleep) appliance that postures the jaw forward at night can drive a traumatic edge-to-edge bite with wear → limited aligners + Class III elastics restore positive overjet.
Minor Occlusal Changes

Other limited-aligner uses: supra-eruption from a coverage-deficient retainer/night-guard (very minor only), small spaces before restorations, mild Class II relapse, minor transverse change opening the bite.
Other Challenges
XIII Handling Missing Teeth
Handling Missing Teeth

Painted aligner — a virtual pontic is placed in the plan, leaving a space in the tray; made slightly undersized so adjacent contours still engage , then pontic paint of the right shade is applied to the facial of that space.
Handling Missing Teeth
Removable pontic / tooth-coloured wax moved tray-to-tray by the patient — convenient, but no tight seal so discoloration can occur .
Handling Missing Teeth
Cantilever resin-bonded bridge — potentially the best provisional when the adjacent tooth needs only minimal tip/rotation (implant usually waits until after movement).
Handling Missing Teeth
Few adults accept a visible space in the esthetic zone during months of treatment. Three solutions:
XIV Orthognathic Surgery
Orthognathic Surgery
Pre- and post-surgical movement can be done with aligners just like fixed appliances; the difference is providing support for intermaxillary fixation (IMF)/elastics during and after surgery.
Orthognathic Surgery

Single-jaw cases: bond buttons to posterior teeth and hold the teeth into the splint with elastic chain / steel ligature during rigid fixation. More complex movements: place TADs in each quadrant for stable support.
Orthognathic Surgery

Some surgeons still want fixed appliances placed for surgery and kept through immediate healing for flexibility. Aligner wear is very difficult immediately after surgery — some discontinue it for a few weeks to let the occlusion settle.
