III Esthetic and Psychosocial Considerations
Esthetic and Psychosocial Considerations

A few patients have great difficulty in adapting to significant changes in their facial appearance. This is more likely to be a problem in older individuals. Psychologic support and counseling therefore are particularly important for older patients , and major esthetic changes in older adults may not be desirable.
Esthetic and Psychosocial Considerations

Whatever the age of the patient, a period of psychologic adjustment following a facial surgical procedure must be expected Fig 20.5 . In part, this is related to the use of steroids at operation to minimize postoperative swelling and edema (steroid withdrawal)
Esthetic and Psychosocial Considerations
By the time orthodontic treatment resumes at 3 to 6 weeks after operation, the patients are usually‒but not always‒on the positive side of the psychologic scales.
Esthetic and Psychosocial Considerations

Interestingly, orthognathic surgery does not rate high on discomfort and morbidity scales. Operations involving the mandibular ramus require about the same amount of pain medication as extraction of impacted wisdom teeth; maxillary procedures are tolerated better than that.
Esthetic and Psychosocial Considerations
In a randomized trial, those who saw the prediction images before operation were more likely to be satisfied with their result.
IV Extraction of Teeth and the Camouflage Versus Surgery Decision
Extraction of Teeth and the Camouflage Versus Surgery Decision

It is a serious error to attempt camouflage on the theory that if it fails, the patient can then be referred for surgical correction. At that point, another phase of "reverse orthodontics" to eliminate the effects of the original treatment will be required before surgery

Contemporary Surgical Techniques
Contemporary Surgical Techniques

I Mandibular Surgery
Mandibular Surgery
The mandible can be moved forward or back as desired, and the tooth-bearing segment can be rotated down anteriorly (increasing the mandibular plane angle).
Mandibular Surgery
This procedure is quite compatible with the use of rigid intraoral fixation (RIF) , so immobilization of the jaws during healing is not required.
Mandibular Surgery
Excellent bone-to-bone contact after the osteotomy means that problems with healing are minimized, and postsurgical stability is good.
Mandibular Surgery
The sagittal split osteotomy now is used for almost all mandibular surgery because of several advantages over alternative techniques for ramus surgery:
Mandibular Surgery

Lower border osteotomy of the mandible to reposition the chin relative to the mandibular body Fig 20.10 is a major adjunct to ramus procedures, especially when the mandible is advanced. (30% of orthognathic patients)
Mandibular Surgery
Other mandibular procedures are used primarily for major advancements or surgery involving the condyles. An extraoral approach and a bone graft are likely to be needed.
Mandibular Surgery
Rarely, a midline osteotomy with removal of an incisor is used to narrow it anteriorly.
II Maxillary Surgery
Maxillary Surgery
The Le Fort I osteotomy with downfracture of the maxilla dominates contemporary maxillary surgery.
Maxillary Surgery
Allows the maxilla to be moved up and/or forward with excellent stability.
Maxillary Surgery
Moving the entire maxilla back is quite difficult because of the structures behind it.
Maxillary Surgery

A segmental osteotomy , closing the space where a premolar was extracted, allows the anterior teeth to be retracted and posterior teeth to be moved superiorly so that anterior open bite is closed as the mandible rotates upward and forward Fig 20.12 . Also allow the posterior maxilla to be widened or (less frequently) narrowed.
Maxillary Surgery
If constriction is desired, bone is removed at the parasagittal osteotomy sites.
Maxillary Surgery
In expansion, either bone harvested in the downfracture or bank bone is used to fill the void created by lateral movement of the posterior segments.
Maxillary Surgery

The original idea of SARPE that cuts in the lateral buttress of the maxilla would decrease resistance to the point that the midpalatal suture could be forced open (i.e., microfractured) in older patients.
Maxillary Surgery

For SARPE now, surgeons usually make all the cuts needed for a Le Fort I osteotomy, omitting only the final step of downfracture. This allows widening of the maxilla against only soft tissue resistance, manipulating the osteotomy sites with what amounts to distraction osteogenesis.
Maxillary Surgery
If only expansion is desired, this provides a somewhat less invasive approach than segmental osteotomy.
Maxillary Surgery
Unfortunately, there is no guarantee of symmetric expansion‒one of the main disadvantages
Maxillary Surgery
The implication of SARPE is that the problem affects only the transverse plane of space.
Maxillary Surgery
Current data show that relapse of the dental expansion accompanies SARPE Fig 20.14 and that its long-term stability is similar to that with segmental osteotomy.
Maxillary Surgery

The primary indication for preliminary SARPE (two phases surgery) is such severe maxillary constriction that segmental expansion of the maxilla in the Le Fort I procedure might compromise the blood supply to the segments.

III Dentoalveolar Surgery
Dentoalveolar Surgery
Recovery From Inadvertent Tooth Movement
Dentoalveolar Surgery

Induction of new bone formation now is possible with local bone-stimulating hormone therapy and bone grafts so that when displaced roots are repositioned into the alveolar process with torque force, root fenestration can be corrected as well.
Dentoalveolar Surgery
Repositioning Alveolar Segments
Dentoalveolar Surgery
The distance of movement that is possible: in most instances, only a few millimeters.
Dentoalveolar Surgery
The size of the segment: a three-tooth or larger segment is preferred, a two-tooth segment is acceptable but less predictable, and a one-tooth segment is a problem waiting to occur.
Dentoalveolar Surgery
Segments of the dentoalveolar process can be repositioned surgically in all three planes of space Fig 20.16 , but there are important limitations with this procedure:
Dentoalveolar Surgery

Blood Supply: after an osteotomy beneath the bone segment and teeth, the blood supply is the surprisingly good collateral circulation via the facial and lingual mucosa. The further a segment is moved and the smaller it is, the greater the chance of interrupting not only the usual blood supply but also the collateral supply.
Dentoalveolar Surgery

Innervation: there is no collateral innervation. The short-term result is: a vital but denervated pulp that does not respond to electrical stimulation. At that point, pulp vitality can be demonstrated by the maintenance of either normal pulp temperature (temperature probe) or blood flow (Doppler flow meter), and re-innervation of the pulp often occurs after a few months.

Distraction Osteogenesis
Based on manipulation of a healing bone, stretching an osteotomized area before calcification has occurred to generate the formation of additional bone and investing soft tissue
Distraction Osteogenesis
Larger distances of movement are possible than with conventional orthognathic surgery
Distraction Osteogenesis
Deficient jaws can be increased in size at an earlier age.

Postsurgical Stability and Clinical Success
The Hierarchy of Stability and Predictability Fig 20.24
Postsurgical Stability and Clinical Success
Stability after surgical repositioning of the jaws depends on the direction of movement, the type of fixation, and the surgical technique , largely in that order of importance.
Postsurgical Stability and Clinical Success
Influences on Stability
Postsurgical Stability and Clinical Success
Three principles that influence postsurgical stability help to put this in perspective:
Postsurgical Stability and Clinical Success

Fortunately, there is good neuromuscular adaptation to most orthognathic procedures. When the maxilla is moved up, the postural position of the mandible alters in concert with the new maxillary position, and occlusal forces tend to increase rather than decrease. This controls any tendency for the maxilla to immediately relapse downward and contributes to the excellent stability of this surgical movement.
Postsurgical Stability and Clinical Success

Repositioning of the tongue to maintain airway dimensions (i.e., a change in tongue posture) occurs as an adaptation to changes produced by mandibular osteotomy, so surgical reduction of the tongue is not needed when the mandible is set back Fig 20.25 . When the mandible is moved forward, a similar adaptation in tongue posture can be advantageous in patients with sleep-disordered breathing, and a lower border osteotomy to bring the chin forward also produces forward movement of the tongue because the tongue is attached to the genial tubercles.
Postsurgical Stability and Clinical Success

In contrast, neuromuscular adaptation does not occur when the pterygomandibular sling is stretched during mandibular osteotomy, as when the mandible is rotated to close an open bite as it is advanced or set back, so movement of the mandible that stretches the elevator muscles should be avoided.
Postsurgical Stability and Clinical Success
Neuromuscular adaptation is essential for stability
Postsurgical Stability and Clinical Success

Moving the maxilla up relaxes tissues. Moving the mandible forward stretches tissues, but rotating it up at the gonial angle and down at the chin decreases the amount of stretch. The most stable mandibular advancements rotate the mandible in this way, whereas the least stable advancements are those that rotate it in the opposite direction, lengthening the ramus and rotating the chin up.
Postsurgical Stability and Clinical Success
The least stable orthognathic surgical procedure, widening the maxilla, stretches the heavy, relatively inelastic palatal mucosa.
Postsurgical Stability and Clinical Success
Stability is greatest when soft tissues are relaxed during the surgical procedure and least when they are stretched.
Postsurgical Stability and Clinical Success
Successful mandibular advancement requires keeping the ramus in an upright position rather than letting it incline forward as the mandibular body is brought forward.
Postsurgical Stability and Clinical Success

The same is true, in reverse, when the mandible is set back: a major cause of instability appears to be the tendency at operation to push the ramus posteriorly, thus changing its orientation. The orientation is restored when jaw function resumes after operation, and that moves the jaw forward again.
Postsurgical Stability and Clinical Success
Neuromuscular adaptation affects the length of the masticatory muscles but not their orientation , and adaptation to a new orientation cannot be expected.

Incision lines contract somewhat as they heal, and when incisions are placed in the vestibule, this can stress the gingival attachment, leading to stripping or recession of the gingiva.
